title: The Sigmoid Nonlinearity in Prepyriform Cortex

abstract: Experiments demonstrated that sigmoid multilayer perceptron (MLP) networks provide slightly better risk prediction than conventional logistic regression when used to predict the risk of death, stroke, and renal failure on 1257 patients who underwent coronary artery bypass operations at the Lahey Clinic. MLP networks with no hidden layer and networks with one hidden layer were trained using stochastic gradient descent with early stopping. MLP networks and logistic regression used the same input features and were evaluated using bootstrap sampling with 50 replications. ROC areas for predicting mortality using preoperative input features were 70.5% for logistic regression and 76.0% for MLP networks. Regularization provided by early stopping was an important component of improved perfonnance. A simplified approach to generating confidence intervals for MLP risk predictions using an auxiliary "confidence MLP" was developed. The confidence MLP is trained to reproduce confidence intervals that were generated during training using the outputs of 50 MLP networks trained with different bootstrap samples.

paragraphs: The paper compares neural networks with logistic regression for predicting death, stroke, and renal failure after coronary artery bypass surgery. The study uses records from 1,257 patients at the Lahey Clinic. Both approaches receive the same input features, and evaluation uses 50 bootstrap replications to assess performance across resampled data.

The neural models are sigmoid multilayer perceptrons with either no hidden layer or one hidden layer. They are trained with stochastic gradient descent and early stopping. The authors report slightly better risk prediction overall, with mortality ROC areas of 76.0% for the networks and 70.5% for logistic regression using preoperative features. These areas concern discrimination between outcomes, rather than the percentage of patients classified correctly.

Early stopping provides regularization and is identified as an important contributor to the improvement. The paper also develops an auxiliary confidence network that learns to reproduce prediction intervals derived from 50 bootstrap-trained networks. This adds a way to approximate the uncertainty information produced by the collection of fitted models.
summary.tldr: Neural networks modestly improve surgical complication risk prediction, with early stopping helping performance and an auxiliary network estimating confidence intervals.

title: Predicting the Risk of Complications in Coronary Artery Bypass Operations using Neural Networks

abstract: The maximization of diversity of neuronal response properties has been recently suggested as an organizing principle for the formation of such prominent features of the functional architecture of the brain as the corti(cid:173) cal columns and the associated patchy projection patterns (Malach, 1994). We show that (1) maximal diversity is attained when the ratio of dendritic and axonal arbor sizes is equal to one, as found in many cortical areas and across species (Lund et al., 1993; Malach, 1994), and (2) that maxi(cid:173) mization of diversity leads to better performance in systems of receptive fields implementing steerable/shiftable filters, and in matching spatially distributed signals, a problem that arises in many high-level visual tasks. 1 Anatomical substrate for sampling diversity A fundamental feature of cortical architecture is its columnar organization, mani(cid:173) fested in the tendency of neurons with similar properties to be organized in columns that run perpendicular to the cortical surface. This organization of the cortex was ini(cid:173) tially discovered by physiological experiments (Mouncastle, 1957; Hubel and Wiesel, 1962), and subsequently confirmed with the demonstration of histologically defined columns. Tracing experiments have shown that axonal projections throughout the cerebral cortex tend to be organized in vertically aligned clusters or patches. In par(cid:173) ticular, intrinsic horizontal connections linking neighboring cortical sites, which may extend up to 2 - 3 mm, have a striking tendency to arborize selectively in preferred sites, forming distinct axonal patches 200 - 300 J.lm in diameter. Recently, it has been observed that the size of these patches matches closely the average diameter of individual dendritic arbors of upper-layer pyramidal cells 118 Kalanit Grill Spector, Shimon Edelman, Rafael Malach

paragraphs: The paper investigates whether diversity in neuronal responses can explain aspects of cortical organization. The proposed organizing principle is that the arrangement of connections promotes a varied collection of response properties. The authors connect this idea to the relative sizes of dendritic and axonal branching structures, linking anatomical geometry to the information neurons can represent.

Their analysis finds that response diversity is maximized when dendritic and axonal arbor sizes have a ratio of one. The supplied evidence notes that similar size matching occurs in multiple cortical areas and species. This agreement gives the diversity principle a specific anatomical consequence, beyond a general preference for varied neural responses.

The authors also examine what that diversity contributes computationally. Maximizing it improves performance in receptive-field systems implementing steerable or shiftable filters and in matching signals distributed across space. These results connect anatomical organization, response variety, and visual computation. The contribution is the argument that diversity can both correspond to observed structure and improve the operations that such structures support.
summary.tldr: The paper links matched axonal and dendritic sizes to maximal response diversity and improved visual computations.

title: Anatomical origin and computational role of diversity in the response properties of cortical neurons

abstract: A new technique, termed soft assign, is applied for the first time to two classic combinatorial optimization problems, the travel(cid:173) ing salesman problem and graph partitioning. Soft assign , which has emerged from the recurrent neural network/statistical physics framework, enforces two-way (assignment) constraints without the use of penalty terms in the energy functions. The soft assign can also be generalized from two-way winner-take-all constraints to multiple membership constraints which are required for graph par(cid:173) titioning. The soft assign technique is compared to the softmax (Potts glass). Within the statistical physics framework, softmax and a penalty term has been a widely used method for enforcing the two-way constraints common within many combinatorial optimiza(cid:173) tion problems. The benchmarks present evidence that soft assign has clear advantages in accuracy, speed, parallelizabilityand algo(cid:173) rithmic simplicity over softmax and a penalty term in optimization problems with two-way constraints.

paragraphs: Many combinatorial optimization problems require assignments that satisfy constraints in two directions. This paper applies softassign to the traveling salesman problem and graph partitioning. Softassign comes from recurrent neural network and statistical physics approaches, and it enforces assignment constraints without adding penalty terms to the energy being optimized.

The comparison is with softmax combined with a penalty term, an established way of handling two-way constraints in this framework. The authors also generalize softassign beyond two-way winner-take-all assignments to allow multiple membership, as required for graph partitioning. This extends the constraint-handling method to a different kind of assignment structure.

The benchmarks provide evidence of advantages in accuracy, speed, parallel execution, and algorithmic simplicity. The stated scope is optimization problems with two-way constraints. The approach matters because satisfying constraints is part of the assignment procedure itself, avoiding a separate penalty contribution to the energy function. The results indicate that this design choice can improve several practical aspects of solving the tested problems.
summary.tldr: Softassign outperforms softmax with penalties in reported benchmarks by enforcing two-way assignment constraints directly.

title: Softassign versus Softmax: Benchmarks in Combinatorial Optimization

abstract: Recently Sill ito and coworkers (Nature 378, pp. 492,1995) demon(cid:173) strated that stimulation beyond the classical receptive field (cRF) can not only modulate, but radically change a neuron's response to oriented stimuli. They revealed that patch-suppressed cells when stimulated with contrasting orientations inside and outside their cRF can strongly respond to stimuli oriented orthogonal to their nominal preferred orientation. Here we analyze the emergence of such complex response patterns in a simple model of primary vi(cid:173) sual cortex. We show that the observed sensitivity for orientation contrast can be explained by a delicate interplay between local isotropic interactions and patchy long-range connectivity between distant iso-orientation domains. In particular we demonstrate that the observed properties might arise without specific connections be(cid:173) tween sites with cross-oriented cRFs.

paragraphs: A visual neuron's response can depend strongly on stimulation outside its classical receptive field. The paper examines observations in which contrasting orientations inside and outside that field make a cell respond strongly to an orientation perpendicular to its usual preference. The surrounding image can therefore alter the apparent selectivity of the cell.

The authors analyze this behavior in a simple model of primary visual cortex. Their explanation combines local isotropic interactions with patchy, long-range connections between distant regions sharing an orientation preference. The unusual response emerges through the interplay of these local and distant influences, linking an individual cell's activity to the surrounding cortical network.

The model shows that the observed orientation-contrast sensitivity might arise without dedicated connections between locations whose receptive fields prefer perpendicular orientations. This is the central mechanistic finding: a response to cross-oriented context does not by itself require a matching cross-orientation wiring scheme. Interactions among connections organized around similar orientations can produce the more complex response pattern.
summary.tldr: Local interactions and long-range connections between similarly oriented regions can explain strong contextual changes in cortical orientation responses.

title: Orientation Contrast Sensitivity from Long-range Interactions in Visual Cortex

abstract: The three-dimensional motion of humans is underdetermined when the observation is limited to a single camera, due to the inherent 3D ambi(cid:173) guity of 2D video. We present a system that reconstructs the 3D motion of human subjects from single-camera video, relying on prior knowledge about human motion, learned from training data, to resolve those am(cid:173) biguities. After initialization in 2D, the tracking and 3D reconstruction is automatic; we show results for several video sequences. The results show the power of treating 3D body tracking as an inference problem.

We present a system that reconstructs the 3D motion of human subjects from single-camera video, relying on prior knowledge about human motion, learned from training data, to resolve those am(cid:173) biguities. After initialization in 2D, the tracking and 3D reconstruction is automatic; we show results for several video sequences. The results show the power of treating 3D body tracking as an inference problem.

paragraphs: A single camera records a two-dimensional view of a three-dimensional body. As a result, the observed video does not uniquely determine the person's motion in three dimensions. This paper addresses that ambiguity by treating reconstruction as an inference problem that combines the images with knowledge about how humans move.

The system learns prior knowledge of human motion from training data and uses it to resolve ambiguities in the camera observations. The prior supplies information that the two-dimensional projection alone cannot provide. This makes reconstruction depend on both the visible evidence and the motion patterns represented by the learned prior.

After an initialization step in two dimensions, tracking and three-dimensional reconstruction proceed automatically. The authors present results for several video sequences as evidence of the approach's usefulness. The stated achievement is therefore automatic tracking and reconstruction after initialization, supported by learned motion knowledge. The work illustrates how probabilistic inference can make an underdetermined visual task tractable by bringing relevant prior information into the reconstruction process.
summary.tldr: Learned priors about human motion help reconstruct three-dimensional movement from single-camera video after a two-dimensional initialization.

title: Bayesian Reconstruction of 3D Human Motion from Single-Camera Video

abstract: In this paper, we address the problem of statistical learning for multi- topic text categorization (MTC), whose goal is to choose all relevant top- ics (a label) from a given set of topics. The proposed algorithm, Max- imal Margin Labeling (MML), treats all possible labels as independent classes and learns a multi-class classiﬁer on the induced multi-class cate- gorization problem. To cope with the data sparseness caused by the huge number of possible labels, MML combines some prior knowledge about label prototypes and a maximal margin criterion in a novel way. Experi- ments with multi-topic Web pages show that MML outperforms existing learning algorithms including Support Vector Machines. 1 Multi-topic Text Categorization (MTC) This paper addresses the problem of learning for multi-topic text categorization (MTC), whose goal is to select all topics relevant to a text from a given set of topics. In MTC, multiple topics may be relevant to a single text. We thus call a set of topics label, and say that a text is assigned a label, not a topic. In almost all previous text categorization studies (e.g. [1, 2]), the label is predicted by judging each topic’s relevance to the text. In this decomposition approach, the features speciﬁc to a topic, not a label, are regarded as important features. However, the approach may result in inefﬁcient learning as we will explain in the following example. Imagine an MTC problem of scientiﬁc papers where quantum computing papers are as- signed multi-topic label “quantum physics (QP) & computer science (CS)”. (QP and CS are topics in this example.) Since there are some words speciﬁc to quantum computing such as “qbit1”, one can say that efﬁcient MTC learners should use such words to assign label QP & CS. However, the decomposition approach is likely to ignore these words since they are only speciﬁc to a small portion of the whole QP or CS papers (there are many more QP and CS papers than quantum computing papers), and therefore are not discriminative features for either topic QP or CS. 1Qbit is a unit of quantum information, and frequently appears in real quantum computing litera- tures, but rarely seen in other literatures. paragraphs: A document can concern several topics at once. This paper treats the complete set of relevant topics as its label and asks how to predict that set. Its motivation is that a word can strongly indicate a particular topic combination without being especially useful for predicting either topic separately.

Maximal Margin Labeling treats every possible topic set as a distinct class, turning the task into multiclass classification. This makes features associated with combinations directly relevant to the decision. However, the many possible combinations create sparse training data. The method addresses that difficulty by combining prior knowledge about label prototypes with a maximal-margin learning criterion.

Experiments on web pages with multiple topics show the method outperforming existing learning algorithms, including support vector machines. The result supports learning complete topic combinations in the evaluated setting. Its significance is that useful document evidence can belong to the intersection of topics, and a classifier organized around whole labels can use that evidence while drawing on prior structure to address sparsity.
summary.tldr: Maximal Margin Labeling learns whole topic combinations and uses label-prototype knowledge to address sparse data, outperforming comparison methods on multi-topic web pages.

title: Maximal Margin Labeling for Multi-Topic Text Categorization

abstract: Areas of the brain involved in various forms of memory exhibit patterns of neural activity quite unlike those in canonical computational models. We show how to use well-founded Bayesian probabilistic autoassociative recall to derive biologically reasonable neuronal dynamics in recurrently coupled models, together with appropriate values for parameters such as the membrane time constant and inhibition. We explicitly treat two cases. One arises from a standard Hebbian learning rule, and involves activity patterns that are coded by graded firing rates. The other arises from a spike timing dependent learning rule, and involves patterns coded by the phase of spike times relative to a coherent local field potential oscillation. Our model offers a new and more complete understanding of how neural dynamics may support autoassociation.

We show how to use well-founded Bayesian probabilistic autoassociative recall to derive biologically reasonable neuronal dynamics in recurrently coupled models, together with appropriate values for parameters such as the membrane time constant and inhibition. We explicitly treat two cases. One arises from a standard Hebbian learning rule, and involves activity patterns that are coded by graded firing rates. The other arises from a spike timing dependent learning rule, and involves patterns coded by the phase of spike times relative to a coherent local field potential oscillation. Our model offers a new and more complete understanding of how neural dynamics may support autoassociation.

paragraphs: The paper asks how neural dynamics can support autoassociative memory while better resembling activity in brain regions involved in memory. Autoassociative recall concerns recovering a stored activity pattern from related input. The authors start with Bayesian probabilistic recall and use it to derive dynamics for recurrently connected neuronal models.

The derivation also supplies appropriate values for parameters including membrane time constants and inhibition. The paper treats two forms of representation. One follows from a standard Hebbian learning rule and encodes patterns through graded firing rates. The other follows from a spike-timing-dependent learning rule and encodes patterns through the timing of spikes relative to a coherent local field-potential oscillation.

Considering both cases connects a common probabilistic account of recall to distinct neural codes. The firing-rate case represents information through activity levels, while the phase case uses timing relative to an oscillation. The resulting models offer an account of how biologically reasonable recurrent dynamics may implement autoassociation, linking the recall computation to learning rules, activity patterns, and neuronal parameters.
summary.tldr: Bayesian autoassociative recall yields biologically reasonable recurrent dynamics for both firing-rate and spike-phase memory codes.

title: Rate- and Phase-coded Autoassociative Memory

abstract: We use unsupervised probabilistic machine learning ideas to try to ex- plain the kinds of learning observed in real neurons, the goal being to connect abstract principles of self-organisation to known biophysi- cal processes. For example, we would like to explain Spike Timing- Dependent Plasticity (see [5,6] and Figure 3A), in terms of information theory. Starting out, we explore the optimisation of a network sensitiv- ity measure related to maximising the mutual information between input spike timings and output spike timings. Our derivations are analogous to those in ICA, except that the sensitivity of output timings to input tim- ings is maximised, rather than the sensitivity of output ‘ﬁring rates’ to inputs. ICA and related approaches have been successful in explaining the learning of many properties of early visual receptive ﬁelds in rate cod- ing models, and we are hoping for similar gains in understanding of spike coding in networks, and how this is supported, in principled probabilistic ways, by cellular biophysical processes. For now, in our initial simula- tions, we show that our derived rule can learn synaptic weights which can unmix, or demultiplex, mixed spike trains. That is, it can recover inde- pendent point processes embedded in distributed correlated input spike trains, using an adaptive single-layer feedforward spiking network. 1 Maximising Sensitivity. In this section, we will follow the structure of the ICA derivation [4] in developing the spiking theory. We cannot claim, as before, that this gives us an information maximisation algorithm, for reasons that we will delay addressing until Section 3. But for now, to ﬁrst develop our approach, we will explore an interim objective function called sensitivity which we deﬁne as the log Jacobian of how input spike timings affect output spike timings. 1.1 How to maximise the effect of one spike timing on another. Consider a spike in neuron j at time tl that has an effect on the timing of another spike in neuron i at time tk. The neurons are connected by a weight wij. We use i and j to index neurons, and k and l to index spikes, but sometimes for convenience we will use spike indices in place of neuron indices. For example, wkl, the weight between an input spike l and an output spike k, is naturally understood to be just the corresponding wij.

paragraphs: The paper explores whether probabilistic learning principles can help explain learning in spiking neurons. Its focus is the timing of individual spikes and how input timings influence output timings. The broader motivation is to connect self-organization and information-theoretic ideas to biological processes such as spike timing-dependent plasticity.

The authors derive a learning approach by optimizing a sensitivity measure based on the log Jacobian of the mapping from input to output spike timings. The derivation resembles independent component analysis, but works with timing sensitivity instead of firing-rate sensitivity. Although motivated by mutual information, the supplied text explicitly stops short of claiming an information-maximization algorithm.

Initial simulations show that the derived rule can learn synaptic weights that separate mixed spike trains. In a single-layer feedforward spiking network, it recovers independent point processes distributed through correlated inputs. This demonstrates a specific computational ability of the proposed learning rule. Explaining biological spike-based learning remains the broader aim, rather than a conclusion established by the reported separation experiments.
summary.tldr: A spike-timing sensitivity objective yields a learning rule that separates mixed spike trains in initial simulations, without establishing information maximization.

title: Maximising Sensitivity in a Spiking Network

abstract: We address the problem of robust, computationally-efficient design of biological experiments. Classical optimal experiment design methods have not been widely adopted in biological practice, in part because the resulting designs can be very brittle if the nominal parameter estimates for the model are poor, and in part because of computational constraints. We present a method for robust experiment design based on a semidefinite programming relaxation. We present an application of this method to the design of experiments for a complex calcium signal transduction pathway, where we have found that the parameter estimates obtained from the robust design are better than those obtained from an "optimal" design.
originalAbstract: We address the problem of robust, computationally-efficient design of biological experiments. Classical optimal experiment design methods have not been widely adopted in biological practice, in part because the resulting designs can be very brittle if the nominal parameter estimates for the model are poor, and in part because of computational constraints. We present a method for robust experiment design based on a semidefinite programming relaxation. We present an application of this method to the design of experiments for a complex calcium signal transduction pathway, where we have found that the parameter estimates obtained from the robust design are better than those obtained from an "optimal" design.

paragraphs: Choosing a biological experiment through optimization requires a model, but the model's parameter estimates may initially be poor. The paper identifies this as a source of brittleness in classical optimal experiment design. A design selected using inaccurate nominal parameters can perform poorly, and computational constraints create an additional obstacle to using such methods in practice.

The authors propose a robust design method based on a semidefinite programming relaxation. This provides an optimization-based approach intended to address both robustness and computational efficiency. The central motivation is to choose experiments that remain useful when the parameter estimates informing the design are unreliable.

They apply the method to experiment design for a complex calcium signal transduction pathway. In this application, the robust design produces better parameter estimates than an optimal design based on the nominal model. The result illustrates why accounting for uncertainty in the starting estimates can improve the eventual information gained from an experiment, even when the competing design is optimal under its assumed parameters.
summary.tldr: A robust experiment design method improves parameter estimation over a nominally optimal design in a calcium signaling application.

title: Robust design of biological experiments

abstract: We present a new connectionist model for constructive, intuitionistic modal reasoning. We use ensembles of neural networks to represent in- tuitionistic modal theories, and show that for each intuitionistic modal program there exists a corresponding neural network ensemble that com- putes the program. This provides a massively parallel model for intu- itionistic modal reasoning, and sets the scene for integrated reasoning, knowledge representation, and learning of intuitionistic theories in neural networks, since the networks in the ensemble can be trained by examples using standard neural learning algorithms.
originalAbstract: We present a new connectionist model for constructive, intuitionistic modal reasoning. We use ensembles of neural networks to represent in- tuitionistic modal theories, and show that for each intuitionistic modal program there exists a corresponding neural network ensemble that com- putes the program. This provides a massively parallel model for intu- itionistic modal reasoning, and sets the scene for integrated reasoning, knowledge representation, and learning of intuitionistic theories in neural networks, since the networks in the ensemble can be trained by examples using standard neural learning algorithms.

paragraphs: This paper connects formal logical reasoning with computation in neural networks. Its target is constructive, intuitionistic modal reasoning, and its proposed representation uses ensembles of networks to encode theories in that logic. The central question is whether a logical program can be represented by a collection of networks that actually carries out its computation.

The authors establish a correspondence: for every intuitionistic modal program, there is a neural network ensemble that computes it. This is stronger than showing that a network resembles a reasoning procedure on selected examples. It provides a general representational result for the class of programs considered, together with a massively parallel computational model.

The learning connection comes from the fact that the constituent networks can be trained on examples using standard neural learning algorithms. The result therefore lays groundwork for combining explicit knowledge, logical reasoning, and learning within one architecture. The abstract presents that integration as a direction enabled by the model, rather than as an already demonstrated complete learning system.
summary.tldr: Neural network ensembles can compute intuitionistic modal programs, providing a parallel foundation for combining logical reasoning with learning.

title: A Connectionist Model for Constructive Modal Reasoning

abstract: We1 develop Conditional Random Sampling (CRS), a technique particularly suit- able for sparse data. In large-scale applications, the data are often highly sparse. CRS combines sketching and sampling in that it converts sketches of the data into conditional random samples online in the estimation stage, with the sample size determined retrospectively. This paper focuses on approximating pairwise l2 and l1 distances and comparing CRS with random projections. For boolean (0/1) data, CRS is provably better than random projections. We show using real-world data that CRS often outperforms random projections. This technique can be applied in learning, data mining, information retrieval, and database query optimizations.

CRS combines sketching and sampling in that it converts sketches of the data into conditional random samples online in the estimation stage, with the sample size determined retrospectively. This paper focuses on approximating pairwise l2 and l1 distances and comparing CRS with random projections. For boolean (0/1) data, CRS is provably better than random projections. We show using real-world data that CRS often outperforms random projections. This technique can be applied in learning, data mining, information retrieval, and database query optimizations.

paragraphs: Large datasets often contain mostly zero entries, making sparsity an important property for approximation methods to exploit. This paper introduces Conditional Random Sampling, or CRS, which combines sketching with sampling. A sketch serves as a compact representation of the data, and CRS turns that representation into conditional random samples during estimation.

A distinguishing feature is that the sample size is determined retrospectively. Sampling is therefore tied to the estimation stage rather than being described solely as a fixed preprocessing choice. The paper focuses on using this mechanism to approximate pairwise l1 and l2 distances, two ways of measuring how far apart data vectors are.

The authors compare CRS with random projections. For Boolean data, whose entries are zero or one, they establish a theoretical advantage over random projections. On real-world data, they report that CRS often performs better, a qualified empirical finding rather than a claim about every dataset. The method is positioned for applications where approximate comparisons support learning, data mining, information retrieval, or database query optimization.
summary.tldr: Conditional Random Sampling converts sketches into samples for distance estimation, with a proven advantage over random projections on Boolean data.

title: Conditional Random Sampling: A Sketch-based Sampling Technique for Sparse Data

abstract: We consider single-class classification (SCC) as a two-person game between the learner and an adversary. In this game the target distribution is completely known to the learner and the learner's goal is to construct a classifier capable of guaranteeing a given tolerance for the false-positive error while minimizing the false negative error. We identify both "hard" and "soft" optimal classification strategies for different types of games and demonstrate that soft classification can provide a significant advantage. Our optimal strategies and bounds provide worst-case lower bounds for standard, finite-sample SCC and also motivate new approaches to solving SCC.

In this game the target distribution is completely known to the learner and the learner's goal is to construct a classifier capable of guaranteeing a given tolerance for the false-positive error while minimizing the false negative error. We identify both "hard" and "soft" optimal classification strategies for different types of games and demonstrate that soft classification can provide a significant advantage. Our optimal strategies and bounds provide worst-case lower bounds for standard, finite-sample SCC and also motivate new approaches to solving SCC.

paragraphs: Single-class classification asks how to recognize a target class when the learning problem centers on that class. This paper studies an idealized version as a game between a learner and an adversary. The learner is assumed to know the complete target distribution, giving the analysis a stronger starting point than ordinary learning from a finite sample.

The objective is to guarantee a specified tolerance for false-positive errors while making false-negative errors as small as possible. For different versions of the game, the authors identify optimal hard and soft classification strategies. They show that soft classification can offer a significant advantage, so the form of the classifier can matter even when the target distribution is already known.

The resulting strategies and bounds also inform more conventional single-class learning. In particular, they provide worst-case lower bounds for finite-sample problems, establishing benchmarks for what those problems can achieve. The analysis additionally motivates new approaches to classification. Its value lies in separating the strategic difficulty of the decision problem from the extra uncertainty introduced by having only sampled data.
summary.tldr: A game-theoretic analysis derives optimal single-class classifiers and shows that soft strategies can have a significant advantage.

title: Optimal Single-Class Classification Strategies

abstract: We consider methods that try to find a good policy for a Markov decision process by choosing one from a given class. The policy is chosen based on its empirical performance in simulations. We are interested in conditions on the complexity of the policy class that ensure the success of such simulation based policy search methods. We show that under bounds on the amount of computation involved in computing policies, transition dynamics and rewards, uniform convergence of empirical estimates to true value functions occurs. Previously, such results were derived by assuming boundedness of pseudodimension and Lipschitz continuity. These assumptions and ours are both stronger than the usual combinatorial complexity measures. We show, via minimax inequalities, that this is essential: boundedness of pseudodimension or fat-shattering dimension alone is not sufficient.

We show that under bounds on the amount of computation involved in computing policies, transition dynamics and rewards, uniform convergence of empirical estimates to true value functions occurs. Previously, such results were derived by assuming boundedness of pseudodimension and Lipschitz continuity. paragraphs: Simulation-based policy search chooses a policy from a given class by comparing how well candidates perform in simulated runs of a Markov decision process. For this selection to be reliable, empirical performance must reflect true policy value across the class being searched. This paper studies conditions that ensure that agreement.

The authors establish uniform convergence when the computation required to evaluate policies, transition dynamics, and rewards is bounded in the specified way. This supplies a route to guarantees based on computational restrictions. Earlier results instead used assumptions involving bounded pseudodimension and Lipschitz continuity, so the paper offers a different sufficient set of conditions.

The paper also examines why stronger restrictions are needed. Using minimax inequalities, it shows that bounded pseudodimension or fat-shattering dimension alone does not suffice. The positive and negative results work together: they identify conditions under which simulation estimates converge uniformly and demonstrate why familiar measures of class complexity, taken alone, cannot guarantee successful simulation-based policy search.
summary.tldr: Computational bounds ensure uniform convergence in simulation-based policy search, while certain complexity measures alone are insufficient.

title: Sample Complexity of Policy Search with Known Dynamics

abstract: This paper addresses the important tradeoff between privacy and learnability, when designing algorithms for learning from private databases. First we apply an idea of Dwork et al. to design a specific privacy-preserving machine learning algorithm, logistic regression. This involves bounding the sensitivity of logistic regression, and perturbing the learned classifier with noise proportional to the sensitivity. Noting that the approach of Dwork et al. has limitations when applied to other machine learning algorithms, we then present another privacy-preserving logistic regression algorithm. The algorithm is based on solving a perturbed objective, and does not depend on the sensitivity. We prove that our algorithm preserves privacy in the model due to Dwork et al., and we provide a learning performance guarantee. Our work also reveals an interesting connection between regularization and privacy.
originalAbstract: This paper addresses the important tradeoff between privacy and learnability, when designing algorithms for learning from private databases. First we apply an idea of Dwork et al. to design a specific privacy-preserving machine learning algorithm, logistic regression. This involves bounding the sensitivity of logistic regression, and perturbing the learned classifier with noise proportional to the sensitivity. Noting that the approach of Dwork et al. has limitations when applied to other machine learning algorithms, we then present another privacy-preserving logistic regression algorithm. The algorithm is based on solving a perturbed objective, and does not depend on the sensitivity. We prove that our algorithm preserves privacy in the model due to Dwork et al., and we provide a learning performance guarantee. Our work also reveals an interesting connection between regularization and privacy.

paragraphs: The paper studies how to learn a useful logistic regression classifier from private data while protecting the database. Its first approach measures the sensitivity of logistic regression, meaning how much the learned result can change when the underlying data changes. It then adds noise to the fitted classifier in proportion to that sensitivity.

The authors identify limitations in extending this strategy to other learning algorithms and introduce a second approach for logistic regression. This method perturbs the optimization objective itself and solves the modified problem. It therefore places the privacy mechanism inside the learning procedure and does not depend on the sensitivity calculation used by the first method.

For the proposed objective-based algorithm, the paper proves privacy in the stated Dwork framework and supplies a learning-performance guarantee. These results address both sides of the motivating tradeoff: protecting data and retaining the ability to learn. The work also identifies a connection between regularization and privacy, linking a familiar tool for controlling learning behavior to the construction of private algorithms.
summary.tldr: Private logistic regression can be learned by perturbing its objective, with formal privacy and learning guarantees and a connection to regularization.

title: Privacy-preserving logistic regression

abstract: We develop a statistical framework for the simultaneous, unsupervised segmentation and discovery of visual object categories from image databases. Examining a large set of manually segmented scenes, we use chi--square tests to show that object frequencies and segment sizes both follow power law distributions, which are well modeled by the Pitman--Yor (PY) process. This nonparametric prior distribution leads to learning algorithms which discover an unknown set of objects, and segmentation methods which automatically adapt their resolution to each image. Generalizing previous applications of PY processes, we use Gaussian processes to discover spatially contiguous segments which respect image boundaries. Using a novel family of variational approximations, our approach produces segmentations which compare favorably to state--of--the--art methods, while simultaneously discovering categories shared among natural scenes.

paragraphs: The paper combines two tasks: dividing images into regions and discovering object categories shared across an image collection. Its framework is unsupervised, so the categories are learned as part of the process. The statistical design is motivated by an analysis of manually segmented scenes, where chi-square tests support power-law distributions for object frequencies and segment sizes.

A Pitman-Yor process provides a prior suited to those observed distributions. It allows the learning procedure to discover an unknown collection of objects and lets segmentation resolution adapt to individual images. The authors also incorporate Gaussian processes to obtain spatially contiguous regions that respect image boundaries, connecting category discovery with the spatial organization of scenes.

Inference uses a new family of variational approximations. The resulting segmentations compare favorably with state-of-the-art methods while the model simultaneously discovers categories shared across natural scenes. The contribution is this combination: a distributional account of how often objects occur and how large segments are, coupled with spatial modeling and joint discovery across a database.
summary.tldr: A Pitman-Yor-based model jointly segments natural images and discovers shared object categories while adapting region resolution to each image.

title: Shared Segmentation of Natural Scenes Using Dependent Pitman-Yor Processes

abstract: Situations in which people with opposing prior beliefs observe the same evidence and then strengthen those existing beliefs are frequently offered as evidence of human irrationality. This phenomenon, termed belief polarization, is typically assumed to be non-normative. We demonstrate, however, that a variety of cases of belief polarization are consistent with a Bayesian approach to belief revision. Simulation results indicate that belief polarization is not only possible but relatively common within the class of Bayesian models that we consider.
originalAbstract: Situations in which people with opposing prior beliefs observe the same evidence and then strengthen those existing beliefs are frequently offered as evidence of human irrationality. Simulation results indicate that belief polarization is not only possible but relatively common within the class of Bayesian models that we consider.

paragraphs: Belief polarization occurs when people who initially disagree encounter the same evidence and each becomes more convinced of their existing position. This pattern is often interpreted as evidence of irrational reasoning. The paper examines whether the pattern itself is incompatible with Bayesian belief revision, a framework for updating prior beliefs in light of evidence.

The authors demonstrate that a variety of polarization cases can be consistent with a Bayesian approach. The central point is that observing the same evidence does not, by itself, establish that people with opposing prior beliefs must move toward agreement. Some forms of increasing disagreement can occur within the models considered.

Simulations indicate that polarization is relatively common within that particular class of Bayesian models, rather than merely possible in an isolated case. This qualifies the usual interpretation of the phenomenon: polarization alone need not demonstrate irrationality. The stated finding concerns compatibility with Bayesian updating and prevalence within the studied model class; it does not establish that every instance of human polarization is Bayesian.
summary.tldr: Belief polarization can be consistent with Bayesian updating and is relatively common within the model class studied.

title: Bayesian Belief Polarization

abstract: We present a novel linear program for the approximation of the dynamic programming cost-to-go function in high-dimensional stochastic control problems. LP approaches to approximate DP naturally restrict attention to approximations that are lower bounds to the optimal cost-to-go function. Our program -- the `smoothed approximate linear program -- relaxes this restriction in an appropriate fashion while remaining computationally tractable. Doing so appears to have several advantages: First, we demonstrate superior bounds on the quality of approximation to the optimal cost-to-go function afforded by our approach. Second, experiments with our approach on a challenging problem (the game of Tetris) show that the approach outperforms the existing LP approach (which has previously been shown to be competitive with several ADP algorithms) by an order of magnitude.

paragraphs: In stochastic control, a cost-to-go function describes the future cost associated with a situation. Approximating this function is central to dynamic programming when the problem has many dimensions. This paper introduces a linear programming formulation that changes a restriction imposed by existing linear programming approaches: their approximations are constrained to lie below the optimal cost-to-go function.

The proposed smoothed approximate linear program relaxes that lower-bound requirement while preserving computational tractability. This gives the approximation more freedom in how it represents future costs. The contribution concerns both the optimization formulation and its analysis: the authors establish improved bounds on approximation quality, providing theoretical support for allowing this additional flexibility.

The authors also test the method on Tetris, a challenging control problem. They report performance an order of magnitude better than the existing linear programming approach, which had previously been competitive with several approximate dynamic programming algorithms. This experimental result supports the proposed relaxation in that setting, while the improved approximation bounds provide a separate mathematical reason to consider the formulation.
summary.tldr: Relaxing a lower-bound constraint yields a tractable linear program with improved approximation bounds and substantially better reported Tetris performance.

title: A Smoothed Approximate Linear Program

abstract: We propose a novel generative model that is able to reason jointly about the 3D scene layout as well as the 3D location and orientation of objects in the scene. In particular, we infer the scene topology, geometry as well as traffic activities from a short video sequence acquired with a single camera mounted on a moving car. Our generative model takes advantage of dynamic information in the form of vehicle tracklets as well as static information coming from semantic labels and geometry (i.e., vanishing points). Experiments show that our approach outperforms a discriminative baseline based on multiple kernel learning (MKL) which has access to the same image information. Furthermore, as we reason about objects in 3D, we are able to significantly increase the performance of state-of-the-art object detectors in their ability to estimate object orientation.

Experiments show that our approach outperforms a discriminative baseline based on multiple kernel learning (MKL) which has access to the same image information. Furthermore, as we reason about objects in 3D, we are able to significantly increase the performance of state-of-the-art object detectors in their ability to estimate object orientation.

paragraphs: The paper develops a generative model that interprets a road scene and its objects together in three dimensions. From a short video recorded by one camera on a moving car, it infers scene topology and geometry, object positions and orientations, and traffic activities. These quantities are handled within a joint model.

The model combines evidence that changes over time with evidence about the scene’s appearance and geometry. Short vehicle tracks provide dynamic information, while semantic labels and vanishing points provide static information. Bringing these cues together allows the inference process to use both observed motion and the spatial organization visible in the images.

In experiments, the approach outperforms a discriminative baseline based on multiple kernel learning that receives the same image information. The authors also report a significant improvement in the orientation estimates of state-of-the-art object detectors through their three-dimensional reasoning. The findings support the value of joint scene and object interpretation, with the equal-information comparison highlighting the contribution of the modeling approach.
summary.tldr: Joint generative reasoning about road scenes and objects in 3D improves the reported scene interpretation and object-orientation results.

title: Joint 3D Estimation of Objects and Scene Layout

abstract: The olfactory system faces a difficult inference problem: it has to determine what odors are present based on the distributed activation of its receptor neurons. Here we derive neural implementations of two approximate inference algorithms that could be used by the brain. One is a variational algorithm (which builds on the work of Beck. et al., 2012), the other is based on sampling. Importantly, we use a more realistic prior distribution over odors than has been used in the past: we use a spike and slab'' prior, for which most odors have zero concentration. After mapping the two algorithms onto neural dynamics, we find that both can infer correct odors in less than 100 ms, although it takes ~500 ms to eliminate false positives. Thus, at the behavioral level, the two algorithms make very similar predictions. However, they make different assumptions about connectivity and neural computations, and make different predictions about neural activity. Thus, they should be distinguishable experimentally. If so, that would provide insight into the mechanisms employed by the olfactory system, and, because the two algorithms use very different coding strategies, that would also provide insight into how networks represent probabilities."

paragraphs: Smell requires inferring which odors are present from activity distributed across receptor neurons. The paper develops neural implementations of two approximate inference algorithms that could perform this task: one uses a variational approach, and the other uses sampling. Both address how a network could separate the underlying odors from their combined receptor responses.

A central modeling choice is a spike-and-slab prior over odor concentrations. It assigns zero concentration to most odors, expressing the assumption that most possible odors are absent. After translating the algorithms into neural dynamics, the authors find that both identify correct odors in less than 100 milliseconds, while eliminating false positives takes roughly 500 milliseconds.

Those similar time courses lead to similar behavioral predictions, but the models differ in connectivity, neural computations, and predicted activity. The authors therefore propose that experiments could distinguish them at the neural level. Such a distinction could illuminate both the mechanisms of odor inference and the different ways neural networks might represent uncertainty.
summary.tldr: Two neural odor-inference models predict similar recognition timing but different neural activity, offering a possible way to distinguish their coding strategies.

title: Demixing odors - fast inference in olfaction

abstract: The Lasso is a cornerstone of modern multivariate data analysis, yet its performance suffers in the common situation in which covariates are correlated. This limitation has led to a growing number of \emph{Preconditioned Lasso} algorithms that pre-multiply $X$ and $y$ by matrices $P_X$, $P_y$ prior to running the standard Lasso. A direct comparison of these and similar Lasso-style algorithms to the original Lasso is difficult because the performance of all of these methods depends critically on an auxiliary penalty parameter $\lambda$. In this paper we propose an agnostic, theoretical framework for comparing Preconditioned Lasso algorithms to the Lasso without having to choose $\lambda$. We apply our framework to three Preconditioned Lasso instances and highlight when they will outperform the Lasso. Additionally, our theory offers insights into the fragilities of these algorithms to which we provide partial solutions.

paragraphs: The Lasso is widely used for analyzing data with many variables, but correlated predictors can hurt its performance. Preconditioned Lasso methods address this by transforming the predictor matrix and response before applying the standard procedure. The difficulty is deciding whether the transformation actually improves the method, rather than merely benefiting from a different choice of penalty strength.

This paper develops a theoretical framework for making that comparison without first choosing the penalty parameter. That matters because the penalty strongly influences the behavior of both ordinary and preconditioned Lasso. A comparison that avoids fixing it can reveal relationships between the methods that are otherwise entangled with tuning decisions.

The authors apply their framework to three preconditioned variants and identify circumstances in which they outperform the original Lasso. The analysis also exposes vulnerabilities in these methods and offers partial remedies. The contribution is therefore a way to understand both advantages and fragilities; it does not establish that preconditioning always improves Lasso.
summary.tldr: A theoretical framework compares preconditioned Lasso methods without choosing a penalty parameter, identifying advantages and vulnerabilities.

title: A Comparative Framework for Preconditioned Lasso Algorithms

abstract: The adaptive anonymity problem is formalized where each individual shares their data along with an integer value to indicate their personal level of desired privacy. This problem leads to a generalization of $k$-anonymity to the $b$-matching setting. Novel algorithms and theory are provided to implement this type of anonymity. The relaxation achieves better utility, admits theoretical privacy guarantees that are as strong, and, most importantly, accommodates a variable level of anonymity for each individual. Empirical results confirm improved utility on benchmark and social data-sets.
originalAbstract: The adaptive anonymity problem is formalized where each individual shares their data along with an integer value to indicate their personal level of desired privacy. This problem leads to a generalization of $k$-anonymity to the $b$-matching setting. Novel algorithms and theory are provided to implement this type of anonymity. The relaxation achieves better utility, admits theoretical privacy guarantees that are as strong, and, most importantly, accommodates a variable level of anonymity for each individual. Empirical results confirm improved utility on benchmark and social data-sets.

paragraphs: People contributing data may want different amounts of privacy. This paper formalizes an adaptive anonymity problem in which each person supplies both their data and an integer expressing their desired anonymity level. The privacy requirement therefore becomes part of the input for each individual, rather than a single setting imposed uniformly on everyone.

The authors generalize k-anonymity into a formulation based on b-matching and develop algorithms and theory for implementing it. The central change is that the formulation accommodates different anonymity requirements within the same problem. This makes individual preferences a direct part of how the anonymization task is defined and solved.

The abstract reports that the relaxation improves utility while retaining theoretical privacy guarantees of equal strength within the comparison being made. Experiments on benchmark and social datasets also show improved utility. The stated result is that allowing personal anonymity levels can preserve more useful information while providing the formal protections established for this framework.
summary.tldr: A b-matching formulation supports individual anonymity preferences while improving data utility and retaining strong theoretical privacy guarantees.

title: Adaptive Anonymity via $b$-Matching

abstract: We consider the problem of reinforcement learning over episodes of a finite-horizon deterministic system and as a solution propose optimistic constraint propagation (OCP), an algorithm designed to synthesize efficient exploration and value function generalization. We establish that when the true value function lies within the given hypothesis class, OCP selects optimal actions over all but at most K episodes, where K is the eluder dimension of the given hypothesis class. We establish further efficiency and asymptotic performance guarantees that apply even if the true value function does not lie in the given hypothesis space, for the special case where the hypothesis space is the span of pre-specified indicator functions over disjoint sets.
originalAbstract: We consider the problem of reinforcement learning over episodes of a finite-horizon deterministic system and as a solution propose optimistic constraint propagation (OCP), an algorithm designed to synthesize efficient exploration and value function generalization. We establish that when the true value function lies within the given hypothesis class, OCP selects optimal actions over all but at most K episodes, where K is the eluder dimension of the given hypothesis class. We establish further efficiency and asymptotic performance guarantees that apply even if the true value function does not lie in the given hypothesis space, for the special case where the hypothesis space is the span of pre-specified indicator functions over disjoint sets.

paragraphs: This paper addresses reinforcement learning in deterministic systems with episodes of finite length. The learner must explore while using a value-function model to generalize beyond individual observations. The proposed optimistic constraint propagation algorithm, or OCP, is designed to bring these two requirements together within a single learning procedure.

Its main guarantee assumes that the true value function belongs to the supplied hypothesis class. Under that condition, OCP chooses optimal actions in every episode except at most K episodes, where K is the class's eluder dimension. The bound connects exploration difficulty to a property of the chosen function class, making the representation central to the performance guarantee.

The authors also analyze a case where the hypothesis class may fail to contain the true value function. Their additional efficiency and asymptotic guarantees apply when that class is the span of predefined indicator functions over disjoint sets. This extends the analysis beyond exact representation, but only for the specific form of approximation identified in the paper.
summary.tldr: In finite-horizon deterministic systems, OCP limits nonoptimal episodes by the hypothesis class's eluder dimension when the true value function belongs to that class.

title: Efficient Exploration and Value Function Generalization in Deterministic Systems

abstract: We consider the class of optimization problems arising from computationally intensive L1-regularized M-estimators, where the function or gradient values are very expensive to compute. A particular instance of interest is the L1-regularized MLE for learning Conditional Random Fields (CRFs), which are a popular class of statistical models for varied structured prediction problems such as sequence labeling, alignment, and classification with label taxonomy. L1-regularized MLEs for CRFs are particularly expensive to optimize since computing the gradient values requires an expensive inference step. In this work, we propose the use of a carefully constructed proximal quasi-Newton algorithm for such computationally intensive M-estimation problems, where we employ an aggressive active set selection technique. In a key contribution of the paper, we show that our proximal quasi-Newton algorithm is provably super-linearly convergent, even in the absence of strong convexity, by leveraging a restricted variant of strong convexity. In our experiments, the proposed algorithm converges considerably faster than current state-of-the-art on the problems of sequence labeling and hierarchical classification.

A particular instance of interest is the L1-regularized MLE for learning Conditional Random Fields (CRFs), which are a popular class of statistical models for varied structured prediction problems such as sequence labeling, alignment, and classification with label taxonomy. L1-regularized MLEs for CRFs are particularly expensive to optimize since computing the gradient values requires an expensive inference step. paragraphs: For some statistical estimation problems, evaluating the objective or its gradient is itself expensive. This paper focuses on L1-regularized M-estimators with that property. A motivating example is maximum likelihood learning for conditional random fields, where each gradient computation requires an expensive inference step for a structured prediction model.

The authors propose a carefully constructed proximal quasi-Newton algorithm with aggressive active set selection. The approach combines the treatment of L1 regularization with a strategy for choosing which variables to work on. Its design targets the cost of optimization in settings where repeated function and gradient evaluations are a substantial burden.

A central theoretical result establishes superlinear convergence even without full strong convexity, using a restricted form of strong convexity instead. That restricted property is important to the guarantee; the result does not remove curvature requirements altogether. Experiments on sequence labeling and hierarchical classification show considerably faster convergence than the compared state-of-the-art methods. The work therefore combines an analyzed convergence advantage with empirical gains on expensive structured learning problems.
summary.tldr: A proximal quasi-Newton method accelerates expensive L1-regularized estimation and achieves superlinear convergence using a restricted strong-convexity property.

title: Proximal Quasi-Newton for Computationally Intensive L1-regularized M-estimators

abstract: Submodular functions describe a variety of discrete problems in machine learning, signal processing, and computer vision. However, minimizing submodular functions poses a number of algorithmic challenges. Recent work introduced an easy-to-use, parallelizable algorithm for minimizing submodular functions that decompose as the sum of simple" submodular functions. Empirically, this algorithm performs extremely well, but no theoretical analysis was given. In this paper, we show that the algorithm converges linearly, and we provide upper and lower bounds on the rate of convergence. Our proof relies on the geometry of submodular polyhedra and draws on results from spectral graph theory."

However, minimizing submodular functions poses a number of algorithmic challenges. Recent work introduced an easy-to-use, parallelizable algorithm for minimizing submodular functions that decompose as the sum of simple" submodular functions. Empirically, this algorithm performs extremely well, but no theoretical analysis was given. In this paper, we show that the algorithm converges linearly, and we provide upper and lower bounds on the rate of convergence. Our proof relies on the geometry of submodular polyhedra and draws on results from spectral graph theory."

paragraphs: Submodular functions arise in discrete problems across machine learning, signal processing, and computer vision. Minimizing them can nevertheless be algorithmically difficult. This paper studies the case where the objective decomposes into a sum of simpler submodular functions, a structure used by an existing algorithm that is easy to apply and can run in parallel.

That algorithm had already shown strong empirical performance, but lacked a theoretical convergence analysis. The authors establish linear convergence, meaning that progress follows a geometric rate rather than merely a fixed reduction in error per iteration. They also provide both upper and lower bounds on the convergence rate, giving a more informative characterization than eventual convergence alone.

The proof combines the geometry of submodular polyhedra with results from spectral graph theory. Its contribution is to explain the behavior of an existing practical method through mathematical analysis. By bounding its convergence rate in the decomposable setting, the paper supplies theoretical support for an algorithm whose appeal had previously rested on empirical results.
summary.tldr: The paper proves linear convergence and bounds its rate for an existing parallelizable algorithm for decomposable submodular minimization.

title: On the Convergence Rate of Decomposable Submodular Function Minimization

abstract: Contexts are crucial for action recognition in video. Current methods often mine contexts after extracting hierarchical local features and focus on their high-order encodings. This paper instead explores contexts as early as possible and leverages their evolutions for action recognition. In particular, we introduce a novel architecture called deep alternative neural network (DANN) stacking alternative layers. Each alternative layer consists of a volumetric convolutional layer followed by a recurrent layer. The former acts as local feature learner while the latter is used to collect contexts. Compared with feed-forward neural networks, DANN learns contexts of local features from the very beginning. This setting helps to preserve hierarchical context evolutions which we show are essential to recognize similar actions. Besides, we present an adaptive method to determine the temporal size for network input based on optical flow energy, and develop a volumetric pyramid pooling layer to deal with input clips of arbitrary sizes. We demonstrate the advantages of DANN on two benchmarks HMDB51 and UCF101 and report competitive or superior results to the state-of-the-art.

This paper argues for collecting that context early in feature learning and preserving how it develops across the hierarchy. The motivation is that waiting until hierarchical local features have already been extracted can overlook contextual evolution that helps distinguish similar actions.

The proposed deep alternative neural network stacks layers that pair volumetric convolution with recurrence. The convolutional component learns local features, while the recurrent component gathers context. Repeating this arrangement lets contextual information participate from the beginning and continue through successive levels of representation. The authors show that these hierarchical contextual changes are essential to recognizing similar actions in their study.

The system also adapts the temporal extent of its input using optical-flow energy and introduces volumetric pyramid pooling to handle clips of arbitrary sizes. Results on HMDB51 and UCF101 are competitive with or superior to state-of-the-art methods. These evaluations support both the architecture and its emphasis on early, evolving context.
summary.tldr: DANN alternates volumetric convolution and recurrence to capture context early and preserve its evolution for video action recognition.

title: Deep Alternative Neural Network: Exploring Contexts as Early as Possible for Action Recognition

abstract: Dropout is used as a practical tool to obtain uncertainty estimates in large vision models and reinforcement learning (RL) tasks. But to obtain well-calibrated uncertainty estimates, a grid-search over the dropout probabilities is necessary—a prohibitive operation with large models, and an impossible one with RL. We propose a new dropout variant which gives improved performance and better calibrated uncertainties. Relying on recent developments in Bayesian deep learning, we use a continuous relaxation of dropout’s discrete masks. Together with a principled optimisation objective, this allows for automatic tuning of the dropout probability in large models, and as a result faster experimentation cycles. In RL this allows the agent to adapt its uncertainty dynamically as more data is observed. We analyse the proposed variant extensively on a range of tasks, and give insights into common practice in the field where larger dropout probabilities are often used in deeper model layers.

paragraphs: Dropout can help large neural networks estimate uncertainty, but the probability of dropping units affects how well those estimates are calibrated. The paper identifies manual grid search over these probabilities as a major obstacle: it is prohibitively expensive for large models and described as infeasible for reinforcement learning.

Concrete Dropout makes the dropout probability tunable during optimization. Its central mechanism replaces discrete dropout masks with a continuous relaxation. Combined with an optimization objective grounded in Bayesian deep learning, this allows the model to adjust dropout probabilities automatically. The practical benefit is a shorter experimentation cycle because those probabilities no longer require the same external search.

The authors report improved performance and better-calibrated uncertainty across a range of tasks. In reinforcement learning, automatic adjustment also lets an agent change its uncertainty as it observes more data. Their analysis examines the common practice of assigning larger dropout probabilities to deeper layers, providing insight into a design choice that is otherwise often set manually.
summary.tldr: Concrete Dropout learns dropout probabilities through a continuous relaxation, improving reported performance and uncertainty calibration.

title: Concrete Dropout

abstract: Synthesizing programs using example input/outputs is a classic problem in artificial intelligence. We present a method for solving Programming By Example (PBE) problems by using a neural model to guide the search of a constraint logic programming system called miniKanren. Crucially, the neural model uses miniKanren's internal representation as input; miniKanren represents a PBE problem as recursive constraints imposed by the provided examples. We explore Recurrent Neural Network and Graph Neural Network models. We contribute a modified miniKanren, drivable by an external agent, available at https://github.com/xuexue/neuralkanren. We show that our neural-guided approach using constraints can synthesize programs faster in many cases, and importantly, can generalize to larger problems.

paragraphs: Programming by example asks a system to construct a program that matches supplied input-output pairs. The challenge is searching through possible programs efficiently. This paper combines a neural model with miniKanren, a constraint logic programming system, so that learned guidance can influence the symbolic search.

The neural model receives miniKanren's internal representation of the problem. That representation expresses the examples as recursive constraints, giving the learner access to the structure used by the search system itself. The authors explore recurrent and graph neural networks for this role and contribute a modified version of miniKanren that an external agent can drive.

The reported results show faster synthesis in many cases and generalization to larger problems. These are qualified findings, rather than a claim of faster search for every task. The key contribution is the interface between learning and logic: a neural model guides decisions using the search engine's constraints, allowing information from the symbolic reasoning process to inform how the system searches for a matching program.
summary.tldr: Neural models guide miniKanren using its internal constraints, speeding program synthesis in many cases and generalizing to larger problems.

title: Neural Guided Constraint Logic Programming for Program Synthesis

abstract: Variational inference plays a vital role in learning graphical models, especially on large-scale datasets. Much of its success depends on a proper choice of auxiliary distribution class for posterior approximation. However, how to pursue an auxiliary distribution class that achieves both good approximation ability and computation efficiency remains a core challenge. In this paper, we proposed coupled variational Bayes which exploits the primal-dual view of the ELBO with the variational distribution class generated by an optimization procedure, which is termed optimization embedding. This flexible function class couples the variational distribution with the original parameters in the graphical models, allowing end-to-end learning of the graphical models by back-propagation through the variational distribution. Theoretically, we establish an interesting connection to gradient flow and demonstrate the extreme flexibility of this implicit distribution family in the limit sense. Empirically, we demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed method on multiple graphical models with either continuous or discrete latent variables comparing to state-of-the-art methods.
