paragraphs: Variational inference learns graphical models by approximating their posterior distributions with a more manageable family of distributions. Choosing that family creates a central tension: it must be expressive enough to approximate the posterior while remaining computationally useful. This paper proposes coupled variational Bayes as a way to address that choice.

The approach generates the approximation family through an optimization procedure, which the authors call optimization embedding. It uses a primal-dual view of the evidence lower bound, or ELBO, to connect this construction to model learning. The approximate distribution is coupled to the graphical model's parameters, allowing training to backpropagate through the distribution-generating procedure and update the model end to end.

The theoretical analysis connects the method to gradient flow and establishes strong flexibility of the implicit distribution family in a limiting sense. That is a statement about the limit, rather than a promise of exact finite computation. Experiments on graphical models with continuous or discrete latent variables demonstrate effectiveness in comparisons with state-of-the-art methods.
summary.tldr: Coupled variational Bayes generates posterior approximations through optimization, linking their flexibility and training directly to graphical-model parameters.

title: Coupled Variational Bayes via Optimization Embedding

abstract: We consider the problem of transferring value functions in reinforcement learning. We propose an approach that uses the given source tasks to learn a prior distribution over optimal value functions and provide an efficient variational approximation of the corresponding posterior in a new target task. We show our approach to be general, in the sense that it can be combined with complex parametric function approximators and distribution models, while providing two practical algorithms based on Gaussians and Gaussian mixtures. We theoretically analyze them by deriving a finite-sample analysis and provide a comprehensive empirical evaluation in four different domains.
originalAbstract: We consider the problem of transferring value functions in reinforcement learning. We propose an approach that uses the given source tasks to learn a prior distribution over optimal value functions and provide an efficient variational approximation of the corresponding posterior in a new target task. We show our approach to be general, in the sense that it can be combined with complex parametric function approximators and distribution models, while providing two practical algorithms based on Gaussians and Gaussian mixtures. We theoretically analyze them by deriving a finite-sample analysis and provide a comprehensive empirical evaluation in four different domains.

paragraphs: The paper studies transferring value functions between reinforcement-learning tasks. It uses source tasks to learn a prior distribution over optimal value functions. This prior represents knowledge from the available tasks in a probabilistic form that can be brought to a new target task, instead of requiring a single transferred value function.

For the target task, the method constructs an efficient variational approximation to the corresponding posterior distribution. This provides a computational way to update the transferred prior using information from the new task. The approach accommodates complex parametric function approximators and distribution models, while the paper supplies two practical algorithms based on Gaussian distributions and Gaussian mixtures.

The authors derive a finite-sample analysis and evaluate the approach empirically in four domains. These contributions connect the general transfer formulation to concrete algorithms, theoretical analysis with finite data, and experimental assessment. The main idea is to transfer a distribution over value functions and then adapt that distribution to the target task through approximate inference, preserving a probabilistic account of the transferred knowledge.
summary.tldr: The method transfers reinforcement-learning knowledge through a learned prior over value functions and variational posterior inference for a new task.

title: Transfer of Value Functions via Variational Methods

abstract: In this paper we developed a computational hierarchical network model to understand the spatiotemporal sequence learning effects observed in the primate visual cortex. The model is a hierarchical recurrent neural model that learns to predict video sequences using the incoming video signals as teaching signals. The model performs fast feedforward analysis using a deep convolutional neural network with sparse convolution and feedback synthesis using a stack of LSTM modules. The network learns a representational hierarchy by minimizing its prediction errors of the incoming signals at each level of the hierarchy. We found that recurrent feedback in this network lead to the development of semantic cluster of global movement patterns in the population codes of the units at the lower levels of the hierarchy. These representations facilitate the learning of relationship among movement patterns, yielding state-of-the-art performance in long range video sequence predictions on benchmark datasets. Without further tuning, this model automatically exhibits the neurophysiological correlates of visual sequence memories that we observed in the early visual cortex of awake monkeys, suggesting the principle of self-supervised prediction learning might be relevant to understanding the cortical mechanisms of representational learning.

paragraphs: This paper develops a computational model to investigate visual sequence-learning effects observed in primate visual cortex. The network learns by predicting incoming video, using the video itself as its teaching signal. Its training objective minimizes prediction errors at multiple levels, allowing a hierarchy of representations to develop through self-supervised learning.

The architecture combines fast feedforward processing through a sparsely convolutional deep network with feedback synthesis through stacked LSTM modules. Recurrent feedback leads lower-level population representations to form semantic clusters of global movement patterns. These representations help the network learn relationships among movements and support state-of-the-art long-range video prediction on the evaluated benchmarks.

Without additional tuning, the model also exhibits neurophysiological correlates of visual sequence memories observed in the early visual cortex of awake monkeys. This agreement suggests that learning through prediction may help explain cortical representation learning. The result connects a working video-prediction model with neural observations, supporting the proposed principle as a possible account of the observed sequence-learning effects.
summary.tldr: A hierarchical video-prediction network develops movement representations and reproduces observed neural correlates of visual sequence memory without further tuning.

title: Visual Sequence Learning in Hierarchical Prediction Networks and Primate Visual Cortex

abstract: Spectral clustering is one of the most popular, yet still incompletely understood, methods for community detection on graphs. This article studies spectral clustering based on the Bethe-Hessian matrix H r= (r^2−1)I n+D−rA for sparse heterogeneous graphs (following the degree-corrected stochastic block model) in a two-class setting. For a specific value r=ζ, clustering is shown to be insensitive to the degree heterogeneity. We then study the behavior of the informative eigenvector of H_ζ and, as a result, predict the clustering accuracy. The article concludes with an overview of the generalization to more than two classes along with extensive simulations on synthetic and real networks corroborating our findings.

paragraphs: Community detection seeks groups of nodes within a graph, but uneven node degrees can complicate the task. This paper studies spectral clustering with the Bethe-Hessian matrix on sparse graphs with heterogeneous degrees. Its main analysis uses the degree-corrected stochastic block model with two communities, making both the graph model and the two-class setting central to the result.

The Bethe-Hessian matrix has a parameter r. The authors identify a particular choice, r equal to zeta, for which clustering is insensitive to degree heterogeneity in the analyzed setting. They then study the informative eigenvector of that matrix and use its behavior to predict clustering accuracy. This links the matrix’s spectral structure to the quality of the recovered communities.

The paper also outlines an extension to more than two classes and reports extensive simulations on synthetic and real networks that corroborate the findings. Its contribution is an explanation of how parameter selection can prevent degree variation from distorting community detection, together with a prediction of accuracy under the studied model.
summary.tldr: A specific Bethe-Hessian parameter choice makes clustering insensitive to degree heterogeneity in a two-community graph model and enables accuracy prediction.

title: Revisiting the Bethe-Hessian: Improved Community Detection in Sparse Heterogeneous Graphs

abstract: Variational Inference is a powerful tool in the Bayesian modeling toolkit, however, its effectiveness is determined by the expressivity of the utilized variational distributions in terms of their ability to match the true posterior distribution. In turn, the expressivity of the variational family is largely limited by the requirement of having a tractable density function. To overcome this roadblock, we introduce a new family of variational upper bounds on a marginal log-density in the case of hierarchical models (also known as latent variable models). We then derive a family of increasingly tighter variational lower bounds on the otherwise intractable standard evidence lower bound for hierarchical variational distributions, enabling the use of more expressive approximate posteriors. We show that previously known methods, such as Hierarchical Variational Models, Semi-Implicit Variational Inference and Doubly Semi-Implicit Variational Inference can be seen as special cases of the proposed approach, and empirically demonstrate superior performance of the proposed method in a set of experiments.

paragraphs: Variational inference approximates a Bayesian posterior using a more manageable distribution. Its quality depends on whether that distribution can express the posterior's structure. Requiring an easily evaluated density restricts this flexibility, creating a tension between a rich approximation and an objective that can actually be computed and optimized.

The paper develops bounds that help resolve this tension for hierarchical variational distributions. It first introduces a family of upper bounds on marginal log-densities in latent-variable models. From these, it derives increasingly tight lower bounds on the standard evidence lower bound, which can itself be intractable for these richer distributions. This provides usable optimization objectives for more expressive posterior approximations.

The framework also unifies several existing approaches: Hierarchical Variational Models, Semi-Implicit Variational Inference, and Doubly Semi-Implicit Variational Inference emerge as special cases. The authors report superior performance in their experiments. The contribution is thus both a broader mathematical construction for handling difficult densities and empirical evidence that the resulting inference method can improve on the compared approaches.
summary.tldr: New variational bounds make richer hierarchical posterior approximations usable while unifying several existing inference methods.

title: Importance Weighted Hierarchical Variational Inference

abstract: This paper addresses the use of neural networks for the estimation of treatment effects from observational data. Generally, estimation proceeds in two stages. First, we ﬁt models for the expected outcome and the probability of treatment (propensity score). Second, we plug these ﬁtted models into a downstream estimator. Neural networks are a natural choice for the models in the ﬁrst step. Our question is: how can we adapt the design and training of the neural networks used in this ﬁrst step in order to improve the quality of the ﬁnal estimate of the treatment effect? We propose two adaptations based on insights from the statistical literature on the estimation of treatment effects. The ﬁrst is a new architecture, the Dragonnet, that exploits the sufﬁciency of the propensity score for estimation adjustment. The second is a regularization procedure, targeted regularization, that induces a bias towards models that have non-parametrically optimal asymptotic properties ‘out-of-the-box’. Studies on benchmark datasets for causal inference show these adaptations outperform existing methods.

paragraphs: Estimating treatment effects from observational data often involves two stages: predicting outcomes and treatment probabilities, then feeding those predictions into a treatment-effect estimator. This paper asks how neural networks in the first stage should be designed so that they improve the final estimate. The downstream statistical task therefore guides the network design and training.

The authors propose two adaptations. Dragonnet is an architecture that uses the statistical sufficiency of the propensity score, the probability of receiving treatment, for estimation adjustment. Targeted regularization changes training to favor models with nonparametrically optimal asymptotic properties. That describes behavior as data grows; the regularizer encourages models with those properties rather than guaranteeing optimal estimates for every dataset.

Studies on causal-inference benchmark datasets report that these adaptations outperform existing methods. The contribution connects neural-network modeling with statistical insights about treatment-effect estimation. It shows how the purpose of the final estimator can inform both the architecture that produces its inputs and the objective used to train that architecture.
summary.tldr: Dragonnet and targeted regularization adapt neural networks to improve downstream treatment-effect estimates from observational data.

title: Adapting Neural Networks for the Estimation of Treatment Effects

abstract: Despite the development of numerous adaptive optimizers, tuning the learning rate of stochastic gradient methods remains a major roadblock to obtaining good practical performance in machine learning. Rather than changing the learning rate at each iteration, we propose an approach that automates the most common hand-tuning heuristic: use a constant learning rate until "progress stops," then drop. We design an explicit statistical test that determines when the dynamics of stochastic gradient descent reach a stationary distribution. This test can be performed easily during training, and when it fires, we decrease the learning rate by a constant multiplicative factor. Our experiments on several deep learning tasks demonstrate that this statistical adaptive stochastic approximation (SASA) method can automatically find good learning rate schedules and match the performance of hand-tuned methods using default settings of its parameters. The statistical testing helps to control the variance of this procedure and improves its robustness.

paragraphs: Learning-rate schedules remain an important source of manual tuning in stochastic optimization. This paper automates a familiar practice: keep the learning rate fixed while training progresses, then reduce it when progress levels off. The method gives that transition an explicit statistical criterion that can be evaluated during training.

The authors design a test for whether stochastic gradient descent's dynamics have reached a stationary distribution. When the test triggers, the learning rate is multiplied by a fixed reduction factor. Called statistical adaptive stochastic approximation, or SASA, the method uses evidence about the training dynamics to determine when the next learning-rate drop should occur.

Experiments across several deep-learning tasks show that SASA can find effective schedules and match hand-tuned performance with its parameters left at default settings. The authors also report that statistical testing helps control the procedure's variance and improves robustness. The findings support automating schedule timing through a measurable property of optimization dynamics, reducing reliance on manually chosen drop points.
summary.tldr: SASA uses a statistical stationarity test to time learning-rate reductions and matches hand-tuned schedules on the evaluated deep-learning tasks.

title: Using Statistics to Automate Stochastic Optimization

abstract: Many practical graph problems, such as knowledge graph construction and drug-drug interaction prediction, require to handle multi-relational graphs. However, handling real-world multi-relational graphs with Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) is often challenging due to their evolving nature, as new entities (nodes) can emerge over time. Moreover, newly emerged entities often have few links, which makes the learning even more difficult. Motivated by this challenge, we introduce a realistic problem of few-shot out-of-graph link prediction, where we not only predict the links between the seen and unseen nodes as in a conventional out-of-knowledge link prediction task but also between the unseen nodes, with only few edges per node. We tackle this problem with a novel transductive meta-learning framework which we refer to as Graph Extrapolation Networks (GEN). GEN meta-learns both the node embedding network for inductive inference (seen-to-unseen) and the link prediction network for transductive inference (unseen-to-unseen). For transductive link prediction, we further propose a stochastic embedding layer to model uncertainty in the link prediction between unseen entities. We validate our model on multiple benchmark datasets for knowledge graph completion and drug-drug interaction prediction. The results show that our model significantly outperforms relevant baselines for out-of-graph link prediction tasks.

paragraphs: Graphs with multiple relation types often grow as new entities appear. Those entities may initially have very few observed connections, making predictions difficult. This paper formulates few-shot out-of-graph link prediction to include both links connecting familiar and new entities and links joining two new entities, using only a few edges per new node.

The proposed Graph Extrapolation Networks, or GEN, use a transductive meta-learning framework. The system meta-learns a node embedding network for predictions involving seen and unseen nodes, together with a link prediction network for relationships between unseen nodes. A stochastic embedding layer further represents uncertainty when predicting connections between new entities with limited available evidence.

The authors evaluate GEN on multiple benchmarks for knowledge graph completion and drug-drug interaction prediction, reporting significant improvements over relevant baselines on out-of-graph tasks. The work broadens the prediction problem beyond attaching a new node to a familiar graph. It also addresses relationships within the newly arriving group, where both endpoints have sparse observations and the model must account for uncertainty.
summary.tldr: GEN meta-learns link prediction for sparsely connected new graph entities, including uncertain relationships between two unseen nodes.

title: Learning to Extrapolate Knowledge: Transductive Few-shot Out-of-Graph Link Prediction

abstract: Developmental machine learning studies how artificial agents can model the way children learn open-ended repertoires of skills. Such agents need to create and represent goals, select which ones to pursue and learn to achieve them. Recent approaches have considered goal spaces that were either fixed and hand-defined or learned using generative models of states. This limited agents to sample goals within the distribution of known effects. We argue that the ability to imagine out-of-distribution goals is key to enable creative discoveries and open-ended learning. Children do so by leveraging the compositionality of language as a tool to imagine descriptions of outcomes they never experienced before, targeting them as goals during play. We introduce IMAGINE, an intrinsically motivated deep reinforcement learning architecture that models this ability. Such imaginative agents, like children, benefit from the guidance of a social peer who provides language descriptions. To take advantage of goal imagination, agents must be able to leverage these descriptions to interpret their imagined out-of-distribution goals. This generalization is made possible by modularity: a decomposition between learned goal-achievement reward function and policy relying on deep sets, gated attention and object-centered representations. We introduce the Playground environment and study how this form of goal imagination improves generalization and exploration over agents lacking this capacity. In addition, we identify the properties of goal imagination that enable these results and study the impacts of modularity and social interactions.

This generalization is made possible by modularity: a decomposition between learned goal-achievement reward function and policy relying on deep sets, gated attention and object-centered representations. We introduce the Playground environment and study how this form of goal imagination improves generalization and exploration over agents lacking this capacity. In addition, we identify the properties of goal imagination that enable these results and study the impacts of modularity and social interactions.

paragraphs: An agent learning through exploration must decide which outcomes to pursue. Existing goal-generation approaches described in this paper restrict that choice to fixed goals or the distribution of already known effects. IMAGINE explores a broader possibility: using the compositional structure of language to describe and pursue outcomes the agent has not previously experienced.

The architecture combines intrinsically motivated deep reinforcement learning with language descriptions supplied by a social peer. Creating new descriptions is useful only if the agent can interpret them as goals. To support that generalization, the system separates its learned goal-achievement reward function from its policy and uses deep sets, gated attention, and object-centered representations.

The authors introduce the Playground environment to study this capacity. They examine improvements in exploration and generalization relative to agents without goal imagination, and investigate which properties of imagination, modularity, and social interaction contribute. The work frames language as a tool for generating new learning objectives, with the architecture designed to connect imagined descriptions to behavior the agent can learn to perform.
summary.tldr: IMAGINE uses language to construct unfamiliar goals and studies how this ability improves exploration and generalization.

title: Language as a Cognitive Tool to Imagine Goals in Curiosity Driven Exploration

abstract: Shapley values underlie one of the most popular model-agnostic methods within explainable artificial intelligence. These values are designed to attribute the difference between a model's prediction and an average baseline to the different features used as input to the model. Being based on solid game-theoretic principles, Shapley values uniquely satisfy several desirable properties, which is why they are increasingly used to explain the predictions of possibly complex and highly non-linear machine learning models. Shapley values are well calibrated to a user’s intuition when features are independent, but may lead to undesirable, counterintuitive explanations when the independence assumption is violated. In this paper, we propose a novel framework for computing Shapley values that generalizes recent work that aims to circumvent the independence assumption. By employing Pearl's do-calculus, we show how these `causal' Shapley values can be derived for general causal graphs without sacrificing any of their desirable properties. Moreover, causal Shapley values enable us to separate the contribution of direct and indirect effects. We provide a practical implementation for computing causal Shapley values based on causal chain graphs when only partial information is available and illustrate their utility on a real-world example.

paragraphs: Shapley explanations distribute the difference between a model's prediction and an average baseline across its input features. Their game-theoretic properties make them attractive for explaining complex models. However, relationships among input features can produce explanations that conflict with intuition when those relationships are handled through an independence assumption.

This paper introduces a framework that incorporates causal knowledge into Shapley attribution. Using Pearl's do-calculus, the authors derive causal Shapley values for general causal graphs while retaining the desirable properties described for Shapley values. The graph supplies information about how features causally relate, allowing that structure to shape the explanation.

A further benefit is the ability to separate direct contributions from contributions transmitted through indirect causal effects. The authors provide a practical implementation based on causal chain graphs for situations where only partial causal information is available, and illustrate its usefulness on a real-world example. The contribution is therefore both an attribution framework and a way to make supplied causal knowledge operational when explaining an individual prediction.
summary.tldr: Causal Shapley values incorporate causal relationships into feature attribution and separate direct from indirect contributions to a prediction.

title: Causal Shapley Values: Exploiting Causal Knowledge to Explain Individual Predictions of Complex Models

abstract: To make decisions based on a model fit with auto-encoding variational Bayes (AEVB), practitioners often let the variational distribution serve as a surrogate for the posterior distribution. This approach yields biased estimates of the expected risk, and therefore leads to poor decisions for two reasons. First, the model fit with AEVB may not equal the underlying data distribution. Second, the variational distribution may not equal the posterior distribution under the fitted model. We explore how fitting the variational distribution based on several objective functions other than the ELBO, while continuing to fit the generative model based on the ELBO, affects the quality of downstream decisions. For the probabilistic principal component analysis model, we investigate how importance sampling error, as well as the bias of the model parameter estimates, varies across several approximate posteriors when used as proposal distributions. Our theoretical results suggest that a posterior approximation distinct from the variational distribution should be used for making decisions. Motivated by these theoretical results, we propose learning several approximate proposals for the best model and combining them using multiple importance sampling for decision-making. In addition to toy examples, we present a full-fledged case study of single-cell RNA sequencing. In this challenging instance of multiple hypothesis testing, our proposed approach surpasses the current state of the art.

paragraphs: Auto-encoding variational Bayes learns a generative model together with an approximate posterior distribution. Practitioners often reuse that approximation when evaluating decisions. This paper identifies two sources of biased risk estimates: the fitted model can differ from the data-generating distribution, and the approximate posterior can differ from the posterior implied by that fitted model.

The authors investigate fitting posterior approximations with objectives other than the evidence lower bound, while retaining that objective for fitting the generative model. Their theoretical findings suggest that the approximation used for decisions should differ from the variational distribution used during model fitting.

This separates learning a model from constructing the estimates needed for a decision. Beyond toy examples, a single-cell RNA sequencing case study reports improved performance over the current state of the art for a challenging multiple-testing problem.
summary.tldr: Combining separately learned posterior proposals can improve decisions made from models trained with auto-encoding variational Bayes.

title: Decision-Making with Auto-Encoding Variational Bayes

abstract: A central problem in cognitive science and behavioural neuroscience as well as in machine learning and artificial intelligence research is to ascertain whether two or more decision makers---be they brains or algorithms---use the same strategy. Accuracy alone cannot distinguish between strategies: two systems may achieve similar accuracy with very different strategies. The need to differentiate beyond accuracy is particularly pressing if two systems are at or near ceiling performance, like Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) and humans on visual object recognition. Here we introduce trial-by-trial error consistency, a quantitative analysis for measuring whether two decision making systems systematically make errors on the same inputs. Making consistent errors on a trial-by-trial basis is a necessary condition if we want to ascertain similar processing strategies between decision makers. Our analysis is applicable to compare algorithms with algorithms, humans with humans, and algorithms with humans. When applying error consistency to visual object recognition we obtain three main findings: (1.) Irrespective of architecture, CNNs are remarkably consistent with one another. (2.) The consistency between CNNs and human observers, however, is little above what can be expected by chance alone---indicating that humans and CNNs are likely implementing very different strategies. (3.) CORnet-S, a recurrent model termed the "current best model of the primate ventral visual stream", fails to capture essential characteristics of human behavioural data and behaves essentially like a standard purely feedforward ResNet-50 in our analysis; highlighting that certain behavioural failure cases are not limited to feedforward models. Taken together, error consistency analysis suggests that the strategies used by human and machine vision are still very different---but we envision our general-purpose error consistency analysis to serve as a fruitful tool for quantifying future progress.

Thus, the observed behavioral mismatch extends beyond feedforward models. Error consistency provides a way to assess whether future systems move closer to human patterns of decisions.
summary.tldr: Comparing which images cause errors reveals substantial behavioral differences between humans and tested vision networks that overall accuracy can conceal.

title: Beyond accuracy: quantifying trial-by-trial behaviour of CNNs and humans by measuring error consistency

abstract: We consider the fundamental problem of selecting $k$ out of $n$ random variables in a way that the expected highest or second-highest value is maximized. This question captures several applications where we have uncertainty about the quality of candidates (e.g. auction bids, search results) and have the capacity to explore only a small subset due to an exogenous constraint. For example, consider a second price auction where system constraints (e.g., costly retrieval or model computation) allow the participation of only $k$ out of $n$ bidders, and the goal is to optimize the expected efficiency (highest bid) or expected revenue (second highest bid). We study the case where we are given an explicit description of each random variable. We give a PTAS for the problem of maximizing the expected highest value. For the second-highest value, we prove a hardness result: assuming the Planted Clique Hypothesis, there is no constant factor approximation algorithm that runs in polynomial time. Surprisingly, under the assumption that each random variable has monotone hazard rate (MHR), a simple score-based algorithm, namely picking the $k$ random variables with the largest $1/\sqrt{k}$ top quantile value, is a constant approximation to the expected highest and second highest value, \emph{simultaneously}.

paragraphs: Suppose only k of n uncertain candidates can be considered, and success depends on the highest or second-highest value among those selected. This paper studies that selection problem when each random variable has an explicit description. One application is a second-price auction, where participation constraints affect both the winning bid and the payment.

The two objectives have sharply different computational properties. For the expected highest value, the authors give a polynomial-time approximation scheme, allowing increasingly accurate approximation for a fixed accuracy choice. For the expected second-highest value, they show that no polynomial-time constant-factor approximation exists assuming the Planted Clique Hypothesis. That hardness conclusion depends on the stated hypothesis.

A distributional assumption changes the picture. If every random variable has monotone hazard rate, selecting the k variables with the largest upper-tail quantile values at probability 1 divided by the square root of k gives a constant-factor approximation to both objectives simultaneously. Thus, a simple scoring rule becomes provably useful under this assumption, despite the broader difficulty of optimizing the second-highest value.
summary.tldr: Selecting for the expected maximum is approximable, the second maximum is conditionally hard, and a simple quantile rule approximates both under monotone hazard rates.

title: Hitting the High Notes: Subset Selection for Maximizing Expected Order Statistics

abstract: Bayesian optimisation is a popular method for efficient optimisation of expensive black-box functions. Traditionally, BO assumes that the search space is known. However, in many problems, this assumption does not hold. To this end, we propose a novel BO algorithm which expands (and shifts) the search space over iterations based on controlling the expansion rate thought a \emph{hyperharmonic series}. Further, we propose another variant of our algorithm that scales to high dimensions. We show theoretically that for both our algorithms, the cumulative regret grows at sub-linear rates. Our experiments with synthetic and real-world optimisation tasks demonstrate the superiority of our algorithms over the current state-of-the-art methods for Bayesian optimisation in unknown search space.

paragraphs: Bayesian optimization seeks good solutions when evaluating a black-box function is expensive. It traditionally assumes that the region to search is already known. This paper addresses problems where that assumption fails, making the choice of where to search part of the optimization process.

The proposed algorithm expands and shifts its search region over successive iterations. A hyperharmonic series controls the expansion rate, providing a mathematical rule for how the region grows. The authors also introduce a variant designed to scale to high-dimensional problems, extending the approach beyond the initial algorithm's setting.

For both algorithms, the paper proves that cumulative regret grows sublinearly. This means the average accumulated shortfall decreases as the number of iterations increases under the theoretical result. Experiments on synthetic and real optimization tasks show improvements over leading methods for unknown search spaces. Together, the findings support controlled search-region adaptation as a way to retain theoretical progress guarantees while tackling uncertainty about the search boundaries.
summary.tldr: Bayesian optimization with controlled expansion and shifting of its search region achieves sublinear cumulative regret.

title: Sub-linear Regret Bounds for Bayesian Optimisation in Unknown Search Spaces

abstract: Despite the recent success of Bayesian optimization (BO) in a variety of applications where sample efficiency is imperative, its performance may be seriously compromised in settings characterized by high-dimensional parameter spaces. A solution to preserve the sample efficiency of BO in such problems is to introduce domain knowledge into its formulation. In this paper, we propose to exploit the geometry of non-Euclidean search spaces, which often arise in a variety of domains, to learn structure-preserving mappings and optimize the acquisition function of BO in low-dimensional latent spaces. Our approach, built on Riemannian manifolds theory, features geometry-aware Gaussian processes that jointly learn a nested-manifolds embedding and a representation of the objective function in the latent space. We test our approach in several benchmark artificial landscapes and report that it not only outperforms other high-dimensional BO approaches in several settings, but consistently optimizes the objective functions, as opposed to geometry-unaware BO methods.

paragraphs: Bayesian optimization seeks good solutions with relatively few evaluations, but high-dimensional search spaces can compromise that efficiency. This paper addresses problems whose search spaces have non-Euclidean geometry. It uses knowledge of that geometry to learn a smaller space in which optimization can proceed while preserving relevant structure.

The method builds on Riemannian manifolds and geometry-aware Gaussian processes. It jointly learns an embedding through nested manifolds and a model of the objective function in the resulting low-dimensional space. The acquisition function, which guides the search for evaluations, is optimized there. Learning the representation and objective together connects dimensionality reduction directly to the optimization task.

Tests on artificial benchmark landscapes show better performance than other high-dimensional Bayesian optimization approaches in several settings. The authors also report consistent optimization of the objectives, contrasting with geometry-unaware methods in those experiments. The findings support using the structure of non-Euclidean domains as useful information when reducing the dimensionality of a search problem, rather than treating all parameter spaces identically.
summary.tldr: Geometry-aware Bayesian optimization learns low-dimensional manifold representations to improve search in high-dimensional non-Euclidean spaces.

title: High-Dimensional Bayesian Optimization via Nested Riemannian Manifolds

abstract: The recovery of sparse data is at the core of many applications in machine learning and signal processing. While such problems can be tackled using $\ell_1$-regularization as in the LASSO estimator and in the Basis Pursuit approach, specialized algorithms are typically required to solve the corresponding high-dimensional non-smooth optimization for large instances.Iteratively Reweighted Least Squares (IRLS) is a widely used algorithm for this purpose due to its excellent numerical performance. However, while existing theory is able to guarantee convergence of this algorithm to the minimizer, it does not provide a global convergence rate. In this paper, we prove that a variant of IRLS converges \emph{with a global linear rate} to a sparse solution, i.e., with a linear error decrease occurring immediately from any initialization if the measurements fulfill the usual null space property assumption. We support our theory by numerical experiments showing that our linear rate captures the correct dimension dependence. We anticipate that our theoretical findings will lead to new insights for many other use cases of the IRLS algorithm, such as in low-rank matrix recovery.

Iteratively Reweighted Least Squares, or IRLS, is widely used for such recovery and performs well numerically, but previous convergence theory did not provide a global rate.

This paper proves a global linear convergence rate for a variant of IRLS. Here, linear convergence means that the error contracts geometrically as iterations proceed. The guarantee begins immediately from any initialization, provided the measurements satisfy the usual null space property. That condition is central to the claim: the result is not an unconditional guarantee for arbitrary measurement systems.

Numerical experiments support the theory and show that the rate captures the correct dependence on problem dimension. The result therefore strengthens an eventual-convergence statement into a description of how quickly error decreases throughout the run. The authors also anticipate implications for other IRLS applications, including low-rank matrix recovery, presenting that connection as a direction for further insight.
summary.tldr: An IRLS variant has global linear convergence from any initialization when measurements satisfy the null space property.

title: Iteratively Reweighted Least Squares for Basis Pursuit with Global Linear Convergence Rate

abstract: Domain generalization refers to the problem where we aim to train a model on data from a set of source domains so that the model can generalize to unseen target domains. Naively training a model on the aggregate set of data (pooled from all source domains) has been shown to perform suboptimally, since the information learned by that model might be domain-specific and generalize imperfectly to target domains. To tackle this problem, a predominant domain generalization approach is to learn some domain-invariant information for the prediction task, aiming at a good generalization across domains. In this paper, we propose a theoretically grounded method to learn a domain-invariant representation by enforcing the representation network to be invariant under all transformation functions among domains. We next introduce the use of generative adversarial networks to learn such domain transformations in a possible implementation of our method in practice. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our method on several widely used datasets for the domain generalization problem, on all of which we achieve competitive results with state-of-the-art models.

paragraphs: Domain generalization asks a model trained on several source domains to perform well on unseen target domains. Simply pooling the source data can leave the model dependent on information specific to those sources. This paper pursues representations that preserve useful predictive information while remaining invariant across domains.

The proposed method expresses invariance through transformations between domains. It requires the representation network to remain unchanged under all such transformation functions. This gives the approach a concrete learning principle: domain changes represented by those transformations should not alter the learned representation. The authors present the method as theoretically grounded.

For a practical implementation, the paper introduces generative adversarial networks to learn the domain transformations. These learned transformations provide a way to put the invariance principle into a training procedure. Evaluations on several widely used domain-generalization datasets produce results competitive with state-of-the-art models on all of them. The findings support transformation-based invariance as an effective approach in the tested settings, with the adversarial implementation serving as one possible realization of the broader method.
summary.tldr: The method learns domain-invariant representations by enforcing consistency under transformations between source domains.

title: Domain Invariant Representation Learning with Domain Density Transformations

abstract: A central challenge in training classification models in the real-world federated system is learning with non-IID data. To cope with this, most of the existing works involve enforcing regularization in local optimization or improving the model aggregation scheme at the server. Other works also share public datasets or synthesized samples to supplement the training of under-represented classes or introduce a certain level of personalization. Though effective, they lack a deep understanding of how the data heterogeneity affects each layer of a deep classification model. In this paper, we bridge this gap by performing an experimental analysis of the representations learned by different layers. Our observations are surprising: (1) there exists a greater bias in the classifier than other layers, and (2) the classification performance can be significantly improved by post-calibrating the classifier after federated training. Motivated by the above findings, we propose a novel and simple algorithm called Classifier Calibration with Virtual Representations (CCVR), which adjusts the classifier using virtual representations sampled from an approximated gaussian mixture model. Experimental results demonstrate that CCVR achieves state-of-the-art performance on popular federated learning benchmarks including CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, and CINIC-10. We hope that our simple yet effective method can shed some light on the future research of federated learning with non-IID data.

paragraphs: Federated classification becomes difficult when participating clients have different data distributions. This paper investigates where that heterogeneity affects a deep model, rather than treating all layers as equally compromised. An experimental analysis of learned representations finds greater bias in the final classifier than in other layers, and substantial gains from adjusting that classifier after federated training.

Those observations motivate Classifier Calibration with Virtual Representations, or CCVR. The method samples virtual representations from an approximated Gaussian mixture model and uses them to adjust the classifier. Its intervention therefore targets the layer that maps representations to class predictions, following the paper's evidence that this layer is especially affected by heterogeneous training data.

Experiments report state-of-the-art performance on CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, and CINIC-10 federated learning benchmarks. The result suggests that useful representations may already exist in a federated model whose final classification decisions remain biased. Post-training classifier adjustment can exploit that distinction. The findings are experimental evidence for a targeted correction strategy, rather than a universal claim that heterogeneity affects only the classifier.
summary.tldr: CCVR improves federated classifiers by recalibrating their final layer with virtual representations after training on heterogeneous client data.

title: No Fear of Heterogeneity: Classifier Calibration for Federated Learning with Non-IID Data

abstract: Modern neural networks are often quite wide, causing large memory and computation costs. It is thus of great interest to train a narrower network. However, training narrow neural nets remains a challenging task. We ask two theoretical questions: Can narrow networks have as strong expressivity as wide ones? If so, does the loss function exhibit a benign optimization landscape? In this work, we provide partially affirmative answers to both questions for 1-hidden-layer networks with fewer than $n$ (sample size) neurons when the activation is smooth. First, we prove that as long as the width $m \geq 2n/d$ (where $d$ is the input dimension), its expressivity is strong, i.e., there exists at least one global minimizer with zero training loss. Second, we identify a nice local region with no local-min or saddle points. Nevertheless, it is not clear whether gradient descent can stay in this nice region. Third, we consider a constrained optimization formulation where the feasible region is the nice local region, and prove that every KKT point is a nearly global minimizer. It is expected that projected gradient methods converge to KKT points under mild technical conditions, but we leave the rigorous convergence analysis to future work. Thorough numerical results show that projected gradient methods on this constrained formulation significantly outperform SGD for training narrow neural nets.

paragraphs: Narrow networks can reduce memory and computation, but their ability to fit data and their ease of optimization are separate questions. This paper studies both for networks with one hidden layer and smooth activations. It proves that width m at least 2n/d is sufficient for a zero-training-loss solution, where n is sample size and d is input dimension.

The authors also identify a favorable local region without local-minimum or saddle points. However, they do not establish that ordinary gradient descent remains in that region. They therefore formulate a constrained problem whose feasible set is the favorable region and prove that every point satisfying the KKT optimality conditions is nearly a global minimizer.

Projected gradient methods are expected to approach such points under mild technical conditions, but rigorous convergence analysis is left open. Numerical results nevertheless show these methods substantially outperforming SGD on the constrained narrow-network formulation. The contribution thus combines an expressivity guarantee, a local optimization result, and empirical training evidence while preserving the distinction between them.
summary.tldr: Smooth narrow networks can fit training data under a sufficient width condition, and a constrained formulation offers promising optimization properties.

title: When Expressivity Meets Trainability: Fewer than $n$ Neurons Can Work

abstract: The generalization mystery of overparametrized deep nets has motivated efforts to understand how gradient descent (GD) converges to low-loss solutions that generalize well. Real-life neural networks are initialized from small random values and trained with cross-entropy loss for classification (unlike the "lazy" or "NTK" regime of training where analysis was more successful), and a recent sequence of results (Lyu and Li, 2020; Chizat and Bach, 2020; Ji and Telgarsky, 2020) provide theoretical evidence that GD may converge to the "max-margin" solution with zero loss, which presumably generalizes well. However, the global optimality of margin is proved only in some settings where neural nets are infinitely or exponentially wide. The current paper is able to establish this global optimality for two-layer Leaky ReLU nets trained with gradient flow on linearly separable and symmetric data, regardless of the width. The analysis also gives some theoretical justification for recent empirical findings (Kalimeris et al., 2019) on the so-called simplicity bias of GD towards linear or other "simple" classes of solutions, especially early in training. On the pessimistic side, the paper suggests that such results are fragile. A simple data manipulation can make gradient flow converge to a linear classifier with suboptimal margin.

paragraphs: Neural networks can have many low-loss solutions, raising the question of which ones gradient-based training selects. One proposed explanation for generalization is a preference for solutions with large classification margins. This paper investigates when training actually reaches a globally optimal margin and how that behavior relates to a preference for simpler classifiers.

The main positive result concerns two-layer networks with Leaky ReLU activations, trained using gradient flow on data that are both linearly separable and symmetric. Under those conditions, the authors establish global margin optimality regardless of network width. This removes the infinite or exponentially large width requirements present in some earlier results, while retaining explicit assumptions on the data and training dynamics.

The analysis also offers theoretical support for an early-training bias toward linear or other simple solutions. However, the paper demonstrates that the favorable margin result is fragile: a simple manipulation of the data can make gradient flow converge to a linear classifier with a suboptimal margin. Simplicity bias can therefore coexist with failure to find the best-margin solution.
summary.tldr: Gradient flow achieves globally optimal margins for two-layer Leaky ReLU networks under specific data assumptions, but small data changes can undermine that result.

title: Gradient Descent on Two-layer Nets: Margin Maximization and Simplicity Bias

abstract: Self-training is an effective approach to semi-supervised learning. The key idea is to let the learner itself iteratively generate "pseudo-supervision" for unlabeled instances based on its current hypothesis. In combination with consistency regularization, pseudo-labeling has shown promising performance in various domains, for example in computer vision. To account for the hypothetical nature of the pseudo-labels, these are commonly provided in the form of probability distributions. Still, one may argue that even a probability distribution represents an excessive level of informedness, as it suggests that the learner precisely knows the ground-truth conditional probabilities. In our approach, we therefore allow the learner to label instances in the form of credal sets, that is, sets of (candidate) probability distributions. Thanks to this increased expressiveness, the learner is able to represent uncertainty and a lack of knowledge in a more flexible and more faithful manner. To learn from weakly labeled data of that kind, we leverage methods that have recently been proposed in the realm of so-called superset learning. In an exhaustive empirical evaluation, we compare our methodology to state-of-the-art self-supervision approaches, showing competitive to superior performance especially in low-label scenarios incorporating a high degree of uncertainty.

paragraphs: Self-training uses a model's current predictions to create supervision for unlabeled examples. A pseudo-label can be a probability distribution rather than a single class, allowing uncertainty about the answer. This paper argues that specifying one exact distribution can still express more knowledge than the learner actually possesses.

The proposed approach assigns a credal set: a collection of candidate probability distributions. This lets the learner express uncertainty about which distribution should describe an example, rather than committing to one precise allocation of probabilities. To train from these less specific labels, the authors use methods from superset learning, which accommodate supervision expressed through sets of possibilities.

The empirical evaluation compares this approach with state-of-the-art self-supervision methods and finds competitive to superior performance, particularly when labeled examples are scarce and uncertainty is high. The contribution is a more flexible form of pseudo-supervision. Its reported benefits suggest that allowing the model to leave some uncertainty unresolved can be useful when its own predictions become training targets.
summary.tldr: Credal self-training replaces a single probabilistic pseudo-label with a set of candidate distributions, improving reported performance especially in uncertain, low-label settings.

title: Credal Self-Supervised Learning

abstract: Maximum cardinality bipartite matching is an important graph optimization problem with several applications. For instance, maximum cardinality matching in a $\delta$-disc graph can be used in the computation of the bottleneck matching as well as the $\infty$-Wasserstein and the Lévy-Prokhorov distances between probability distributions. For any point sets $A, B \subset \mathbb{R}^2$, the $\delta$-disc graph is a bipartite graph formed by connecting every pair of points $(a,b) \in A\times B$ by an edge if the Euclidean distance between them is at most $\delta$. Using the classical Hopcroft-Karp algorithm, a maximum-cardinality matching on any $\delta$-disc graph can be found in $\tilde{O}(n^{3/2})$ time.~\footnote{We use $\tilde{O}(\cdot)$ to suppress poly-logarithmic terms in the complexity.} In this paper, we present a simplification of a recent algorithm (Lahn and Raghvendra, JoCG 2021) for the maximum cardinality matching problem and describe how a maximum cardinality matching in a $\delta$-disc graph can be computed asymptotically faster than $O(n^{3/2})$ time for any moderately dense point set. As applications, we show that if $A$ and $B$ are point sets drawn uniformly at random from a unit square, an exact bottleneck matching can be computed in $\tilde{O}(n^{4/3})$ time. On the other hand, experiments suggest that the Hopcroft-Karp algorithm seems to take roughly $\Theta (n^{3/2})$ time for this case. This translates to substantial improvements in execution time for larger inputs.

paragraphs: Maximum cardinality bipartite matching pairs members of two sets while making as many pairs as possible, without reusing a member. This paper studies a geometric version: points in two planar sets may be paired only when their distance is within a chosen threshold. Such matching problems support calculations of bottleneck matchings and several distances between probability distributions.

The authors simplify a recent matching algorithm and show how to exploit this geometric setting. For moderately dense point sets, their method computes a maximum matching asymptotically faster than the n-to-the-three-halves running time discussed for the classical Hopcroft–Karp approach. The density qualification matters: the stated improvement is tied to that class of inputs.

For points drawn uniformly at random from a unit square, the paper gives an exact bottleneck matching algorithm taking roughly n-to-the-four-thirds time, with logarithmic factors suppressed. Experiments suggest that Hopcroft–Karp takes roughly n-to-the-three-halves time in this setting. The resulting execution-time improvements become substantial for larger inputs, connecting the theoretical speedup to a practical computational benefit.
summary.tldr: A simplified geometric matching algorithm improves running time for moderately dense planar point sets and accelerates exact bottleneck matching on uniformly random inputs.

title: A Faster Maximum Cardinality Matching Algorithm with Applications in Machine Learning

abstract: Test-time training (TTT) through self-supervised learning (SSL) is an emerging paradigm to tackle distributional shifts. Despite encouraging results, it remains unclear when this approach thrives or fails. In this work, we first provide an in-depth look at its limitations and show that TTT can possibly deteriorate, instead of improving, the test-time performance in the presence of severe distribution shifts. To address this issue, we introduce a test-time feature alignment strategy utilizing offline feature summarization and online moment matching, which regularizes adaptation without revisiting training data. We further scale this strategy in the online setting through batch-queue decoupling to enable robust moment estimates even with limited batch size. Given aligned feature distributions, we then shed light on the strong potential of TTT by theoretically analyzing its performance post adaptation. This analysis motivates our use of more informative self-supervision in the form of contrastive learning for visual recognition problems. We empirically demonstrate that our modified version of test-time training, termed TTT++, outperforms state-of-the-art methods by significant margins on several benchmarks. Our result indicates that storing and exploiting extra information, in addition to model parameters, can be a promising direction towards robust test-time adaptation.

paragraphs: Test-time training adapts a model using self-supervision on incoming data, aiming to handle distribution shifts. This paper shows that adaptation can instead hurt performance when the shift is severe. It investigates that failure mode and introduces TTT++, which adds feature alignment to help regulate the adaptation process.

The method summarizes features offline and matches feature moments online, allowing adaptation to use training-derived information without revisiting the training data. Batch-queue decoupling supports robust moment estimates even when online batches are small. These components make the alignment strategy usable in a setting where incoming data and batch sizes constrain adaptation.

That conditional analysis motivates more informative self-supervision through contrastive learning for visual recognition. TTT++ outperforms state-of-the-art methods by significant margins on several benchmarks. The results suggest that retaining useful information beyond model parameters can improve test-time adaptation, while the paper’s opening finding makes clear that self-supervised adaptation alone need not be beneficial.
summary.tldr: TTT++ combines feature alignment and contrastive self-supervision to improve test-time adaptation, which can otherwise deteriorate under severe shifts.

title: TTT++: When Does Self-Supervised Test-Time Training Fail or Thrive?

abstract: Graph neural networks (GNNs) have recently emerged as revolutionary technologies for machine learning tasks on graphs. In GNNs, the graph structure is generally incorporated with node representation via the message passing scheme, making the explanation much more challenging. Given a trained GNN model, a GNN explainer aims to identify a most influential subgraph to interpret the prediction of an instance (e.g., a node or a graph), which is essentially a combinatorial optimization problem over graph. The existing works solve this problem by continuous relaxation or search-based heuristics. But they suffer from key issues such as violation of message passing and hand-crafted heuristics, leading to inferior interpretability. To address these issues, we propose a RL-enhanced GNN explainer, RG-Explainer, which consists of three main components: starting point selection, iterative graph generation and stopping criteria learning. RG-Explainer could construct a connected explanatory subgraph by sequentially adding nodes from the boundary of the current generated graph, which is consistent with the message passing scheme. Further, we design an effective seed locator to select the starting point, and learn stopping criteria to generate superior explanations. Extensive experiments on both synthetic and real datasets show that RG-Explainer outperforms state-of-the-art GNN explainers. Moreover, RG-Explainer can be applied in the inductive setting, demonstrating its better generalization ability.

paragraphs: Explaining a trained graph neural network often means finding a subgraph that strongly influences a particular prediction. This is a combinatorial problem because many possible node combinations could be considered. The paper argues that existing continuous relaxations and search heuristics can conflict with message passing or rely on hand-designed choices that weaken explanations.

RG-Explainer uses reinforcement learning to organize explanation construction into three parts: selecting a starting point, growing the graph, and deciding when to stop. It adds nodes from the boundary of the current subgraph, allowing it to construct a connected explanation consistent with message passing. A seed locator chooses the initial node, and learned stopping criteria determine the explanation’s extent.

Experiments on synthetic and real datasets show better performance than state-of-the-art GNN explainers. The authors also demonstrate application in an inductive setting, supporting their claim of improved generalization. The approach matters because the structure of the explanation and the process used to produce it are designed together, with connectivity and learned search decisions built into subgraph generation.
summary.tldr: RG-Explainer learns where to start, how to grow, and when to stop constructing connected subgraphs that explain GNN predictions.

title: Reinforcement Learning Enhanced Explainer for Graph Neural Networks

abstract: Recent research has shown that graph neural networks (GNNs) can learn policies for locomotion control that are as effective as a typical multi-layer perceptron (MLP), with superior transfer and multi-task performance. However, results have so far been limited to training on small agents, with the performance of GNNs deteriorating rapidly as the number of sensors and actuators grows. A key motivation for the use of GNNs in the supervised learning setting is their applicability to large graphs, but this benefit has not yet been realised for locomotion control. We show that poor scaling in GNNs is a result of increasingly unstable policy updates, caused by overfitting in parts of the network during training. To combat this, we introduce Snowflake, a GNN training method for high-dimensional continuous control that freezes parameters in selected parts of the network. Snowflake significantly boosts the performance of GNNs for locomotion control on large agents, now matching the performance of MLPs while offering superior transfer properties.

paragraphs: Graph neural networks offer attractive transfer and multitask properties for locomotion policies, but their performance has deteriorated as controlled agents gain more sensors and actuators. This creates a scaling problem: successful control of small agents does not automatically carry over to larger systems with more continuous control dimensions.

The paper attributes this degradation to increasingly unstable policy updates caused by overfitting in parts of the network. Snowflake addresses that mechanism by freezing parameters in selected network components during training. Restricting which parameters change is intended to curb the local overfitting responsible for unstable updates and improve learning on larger agents.

The authors report substantial gains in graph-based locomotion control for large agents. With Snowflake, graph neural networks match multilayer perceptron performance while retaining superior transfer properties. The result highlights training dynamics as a barrier to scaling these policies: changing which components are allowed to learn can improve performance without abandoning the graph-based representation. The stated evidence concerns locomotion control on the evaluated large agents, where both control performance and transfer are relevant.
summary.tldr: Snowflake freezes selected GNN parameters to stabilize learning and improve locomotion control on agents with many sensors and actuators.

title: Snowflake: Scaling GNNs to high-dimensional continuous control via parameter freezing

abstract: Multi-site fMRI studies face the challenge that the pooling introduces systematic non-biological site-specific variance due to hardware, software, and environment. In this paper, we propose to reduce site-specific variance in the estimation of hierarchical Sparsity Connectivity Patterns (hSCPs) in fMRI data via a simple yet effective matrix factorization while preserving biologically relevant variations. Our method leverages unsupervised adversarial learning to improve the reproducibility of the components. Experiments on simulated datasets display that the proposed method can estimate components with higher accuracy and reproducibility, while preserving age-related variation on a multi-center clinical data set.

paragraphs: Combining fMRI data from several sites introduces a problem: differences between measurements can reflect scanners, software, or the collection environment rather than biology. The paper studies how to reduce this site-specific variation when estimating hierarchical Sparsity Connectivity Patterns, or hSCPs. The aim is to obtain reproducible brain connectivity components while retaining biologically relevant differences.

The proposed method uses matrix factorization together with unsupervised adversarial learning. This combination targets unwanted variation associated with the collection site during component estimation. The distinction matters because removing variation indiscriminately would conflict with the goal of preserving meaningful biological patterns in the pooled data.

On simulated datasets, the authors report components with higher accuracy and reproducibility. On a multi-center clinical dataset, they show preservation of age-related variation. These findings address complementary parts of the objective: recovering consistent components and keeping a particular source of biological variation. The evidence supports reducing site effects in this estimation process without losing the age-related differences examined in the clinical data.
summary.tldr: Adversarial matrix factorization improves the reproducibility of hierarchical fMRI connectivity patterns while preserving observed age-related variation.

title: Learning Robust Hierarchical Patterns of Human Brain across Many fMRI Studies

abstract: Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) have emerged as powerful tools to encode graph-structured data. Due to their broad applications, there is an increasing need to develop tools to explain how GNNs make decisions given graph-structured data. Existing learning-based GNN explanation approaches are task-specific in training and hence suffer from crucial drawbacks. Specifically, they are incapable of producing explanations for a multitask prediction model with a single explainer. They are also unable to provide explanations in cases where the GNN is trained in a self-supervised manner, and the resulting representations are used in future downstream tasks. To address these limitations, we propose a Task-Agnostic GNN Explainer (TAGE) that is independent of downstream models and trained under self-supervision with no knowledge of downstream tasks. TAGE enables the explanation of GNN embedding models with unseen downstream tasks and allows efficient explanation of multitask models. Our extensive experiments show that TAGE can significantly speed up the explanation efficiency by using the same model to explain predictions for multiple downstream tasks while achieving explanation quality as good as or even better than current state-of-the-art GNN explanation approaches.

paragraphs: Graph neural networks often produce representations that are reused across several prediction tasks. An explanation method trained for one specific task can be difficult to reuse in that setting. The problem is especially relevant when a graph encoder is trained without supervision and its eventual downstream tasks are not yet known.

TAGE addresses this by learning an explainer through self-supervision without knowledge of downstream tasks. Its training is independent of the downstream prediction models. This allows the same explainer to support graph embedding models used for previously unseen tasks and to explain predictions from multitask models more efficiently.

Experiments show significant gains in explanation efficiency from reusing one model across multiple downstream tasks. Explanation quality is as good as, or better than, the state-of-the-art approaches evaluated. The contribution is therefore both a broader training setup for graph explanations and an empirical efficiency benefit: learning an explainer before the downstream tasks are specified can still support useful explanations when those tasks arrive.
summary.tldr: TAGE learns a self-supervised graph explainer that can be reused across downstream tasks, improving efficiency while maintaining strong explanation quality.

title: Task-Agnostic Graph Explanations

abstract: We introduce a constrained optimization method for policy gradient reinforcement learning, which uses two trust regions to regulate each policy update. In addition to using the proximity of one single old policy as the first trust region as done by prior works, we propose forming a second trust region by constructing another virtual policy that represents a wide range of past policies. We then enforce the new policy to stay closer to the virtual policy, which is beneficial if the old policy performs poorly. We propose a mechanism to automatically build the virtual policy from a memory buffer of past policies, providing a new capability for dynamically selecting appropriate trust regions during the optimization process. Our proposed method, dubbed Memory-Constrained Policy Optimization (MCPO), is examined in diverse environments, including robotic locomotion control, navigation with sparse rewards and Atari games, consistently demonstrating competitive performance against recent on-policy constrained policy gradient methods.

paragraphs: Policy-gradient reinforcement learning improves an agent by updating its action-selection policy. Constrained methods regulate these updates by keeping the new policy near a previous one. The paper examines how to choose this reference more flexibly, particularly when the immediately preceding policy performs poorly and may be an unhelpful guide for the next update.

Memory-Constrained Policy Optimization, or MCPO, uses two trust regions. One constrains proximity to the single old policy, as in earlier approaches. The other uses a virtual policy that represents a broader range of past policies. A mechanism constructs this virtual policy automatically from a memory buffer, allowing the method to select appropriate trust regions dynamically during optimization.

The authors evaluate MCPO on robotic locomotion, navigation with sparse rewards, and Atari games. Across these environments, it consistently delivers competitive performance against recent on-policy constrained policy-gradient methods. The stated result supports using policy history to regulate learning across different tasks. Its distinctive contribution is making past policies an active part of update constraints, with potential benefit when the most recent policy performs poorly.
summary.tldr: MCPO constrains policy updates using both the previous policy and an automatically constructed reference drawn from policy history.

title: Learning to Constrain Policy Optimization with Virtual Trust Region

abstract: We study the problem of list-decodable sparse mean estimation. Specifically, for a parameter $\alpha \in (0, 1/2)$, we are given $m$ points in $\mathbb{R}^n$, $\lfloor \alpha m \rfloor$ of which are i.i.d. samples from a distribution $D$ with unknown $k$-sparse mean $\mu$. No assumptions are made on the remaining points, which form the majority of the dataset. The goal is to return a small list of candidates containing a vector $\hat \mu$ such that $\|\hat \mu - \mu\|_2$ is small. Prior work had studied the problem of list-decodable mean estimation in the dense setting. In this work, we develop a novel, conceptually simpler technique for list-decodable mean estimation. As the main application of our approach, we provide the first sample and computationally efficient algorithm for list-decodable sparse mean estimation. In particular, for distributions with ``certifiably bounded'' $t$-th moments in $k$-sparse directions and sufficiently light tails, our algorithm achieves error of $(1/\alpha)^{O(1/t)}$ with sample complexity $m = (k\log(n))^{O(t)}/\alpha$ and running time $\mathrm{poly}(mn^t)$. For the special case of Gaussian inliers, our algorithm achieves the optimal error guarantee $\Theta (\sqrt{\log(1/\alpha)})$ with quasi-polynomial complexity. We complement our upper bounds with nearly-matching statistical query and low-degree polynomial testing lower bounds.

paragraphs: The paper considers estimating a sparse mean when reliable observations are a minority of the dataset. An unknown fraction alpha, below one half, consists of independent samples from a distribution with a k-sparse mean; the remaining points are unrestricted. The goal is a short list of candidate means containing at least one accurate estimate.

The authors introduce a conceptually simpler filtering technique and use it to obtain the first sample- and computationally efficient algorithm for this sparse setting. Its guarantees require certifiably bounded moments in sparse directions and sufficiently light tails. Under those assumptions, the sample requirement depends on sparsity and the logarithm of ambient dimension, with additional dependence on moment order and the reliable fraction.

For Gaussian inliers, the algorithm achieves optimal error proportional to the square root of log(1/alpha), with quasi-polynomial complexity. Nearly matching lower bounds in statistical query and low-degree polynomial testing frameworks complement the upper bounds. These results clarify both achievable estimation accuracy and computational barriers when arbitrary contamination makes up most of the data.
summary.tldr: A new filtering technique estimates sparse means from minority inliers by returning a short candidate list with conditional accuracy guarantees.

title: List-Decodable Sparse Mean Estimation via Difference-of-Pairs Filtering

abstract: We study to what extent may stochastic gradient descent (SGD) be understood as a ``conventional'' learning rule that achieves generalization performance by obtaining a good fit to training data. We consider the fundamental stochastic convex optimization framework, where (one pass, $\textit{without}$-replacement) SGD is classically known to minimize the population risk at rate $O(1/\sqrt n)$, and prove that, surprisingly, there exist problem instances where the SGD solution exhibits both empirical risk and generalization gap of $\Omega(1)$. Consequently, it turns out that SGD is not algorithmically stable in $\textit{any}$ sense, and its generalization ability cannot be explained by uniform convergence or any other currently known generalization bound technique for that matter (other than that of its classical analysis). We then continue to analyze the closely related $\textit{with}$-replacement SGD, for which we show that an analogous phenomenon does not occur and prove that its population risk does in fact converge at the optimal rate. Finally, we interpret our main results in the context of without-replacement SGD for finite-sum convex optimization problems, and derive upper and lower bounds for the multi-epoch regime that significantly improve upon previously known results.
