paragraphs: A familiar explanation of learning is that a model fits its training data and that this fit transfers to the broader population. This paper shows why that explanation can fail for stochastic gradient descent in stochastic convex optimization. The central setting is one pass through the data without replacement, so each training example is used once.

Although this procedure has a classical population-risk convergence rate of O(1/sqrt(n)), the authors construct problems where empirical risk and the generalization gap remain bounded away from zero. Thus, good population performance can coexist with persistent underfitting. They show that familiar explanations based on algorithmic stability or uniform convergence do not account for this behavior; the classical analysis still does.

The sampling rule matters. For SGD with replacement, the authors show that the analogous phenomenon does not occur and establish optimal population-risk convergence. They also extend the implications to finite-sum convex optimization, deriving improved upper and lower bounds for multiple epochs. The results distinguish successful population optimization from the usual story of learning through a good training fit.
summary.tldr: One-pass SGD without replacement can achieve good population performance while retaining substantial training error and a nonvanishing generalization gap.

title: Benign Underfitting of Stochastic Gradient Descent

abstract: Increasing concerns about disparate effects of AI have motivated a great deal of work on fair machine learning. Existing works mainly focus on independence- and separation-based measures (e.g., demographic parity, equality of opportunity, equalized odds), while sufficiency-based measures such as predictive parity are much less studied. This paper considers predictive parity, which requires equalizing the probability of success given a positive prediction among different protected groups. We prove that, if the overall performances of different groups vary only moderately, all fair Bayes-optimal classifiers under predictive parity are group-wise thresholding rules. Perhaps surprisingly, this may not hold if group performance levels vary widely; in this case, we find that predictive parity among protected groups may lead to within-group unfairness. We then propose an algorithm we call FairBayes-DPP, aiming to ensure predictive parity when our condition is satisfied. FairBayes-DPP is an adaptive thresholding algorithm that aims to achieve predictive parity, while also seeking to maximize test accuracy. We provide supporting experiments conducted on synthetic and empirical data.

paragraphs: The paper examines predictive parity, a fairness requirement under which a positive prediction has the same probability of being correct across protected groups. It asks what the most accurate classifiers satisfying this requirement look like. This focuses on the reliability of positive predictions, a different fairness question from equalizing how frequently groups receive them.

The main theorem is conditional: when overall group performance levels differ only moderately, every fair Bayes-optimal classifier takes the form of group-specific threshold rules. When performance differs widely, that conclusion may fail. The authors also find that enforcing parity between groups can then produce unfairness within a group, revealing a tension that group-level measurements alone may obscure.

The proposed FairBayes-DPP algorithm adaptively selects thresholds, seeking predictive parity and high test accuracy when the stated condition holds. Experiments on synthetic and empirical data support the approach. The paper's contribution is both constructive and cautionary: it identifies a setting where thresholding has a theoretical foundation and a setting where that structure need not apply.
summary.tldr: Under a condition on group performance differences, optimal predictive-parity classifiers use group-specific thresholds, motivating FairBayes-DPP.

title: Fair Bayes-Optimal Classifiers Under Predictive Parity

abstract: Providing a timely intervention before the onset of a critical event, such as a system failure, is of importance in many industrial settings. Before the onset of the critical event, systems typically exhibit behavioral changes which often manifest as stochastic co-variate observations which may be leveraged to trigger intervention. In this paper, for the first time, we formulate the problem of finding an optimally timed intervention (OTI) policy as minimizing the expected residual time to event, subject to a constraint on the probability of missing the event. Existing machine learning approaches to intervention on critical events focus on predicting event occurrence within a pre-defined window (a classification problem) or predicting time-to-event (a regression problem). Interventions are then triggered by setting model thresholds. These are heuristic-driven, lacking guarantees regarding optimality. To model the evolution of system behavior, we introduce the concept of a hazard rate process. We show that the OTI problem is equivalent to an optimal stopping problem on the associated hazard rate process. This key link has not been explored in literature. Under Markovian assumptions on the hazard rate process, we show that an OTI policy at any time can be analytically determined from the conditional hazard rate function at that time. Further, we show that our theory includes, as a special case, the important class of neural hazard rate processes generated by recurrent neural networks (RNNs). To model such processes, we propose a dynamic deep recurrent survival analysis (DDRSA) architecture, introducing an RNN encoder into the static DRSA setting. Finally, we demonstrate RNN-based OTI policies with experiments and show that they outperform popular intervention methods

paragraphs: Predicting a critical event does not by itself determine when an intervention should occur. This paper formulates timing directly: minimize the expected time remaining until the event when intervention happens, subject to a bound on the probability of missing it. That objective captures a preference for intervening close to the event while controlling the risk of waiting too long.

The authors introduce a hazard rate process to describe how event risk evolves with observations of system behavior. They show that the intervention problem is equivalent to an optimal stopping problem on this process. Under Markovian assumptions, the optimal policy at a given time can be determined analytically from the conditional hazard rate function.

The theory also covers a class of neural hazard processes generated by recurrent networks. To model these, the authors introduce dynamic deep recurrent survival analysis, adding a recurrent encoder to the static DRSA setting. Experiments show that the resulting recurrent-network intervention policies outperform popular intervention methods. The contribution connects risk modeling to an explicit timing objective and derives the decision rule under the stated assumptions.
summary.tldr: The paper derives intervention timing as an optimal stopping problem and learns recurrent risk models to support the resulting policies.

title: When to Intervene: Learning Optimal Intervention Policies for Critical Events

abstract: Covering option discovery has been developed to improve the exploration of RL in single-agent scenarios with sparse reward signals, through connecting the most distant states in the embedding space provided by the Fiedler vector of the state transition graph. Given that joint state space grows exponentially with the number of agents in multi-agent systems, existing researches still relying on single-agent option discovery either become prohibitive or fail to directly discover joint options that improve the connectivity of the joint state space. In this paper, we show how to directly compute multi-agent options with collaborative exploratory behaviors while still enjoying the ease of decomposition. Our key idea is to approximate the joint state space as a Kronecker graph, based on which we can directly estimate its Fiedler vector using the Laplacian spectrum of individual agents' transition graphs. Further, considering that directly computing the Laplacian spectrum is intractable for tasks with infinite-scale state spaces, we further propose a deep learning extension of our method by estimating eigenfunctions through NN-based representation learning techniques. The evaluation on multi-agent tasks built with simulators like Mujoco, shows that the proposed algorithm can successfully identify multi-agent options, and significantly outperforms the state-of-the-art. Codes are available at: https://github.itap.purdue.edu/Clan-labs/Scalable_MAOD_via_KP.

paragraphs: Covering options support exploration by connecting distant states identified through the structure of a state-transition graph. Extending this idea to multiple agents is difficult because the joint state space grows exponentially with the number of agents. Applying single-agent discovery methods can become prohibitively expensive or fail to discover genuinely collaborative exploration behaviors.

The authors approximate the joint state space using a Kronecker graph. This allows them to estimate its Fiedler vector, which supplies the relevant embedding, from the Laplacian spectra of individual agents' transition graphs. The approach therefore discovers joint options while retaining a decomposition into information about individual agents.

For settings with infinite-scale state spaces, directly computing those spectra is also intractable. The paper adds a deep-learning extension that estimates eigenfunctions using neural representations. Evaluations on multi-agent tasks built with simulators including MuJoCo show successful discovery of multi-agent options and significant improvements over the compared state of the art. The main contribution is a scalable approximation that preserves the goal of coordinated exploration.
summary.tldr: A Kronecker-graph approximation enables collaborative exploration-option discovery from individual agents' transition structures.

title: Scalable Multi-agent Covering Option Discovery based on Kronecker Graphs

abstract: We address the problem of learning a risk-sensitive policy based on the CVaR risk measure using distributional reinforcement learning. In particular, we show that the standard action-selection strategy when applying the distributional Bellman optimality operator can result in convergence to neither the dynamic, Markovian CVaR nor the static, non-Markovian CVaR. We propose modifications to the existing algorithms that include a new distributional Bellman operator and show that the proposed strategy greatly expands the utility of distributional RL in learning and representing CVaR-optimized policies. Our proposed approach is a simple extension of standard distributional RL algorithms and can therefore take advantage of many of the recent advances in deep RL. On both synthetic and real data, we empirically show that our proposed algorithm is able to learn better CVaR-optimized policies.

paragraphs: This paper studies how distributional reinforcement learning can learn policies optimized for the CVaR risk measure. Modeling a distribution of outcomes provides information relevant to risk-sensitive decisions, but the authors show that the usual action-selection procedure does not necessarily optimize the intended CVaR objective. Representing outcome uncertainty and choosing actions consistently with a risk objective are separate challenges.

Specifically, standard action selection with the distributional Bellman optimality operator can converge to neither dynamic, Markovian CVaR nor static, non-Markovian CVaR. The authors respond by modifying existing algorithms, including introducing a new distributional Bellman operator. These changes expand the ability of distributional methods to learn and represent CVaR-optimized policies.

The approach is a simple extension of standard distributional reinforcement learning algorithms, allowing it to benefit from advances in deep reinforcement learning. Experiments on synthetic and real data show better CVaR-optimized policies. The findings establish both a failure mode in conventional action selection and an empirically supported way to address it.
summary.tldr: Modified distributional reinforcement learning updates address a failure of standard action selection to optimize CVaR risk objectives.

title: Distributional Reinforcement Learning for Risk-Sensitive Policies

abstract: Temporal graph networks (TGNs) have gained prominence as models for embedding dynamic interactions, but little is known about their theoretical underpinnings. We establish fundamental results about the representational power and limits of the two main categories of TGNs: those that aggregate temporal walks (WA-TGNs), and those that augment local message passing with recurrent memory modules (MP-TGNs). Specifically, novel constructions reveal the inadequacy of MP-TGNs and WA-TGNs, proving that neither category subsumes the other. We extend the 1-WL (Weisfeiler-Leman) test to temporal graphs, and show that the most powerful MP-TGNs should use injective updates, as in this case they become as expressive as the temporal WL. Also, we show that sufficiently deep MP-TGNs cannot benefit from memory, and MP/WA-TGNs fail to compute graph properties such as girth. These theoretical insights lead us to PINT --- a novel architecture that leverages injective temporal message passing and relative positional features. Importantly, PINT is provably more expressive than both MP-TGNs and WA-TGNs. PINT significantly outperforms existing TGNs on several real-world benchmarks.

paragraphs: Temporal graph networks represent interactions that change over time. This paper compares two major approaches: aggregating temporal walks and combining local message passing with recurrent memory. Its theoretical constructions show that neither family contains the other's representational abilities. Each can distinguish some situations that the other cannot, so neither provides a universally stronger foundation.

The authors extend the Weisfeiler–Leman graph test to temporal graphs and connect it to message-passing networks. With injective updates, which preserve distinctions between different inputs, these networks reach the expressive power of the temporal test. The analysis also shows that sufficiently deep message-passing networks gain no additional expressiveness from memory, and that both studied families fail to compute properties such as girth.

These findings motivate PINT, an architecture combining injective temporal message passing with relative positional features. The paper proves that PINT is more expressive than both original families and reports significant improvements over existing temporal graph networks on several real-world benchmarks. The work thus turns representational limits into concrete architectural choices supported by both proofs and empirical results.
summary.tldr: PINT combines injective temporal message passing and relative positions to exceed the proven expressiveness of two major temporal graph network families.

title: Provably expressive temporal graph networks

abstract: Existing statistical learning guarantees for general kernel regressors often yield loose bounds when used with finite-rank kernels. Yet, finite-rank kernels naturally appear in a number of machine learning problems, e.g. when fine-tuning a pre-trained deep neural network's last layer to adapt it to a novel task when performing transfer learning. We address this gap for finite-rank kernel ridge regression (KRR) by deriving sharp non-asymptotic upper and lower bounds for the KRR test error of any finite-rank KRR. Our bounds are tighter than previously derived bounds on finite-rank KRR and, unlike comparable results, they also remain valid for any regularization parameters.
originalAbstract: Existing statistical learning guarantees for general kernel regressors often yield loose bounds when used with finite-rank kernels. Yet, finite-rank kernels naturally appear in a number of machine learning problems, e.g. when fine-tuning a pre-trained deep neural network's last layer to adapt it to a novel task when performing transfer learning. We address this gap for finite-rank kernel ridge regression (KRR) by deriving sharp non-asymptotic upper and lower bounds for the KRR test error of any finite-rank KRR. Our bounds are tighter than previously derived bounds on finite-rank KRR and, unlike comparable results, they also remain valid for any regularization parameters.

paragraphs: This paper studies how accurately finite-rank kernel ridge regression predicts on unseen data. Existing guarantees for more general kernel regression can give overly loose bounds in this setting. That leaves a gap between having a theoretical guarantee and having one that usefully describes the particular model being trained.

The authors address this gap by deriving both upper and lower bounds on test error specifically for finite-rank kernel ridge regression. Together, these bounds constrain the error from both directions. The results are non-asymptotic, meaning they apply at finite sample sizes rather than only describing behavior as the amount of training data grows indefinitely.

The stated bounds improve on earlier finite-rank results and remain valid for any regularization parameter. This matters because the analysis continues to apply across choices of regularization strength. The setting also connects to transfer learning: adapting the last layer of a pretrained neural network is one situation where finite-rank kernels naturally arise. The contribution is therefore a sharper account of prediction error for a model class with practical relevance.
summary.tldr: The paper derives tighter finite-sample bounds on finite-rank kernel ridge regression test error that remain valid across all regularization parameters.

title: A Theoretical Analysis of the Test Error of Finite-Rank Kernel Ridge Regression

abstract: Due to the high price and heavy energy consumption of GPUs, deploying deep models on IoT devices such as microcontrollers makes significant contributions for ecological AI. Conventional methods successfully enable convolutional neural network inference of high resolution images on microcontrollers, while the framework for vision transformers that achieve the state-of-the-art performance in many vision applications still remains unexplored. In this paper, we propose a hardware-algorithm co-optimizations method called MCUFormer to deploy vision transformers on microcontrollers with extremely limited memory, where we jointly design transformer architecture and construct the inference operator library to fit the memory resource constraint. More specifically, we generalize the one-shot network architecture search (NAS) to discover the optimal architecture with highest task performance given the memory budget from the microcontrollers, where we enlarge the existing search space of vision transformers by considering the low-rank decomposition dimensions and patch resolution for memory reduction. For the construction of the inference operator library of vision transformers, we schedule the memory buffer during inference through operator integration, patch embedding decomposition, and token overwriting, allowing the memory buffer to be fully utilized to adapt to the forward pass of the vision transformer. Experimental results demonstrate that our MCUFormer achieves 73.62\% top-1 accuracy on ImageNet for image classification with 320KB memory on STM32F746 microcontroller. Code is available at https://github.com/liangyn22/MCUFormer.

paragraphs: MCUFormer addresses running vision Transformers on microcontrollers with extremely small memory budgets. The paper treats model architecture and inference implementation as a joint design problem. A network must fit the available memory, and the operations executing that network must use their temporary storage carefully enough for the forward pass to succeed.

The architecture component extends one-shot neural architecture search to optimize task performance subject to a device’s memory budget. Its search space includes low-rank decomposition dimensions and patch resolution, giving the search additional ways to reduce memory needs. The implementation component builds a Transformer operator library with explicit attention to buffer scheduling.

Operator integration, patch embedding decomposition, and token overwriting help reuse the available inference memory. Combining these choices, MCUFormer achieves a reported 73.62% ImageNet top-1 accuracy with 320 KB of memory on an STM32F746 microcontroller. This result demonstrates a concrete deployment under severe memory constraints and highlights why architecture selection and execution-level memory management need to be designed together.
summary.tldr: MCUFormer jointly optimizes Transformer architecture and memory use, reporting 73.62% ImageNet top-1 accuracy with 320 KB on a microcontroller.

title: MCUFormer: Deploying Vision Tranformers on Microcontrollers with Limited Memory

abstract: Research on adversarial robustness is primarily focused on image and text data. Yet, many scenarios in which lack of robustness can result in serious risks, such as fraud detection, medical diagnosis, or recommender systems often do not rely on images or text but instead on tabular data. Adversarial robustness in tabular data poses two serious challenges. First, tabular datasets often contain categorical features, and therefore cannot be tackled directly with existing optimization procedures. Second, in the tabular domain, algorithms that are not based on deep networks are widely used and offer great performance, but algorithms to enhance robustness are tailored to neural networks (e.g. adversarial training).In this paper, we tackle both challenges. We present a method that allows us to train adversarially robust deep networks for tabular data and to transfer this robustness to other classifiers via universal robust embeddings tailored to categorical data. These embeddings, created using a bilevel alternating minimization framework, can be transferred to boosted trees or random forests making them robust without the need for adversarial training while preserving their high accuracy on tabular data. We show that our methods outperform existing techniques within a practical threat model suitable for tabular data.

paragraphs: Adversarial robustness for tabular data presents challenges that differ from those emphasized in image and text research. Categorical features do not directly fit existing optimization procedures. Meanwhile, effective tabular classifiers such as boosted trees and random forests cannot directly use robustness methods designed specifically for neural networks.

The paper addresses both issues with universal robust embeddings tailored to categorical data. It first supports adversarially robust deep-network training, then transfers robustness through the learned embeddings to other classifiers. The embeddings are produced using a bilevel alternating minimization framework, connecting representation learning with the robustness objective.

The authors show that boosted trees and random forests can use these embeddings to gain robustness without undergoing adversarial training themselves, while preserving high tabular-data accuracy. They also report better results than existing techniques within a practical threat model suited to tabular data. The contribution is a transferable representation: robustness learned through a neural approach can benefit other classifier families under the evaluated threat model.
summary.tldr: Robust categorical embeddings transfer adversarial robustness from deep-network training to boosted trees and random forests while preserving high accuracy.

title: Transferable Adversarial Robustness for Categorical Data via Universal Robust Embeddings

abstract: Self-play is a technique for machine learning in multi-agent systems where a learning algorithm learns by interacting with copies of itself. Self-play is useful for generating large quantities of data for learning, but has the drawback that the agents the learner will face post-training may have dramatically different behavior than the learner came to expect by interacting with itself. For the special case of two-player constant-sum games, self-play that reaches Nash equilibrium is guaranteed to produce strategies that perform well against any post-training opponent; however, no such guarantee exists for multiplayer games. We show that in games that approximately decompose into a set of two-player constant-sum games (called constant-sum polymatrix games) where global $\epsilon$-Nash equilibria are boundedly far from Nash equilibria in each subgame (called subgame stability), any no-external-regret algorithm that learns by self-play will produce a strategy with bounded vulnerability. For the first time, our results identify a structural property of multiplayer games that enable performance guarantees for the strategies produced by a broad class of self-play algorithms. We demonstrate our findings through experiments on Leduc poker.

Self-play is useful for generating large quantities of data for learning, but has the drawback that the agents the learner will face post-training may have dramatically different behavior than the learner came to expect by interacting with itself. For the special case of two-player constant-sum games, self-play that reaches Nash equilibrium is guaranteed to produce strategies that perform well against any post-training opponent; however, no such guarantee exists for multiplayer games. We show that in games that approximately decompose into a set of two-player constant-sum games (called constant-sum polymatrix games) where global $\epsilon$-Nash equilibria are boundedly far from Nash equilibria in each subgame (called subgame stability), any no-external-regret algorithm that learns by self-play will produce a strategy with bounded vulnerability. For the first time, our results identify a structural property of multiplayer games that enable performance guarantees for the strategies produced by a broad class of self-play algorithms. We demonstrate our findings through experiments on Leduc poker.

paragraphs: Self-play generates training experience by having a learner interact with copies of itself. The resulting strategy may encounter very different opponents after training. Two-player constant-sum games offer equilibrium-based protection against this mismatch, but multiplayer games do not generally inherit that guarantee. This paper identifies structural conditions under which a broader guarantee becomes possible.

The first condition is that the multiplayer game approximately decomposes into pairwise constant-sum games. The second, called subgame stability, requires approximate equilibria of the overall game to remain boundedly close to equilibria in the pairwise subgames. Together, these conditions connect whole-game behavior to the more controlled structure of two-player interactions.

For games satisfying those conditions, self-play with any no-external-regret algorithm produces strategies with bounded vulnerability. This bounds exposure to different opponents after training rather than asserting universal protection for multiplayer self-play. Experiments on Leduc poker demonstrate the findings. The contribution is a sufficient structural basis for guarantees that applies to a broad algorithm class when the game has the required properties.
summary.tldr: Approximate constant-sum pairwise structure and subgame stability give no-external-regret self-play bounded vulnerability in certain multiplayer games.

title: Guarantees for Self-Play in Multiplayer Games via Polymatrix Decomposability

abstract: Intermediate-level attacks that attempt to perturb feature representations following an adversarial direction drastically have shown favorable performance in crafting transferable adversarial examples. Existing methods in this category are normally formulated with two separate stages, where a directional guide is required to be determined at first and the scalar projection of the intermediate-level perturbation onto the directional guide is enlarged thereafter. The obtained perturbation deviates from the guide inevitably in the feature space, and it is revealed in this paper that such a deviation may lead to sub-optimal attack. To address this issue, we develop a novel intermediate-level method that crafts adversarial examples within a single stage of optimization. In particular, the proposed method, named intermediate-level perturbation decay (ILPD), encourages the intermediate-level perturbation to be in an effective adversarial direction and to possess a great magnitude simultaneously. In-depth discussion verifies the effectiveness of our method. Experimental results show that it outperforms state-of-the-arts by large margins in attacking various victim models on ImageNet (+10.07% on average) and CIFAR-10 (+3.88% on average). Our code is at https://github.com/qizhangli/ILPD-attack.

paragraphs: Transferable adversarial examples are altered inputs that can fool models beyond the one used to construct them. Intermediate-level attacks pursue this by changing internal feature representations. Existing approaches often first choose an adversarial direction and then increase the feature perturbation’s projection onto that direction, treating guidance and perturbation growth as separate stages.

The paper identifies a weakness in that separation: the actual feature change inevitably deviates from the guide, and this deviation may produce a suboptimal attack. Intermediate-level Perturbation Decay, or ILPD, instead uses one optimization stage. It simultaneously encourages the perturbation to point in an effective adversarial direction and to have a large magnitude, addressing direction and strength together.

Experiments across various victim models report average improvements of 10.07% on ImageNet and 3.88% on CIFAR-10 over state-of-the-art approaches. These findings support the proposed joint treatment of direction and magnitude for improving attack transferability. The explanation concerns the behavior of intermediate feature perturbations, connecting a geometric weakness in prior methods to the observed empirical gains.
summary.tldr: ILPD jointly optimizes the direction and magnitude of intermediate feature perturbations to improve adversarial transferability.

title: Improving Adversarial Transferability via Intermediate-level Perturbation Decay

abstract: Synthetic image datasets offer unmatched advantages for designing and evaluating deep neural networks: they make it possible to (i) render as many data samples as needed, (ii) precisely control each scene and yield granular ground truth labels (and captions), (iii) precisely control distribution shifts between training and testing to isolate variables of interest for sound experimentation.Despite such promise, the use of synthetic image data is still limited -- and often played down -- mainly due to their lack of realism. Most works therefore rely on datasets of real images, which have often been scraped from public images on the internet, and may have issues with regards to privacy, bias, and copyright, while offering little control over how objects precisely appear.In this work, we present a path to democratize the use of photorealistic synthetic data: we develop a new generation of interactive environments for representation learning research, that offer both controllability and realism. We use the Unreal Engine, a powerful game engine well known in the entertainment industry, to produce PUG (Photorealistic Unreal Graphics) environments and datasets for representation learning. Using PUG for evaluation and fine-tuning, we demonstrate the potential of PUG to both enable more rigorous evaluations and to improve model training.

paragraphs: Synthetic images let researchers choose what appears in a scene and precisely control differences between training and testing data. They can also provide detailed labels and captions. However, insufficient realism has limited their use in representation learning. PUG addresses this tension by combining scene control with photorealistic rendering.

The authors build interactive environments and datasets using Unreal Engine. These environments support controlled image generation, giving researchers a way to vary scene content while retaining knowledge of how each image was produced. That control is valuable for isolating a variable of interest in an evaluation, something that collections of existing real images offer much less directly.

The paper uses PUG for both evaluation and model fine-tuning, demonstrating its potential to improve experimental rigor and training. Its contribution includes the environments as a research tool, not just a fixed image collection. By making realistic scenes controllable, PUG supports experiments in which changes in model behavior can be examined alongside deliberately chosen changes in the input data.
summary.tldr: PUG uses Unreal Engine to create realistic, controllable synthetic images for more rigorous evaluation and improved model training.

title: PUG: Photorealistic and Semantically Controllable Synthetic Data for Representation Learning

abstract: Decision trees are a well-established tool in machine learning for classification and regression tasks. In this paper, we introduce a novel non-parametric Bayesian model that uses variational inference to approximate a posterior distribution over the space of stochastic decision trees. We evaluate the model's performance on 18 datasets and demonstrate its competitiveness with other state-of-the-art methods in regression tasks. We also explore its application to causal inference problems. We provide a fully vectorized implementation of our algorithm in PyTorch.
originalAbstract: Decision trees are a well-established tool in machine learning for classification and regression tasks. In this paper, we introduce a novel non-parametric Bayesian model that uses variational inference to approximate a posterior distribution over the space of stochastic decision trees. We evaluate the model's performance on 18 datasets and demonstrate its competitiveness with other state-of-the-art methods in regression tasks. We also explore its application to causal inference problems. We provide a fully vectorized implementation of our algorithm in PyTorch.

paragraphs: VaRT develops a Bayesian approach to regression with decision trees. Instead of representing the result only as one selected tree, the model approximates a posterior distribution over stochastic trees. This makes a collection of possible tree-based explanations the object of inference, bringing uncertainty over the trees into the modeling framework.

The model is non-parametric and uses variational inference to approximate that posterior. The central computational task is therefore to find an approximation to the distribution over trees supported by the data. This combines the familiar tree approach to prediction with a method for making Bayesian inference over that space computationally manageable.

The authors evaluate regression performance on 18 datasets and report competitiveness with state-of-the-art methods. They also explore causal inference applications and provide a fully vectorized PyTorch implementation. The stated evidence supports VaRT as a competitive regression approach, with causal inference presented as an additional application explored by the paper rather than a separately established claim of superiority.
summary.tldr: VaRT uses variational Bayesian inference over stochastic decision trees and reports competitive regression performance across 18 datasets.

title: VaRT: Variational Regression Trees

abstract: Webly supervised learning has attracted increasing attention for its effectiveness in exploring publicly accessible data at scale without manual annotation. However, most existing methods of learning with web datasets are faced with challenges from label noise, and they have limited assumptions on clean samples under various noise. For instance, web images retrieved with queries of ”tiger cat“ (a cat species) and ”drumstick“ (a musical instrument) are almost dominated by images of tigers and chickens, which exacerbates the challenge of fine-grained visual concept learning. In this case, exploiting both web images and their associated texts is a requisite solution to combat real-world noise. In this paper, we propose Cross-modality Aligned Prototypes (CAPro), a unified prototypical contrastive learning framework to learn visual representations with correct semantics. For one thing, we leverage textual prototypes, which stem from the distinct concept definition of classes, to select clean images by text matching and thus disambiguate the formation of visual prototypes. For another, to handle missing and mismatched noisy texts, we resort to the visual feature space to complete and enhance individual texts and thereafter improve text matching. Such semantically aligned visual prototypes are further polished up with high-quality samples, and engaged in both cluster regularization and noise removal. Besides, we propose collective bootstrapping to encourage smoother and wiser label reference from appearance-similar instances in a manner of dictionary look-up. Extensive experiments on WebVision1k and NUS-WIDE (Web) demonstrate that CAPro well handles realistic noise under both single-label and multi-label scenarios. CAPro achieves new state-of-the-art performance and exhibits robustness to open-set recognition. Codes are available at https://github.com/yuleiqin/capro.

paragraphs: Web images provide abundant training data, but their labels and accompanying text can be misleading. Ambiguous queries may retrieve images dominated by the wrong concept, making fine-grained categories especially difficult to learn. CAPro addresses this problem by using images and text together to build class representatives, or prototypes, whose meaning matches the intended category.

Textual prototypes come from class definitions and help identify clean images through text matching. Those images guide the visual prototypes. Because accompanying text may be missing or mismatched, visual features also help complete and improve the text information. High-quality samples further refine the visual prototypes, which support clustering and noise removal. A collective bootstrapping mechanism draws label guidance from visually similar examples.

Experiments on WebVision1k and NUS-WIDE (Web) report state-of-the-art performance under realistic noise in both single-label and multi-label settings, alongside robustness in open-set recognition. The central finding is that aligning category meaning across text and images helps the evaluated models learn useful visual concepts even when web supervision is unreliable.
summary.tldr: CAPro aligns text and image prototypes to learn visual categories from web data with noisy labels and unreliable accompanying text.

title: CAPro: Webly Supervised Learning with Cross-modality Aligned Prototypes

abstract: Machine Learning as a Service (MLaaS) APIs provide ready-to-use and high-utility encoders that generate vector representations for given inputs. Since these encoders are very costly to train, they become lucrative targets for model stealing attacks during which an adversary leverages query access to the API to replicate the encoder locally at a fraction of the original training costs. We propose *Bucks for Buckets (B4B)*, the first *active defense* that prevents stealing while the attack is happening without degrading representation quality for legitimate API users. Our defense relies on the observation that the representations returned to adversaries who try to steal the encoder's functionality cover a significantly larger fraction of the embedding space than representations of legitimate users who utilize the encoder to solve a particular downstream task. B4B leverages this to adaptively adjust the utility of the returned representations according to a user's coverage of the embedding space. To prevent adaptive adversaries from eluding our defense by simply creating multiple user accounts (sybils), B4B also individually transforms each user's representations. This prevents the adversary from directly aggregating representations over multiple accounts to create their stolen encoder copy. Our active defense opens a new path towards securely sharing and democratizing encoders over public APIs.

paragraphs: Encoder APIs turn inputs into vector representations that users can reuse for machine learning tasks. Because the underlying encoders are expensive to train, an attacker may collect API outputs to build a cheaper local copy. Bucks for Buckets, or B4B, introduces an active defense that changes what the API returns while a stealing attempt is underway.

The defense rests on an observed difference in usage. Attackers trying to reproduce broad encoder functionality cover substantially more of the embedding space than legitimate users solving a particular downstream task. B4B tracks that coverage and adaptively adjusts the usefulness of returned representations. The authors present this as a way to interfere with stealing while preserving representation quality for legitimate use.

B4B also addresses attackers who spread queries across multiple accounts. It applies a different transformation to each user's representations, preventing straightforward pooling of outputs from those accounts into one training collection. Together, coverage-sensitive responses and account-specific transformations target both broad collection and direct cross-account aggregation, making the API itself part of the proposed defense.
summary.tldr: B4B actively defends encoder APIs by adjusting outputs according to embedding-space coverage and transforming representations separately for each user.

title: Bucks for Buckets (B4B): Active Defenses Against Stealing Encoders

abstract: Combining the signed distance function (SDF) and differentiable volume rendering has emerged as a powerful paradigm for surface reconstruction from multi-view images without 3D supervision. However, current methods are impeded by requiring long-time per-scene optimizations and cannot generalize to new scenes. In this paper, we present GenS, an end-to-end generalizable neural surface reconstruction model. Unlike coordinate-based methods that train a separate network for each scene, we construct a generalized multi-scale volume to directly encode all scenes. Compared with existing solutions, our representation is more powerful, which can recover high-frequency details while maintaining global smoothness. Meanwhile, we introduce a multi-scale feature-metric consistency to impose the multi-view consistency in a more discriminative multi-scale feature space, which is robust to the failures of the photometric consistency. And the learnable feature can be self-enhanced to continuously improve the matching accuracy and mitigate aggregation ambiguity. Furthermore, we design a view contrast loss to force the model to be robust to those regions covered by few viewpoints through distilling the geometric prior from dense input to sparse input. Extensive experiments on popular benchmarks show that our model can generalize well to new scenes and outperform existing state-of-the-art methods even those employing ground-truth depth supervision. Code will be available at https://github.com/prstrive/GenS.

paragraphs: Reconstructing surfaces from multiple images can combine signed distance functions with differentiable rendering, avoiding direct three-dimensional supervision. However, existing approaches often require lengthy optimization for each scene. GenS addresses this bottleneck with an end-to-end model designed to transfer to new scenes rather than train a separate network for each one.

Its representation uses a generalized volume at multiple scales to encode scenes, aiming to retain fine detail alongside globally smooth surfaces. A multi-scale feature consistency objective compares views in a learned feature space. This helps when direct photometric agreement fails, while self-enhancement of the features improves matching and reduces ambiguity when information is aggregated.

GenS also uses a view contrast loss that transfers geometric knowledge from dense inputs to sparse inputs. This targets regions visible from only a few viewpoints. Benchmark experiments show generalization to new scenes and performance exceeding the compared leading methods, including methods trained with ground-truth depth. The findings support combining a transferable representation with explicit mechanisms for matching views and handling sparse coverage.
summary.tldr: GenS learns transferable multi-scale scene representations and view-consistency objectives for detailed surface reconstruction on new scenes.

title: GenS: Generalizable Neural Surface Reconstruction from Multi-View Images

abstract: We show that many definitions of stability found in the learning theory literature are equivalent to one another. We distinguish between two families of definitions of stability: distribution-dependent and distribution-independent Bayesian stability. Within each family, we establish equivalences between various definitions, encompassing approximate differential privacy, pure differential privacy, replicability, global stability, perfect generalization, TV stability, mutual information stability, KL-divergence stability, and Rényi-divergence stability. Along the way, we prove boosting results that enable the amplification of the stability of a learning rule. This work is a step towards a more systematic taxonomy of stability notions in learning theory, which can promote clarity and an improved understanding of an array of stability concepts that have emerged in recent years.

We distinguish between two families of definitions of stability: distribution-dependent and distribution-independent Bayesian stability. Within each family, we establish equivalences between various definitions, encompassing approximate differential privacy, pure differential privacy, replicability, global stability, perfect generalization, TV stability, mutual information stability, KL-divergence stability, and Rényi-divergence stability. paragraphs: Learning theory contains many definitions of stability, making it difficult to see which capture distinct requirements and which express related guarantees. This paper develops a more systematic organization by dividing Bayesian stability into two families: definitions that depend on the data distribution and definitions that are distribution-independent.

Within each family, the authors establish equivalences among a range of stability notions. These encompass pure and approximate differential privacy, replicability, global stability, perfect generalization, and stability measured through total variation, mutual information, KL divergence, and Rényi divergence. The family distinction is central to the result: the abstract states equivalences within each family, rather than identifying all definitions across both families.

The paper also proves boosting results that amplify the stability of a learning rule. This adds a constructive component to the taxonomy, showing how stability can be strengthened as well as how its definitions relate. The contribution is a set of mathematical connections that helps clarify a crowded conceptual landscape and supports a more unified understanding of guarantees previously described using different terminology.
summary.tldr: The paper establishes equivalences within two families of Bayesian stability notions and proves methods for amplifying stability.

title: The Bayesian Stability Zoo

abstract: In this paper, we consider how to construct best-of-both-worlds linear bandit algorithms that achieve nearly optimal performance for both stochastic and adversarial environments. For this purpose, we show that a natural approach referred to as exploration by optimization [Lattimore and Szepesvári, 2020] works well. Specifically, an algorithm constructed using this approach achieves $O(d \sqrt{ T \log{T}})$-regret in adversarial environments and $O(\frac{d^2 \log T}{\Delta_{\min}} )$-regret in stochastic environments. Symbols $d$, $T$ and $\Delta_{\min}$ here represent the dimensionality of the action set, the time horizon, and the minimum sub-optimality gap, respectively. We also show that this algorithm has even better theoretical guarantees for important special cases including the multi-armed bandit problem and multitask bandits.

Specifically, an algorithm constructed using this approach achieves $O(d \sqrt{ T \log{T}})$-regret in adversarial environments and $O(\frac{d^2 \log T}{\Delta_{\min}} )$-regret in stochastic environments. Symbols $d$, $T$ and $\Delta_{\min}$ here represent the dimensionality of the action set, the time horizon, and the minimum sub-optimality gap, respectively. paragraphs: A linear bandit algorithm repeatedly chooses actions while learning from limited feedback about their outcomes. This paper asks how one algorithm can perform well both when outcomes follow a stable statistical pattern and when the environment behaves adversarially. These settings place different demands on exploration, so the goal is a method with strong guarantees in both.

The authors construct an algorithm using exploration by optimization. Their analysis gives an adversarial regret bound of O(d sqrt(T log T)) and a stochastic bound of O(d² log T / Δ_min). Here, regret measures the accumulated performance shortfall, d is the action set's dimension, T is the number of rounds, and Δ_min is the smallest gap separating an inferior action from the best one.

The bounds show nearly optimal performance across the two environments: the stochastic guarantee grows logarithmically with time, while the adversarial guarantee accommodates a harder setting. The paper also derives stronger guarantees for special cases, including ordinary multi-armed bandits and multitask bandits.
summary.tldr: Exploration by optimization yields a linear bandit algorithm with nearly optimal regret guarantees in both stochastic and adversarial environments.

title: An Exploration-by-Optimization Approach to Best of Both Worlds in Linear Bandits

abstract: While direction of arrival (DOA) of sound events is generally estimated from multichannel audio data recorded in a microphone array, sound events usually derive from visually perceptible source objects, e.g., sounds of footsteps come from the feet of a walker. This paper proposes an audio-visual sound event localization and detection (SELD) task, which uses multichannel audio and video information to estimate the temporal activation and DOA of target sound events. Audio-visual SELD systems can detect and localize sound events using signals from a microphone array and audio-visual correspondence. We also introduce an audio-visual dataset, Sony-TAu Realistic Spatial Soundscapes 2023 (STARSS23), which consists of multichannel audio data recorded with a microphone array, video data, and spatiotemporal annotation of sound events. Sound scenes in STARSS23 are recorded with instructions, which guide recording participants to ensure adequate activity and occurrences of sound events. STARSS23 also serves human-annotated temporal activation labels and human-confirmed DOA labels, which are based on tracking results of a motion capture system. Our benchmark results demonstrate the benefits of using visual object positions in audio-visual SELD tasks. The data is available at https://zenodo.org/record/7880637.

paragraphs: Detecting a sound involves identifying when it occurs, while localization estimates the direction it comes from. This paper combines those tasks with visual information, motivated by the fact that sound-producing objects are often visible. Its audio-visual task uses microphone-array recordings and video to estimate both sound-event activity and direction of arrival.

The authors introduce STARSS23, a dataset containing multichannel audio, video, and sound-event annotations across space and time. Participants receive recording instructions intended to ensure adequate activity and occurrences of sound events. Event timing is annotated by people, while direction labels are based on motion-capture tracking and confirmed by people.

The benchmark results demonstrate benefits from using the visible positions of objects in audio-visual sound-event localization and detection. The contribution provides both a task formulation and data for studying it. By connecting sounds with visual source information, the work creates a concrete setting for evaluating whether the two forms of evidence together improve understanding of where and when sound events happen.
summary.tldr: STARSS23 pairs spatial audio, video, and verified event annotations to study sound detection and localization aided by visual object positions.

title: STARSS23: An Audio-Visual Dataset of Spatial Recordings of Real Scenes with Spatiotemporal Annotations of Sound Events

abstract: We introduce a novel reinforcement learning framework of LLM agents named AGILE (AGent that Interacts and Learns from Environments) designed to perform complex conversational tasks with users, leveraging LLMs, memory, tools, and interactions with experts. The agent possesses capabilities beyond conversation, including reflection, tool usage, and expert consultation. We formulate the construction of such an LLM agent as a reinforcement learning (RL) problem, in which the LLM serves as the policy model. We fine-tune the LLM using labeled data of actions and the PPO algorithm. We focus on question answering and release a dataset for agents called ProductQA, comprising challenging questions in online shopping. Our extensive experiments on ProductQA, MedMCQA and HotPotQA show that AGILE agents based on 7B and 13B LLMs trained with PPO can outperform GPT-4 agents. Our ablation study highlights the indispensability of memory, tools, consultation, reflection, and reinforcement learning in achieving the agent's strong performance. Datasets and code are available at https://github.com/bytarnish/AGILE.

paragraphs: AGILE treats a conversational agent as a system that learns how to act while answering questions. Its language model can draw on memory, use tools, reflect on its progress, and consult experts. The central problem is therefore broader than generating an answer: the agent must also decide which supporting actions will help.

The framework expresses these decisions as a reinforcement learning problem, with the language model serving as the policy that selects actions. Training uses labeled action data and the PPO reinforcement learning algorithm. This connects the model’s conversational abilities to learning how to use the resources available in its environment.

The authors introduce ProductQA, a dataset of challenging online shopping questions, and evaluate on it alongside MedMCQA and HotPotQA. In these experiments, PPO-trained agents using 7B and 13B models can outperform GPT-4 agents. Ablation experiments identify memory, tools, consultation, reflection, and reinforcement learning as essential contributors to the reported performance. The findings emphasize the importance of training the agent’s behavior as well as choosing its underlying language model.
summary.tldr: AGILE trains language models to coordinate memory, tools, reflection, and expert consultation through reinforcement learning.

title: AGILE: A Novel Reinforcement Learning Framework of LLM Agents

abstract: Recent advances in generative modeling with diffusion processes (DPs) enabled breakthroughs in image synthesis. Despite impressive image quality, these models have various prompt compliance problems, including low recall in generating multiple objects, difficulty in generating text in images, and meeting constraints like object locations and pose. For fine-grained editing and manipulation, they also require fine-grained semantic or instance maps that are tedious to produce manually. While prompt compliance can be enhanced by addition of loss functions at inference, this is time consuming and does not scale to complex scenes. To overcome these limitations, this work introduces a new family of $\textit{Factor Graph Diffusion Models}$ (FG-DMs) that models the joint distribution of images and conditioning variables, such as semantic, sketch, depth or normal maps via a factor graph decomposition. This joint structure has several advantages, including support for efficient sampling based prompt compliance schemes, which produce images of high object recall, semi-automated fine-grained editing, explainability at intermediate levels, ability to produce labeled datasets for the training of downstream models such as segmentation or depth, training with missing data, and continual learning where new conditioning variables can be added with minimal or no modifications to the existing structure. We propose an implementation of FG-DMs by adapting a pre-trained Stable Diffusion (SD) model to implement all FG-DM factors, using only COCO dataset, and show that it is effective in generating images with 15\% higher recall than SD while retaining its generalization ability. We introduce an attention distillation loss that encourages consistency among the attention maps of all factors, improving the fidelity of the generated conditions and image. We also show that training FG-DMs from scratch on MM-CelebA-HQ, Cityscapes, ADE20K, and COCO produce images of high quality (FID) and diversity (LPIPS).

title: Adapting Diffusion Models for Improved Prompt Compliance and Controllable Image Synthesis

abstract: Consider a hiring process with candidates coming from different universities. It is easy to order candidates with the same background, yet it can be challenging to compare them otherwise. The latter case requires additional costly assessments, leading to a potentially high total cost for the hiring organization. Given an assigned budget, what would be an optimal strategy to select the most qualified candidate?We model the above problem as a multicolor secretary problem, allowing comparisons between candidates from distinct groups at a fixed cost. Our study explores how the allocated budget enhances the success probability of online selection algorithms.

paragraphs: The paper studies selection when candidates arrive over time and comparisons are easier within groups than across them. Its motivating example is hiring from different universities: candidates with similar backgrounds may be straightforward to rank, while comparing candidates from different backgrounds requires an additional assessment. Those assessments cost money, so a fixed budget constrains how much information the selector can obtain.

The authors express this situation as a multicolor secretary problem, using group membership to distinguish the different candidate populations. The model permits comparisons across groups at a fixed cost. This makes the allocation of comparison resources part of the selection problem, alongside the objective of choosing the most qualified candidate.

The study examines how the available budget affects an online algorithm’s probability of selecting the best candidate. Its contribution is a mathematical framework connecting unequal comparability, paid assessments, and selection success. The central question is how to spend limited comparison opportunities effectively when candidates from different groups must ultimately be considered together.
summary.tldr: The paper models online candidate selection when comparisons across groups cost money and studies how the comparison budget affects success.

title: Addressing Bias in Online Selection with Limited Budget of Comparisons

abstract: We study a class of optimization problems in the Wasserstein space (the space of probability measures) where the objective function is nonconvex along generalized geodesics. Specifically, the objective exhibits some difference-of-convex structure along these geodesics. The setting also encompasses sampling problems where the logarithm of the target distribution is difference-of-convex. We derive multiple convergence insights for a novel semi Forward-Backward Euler scheme under several nonconvex (and possibly nonsmooth) regimes. Notably, the semi Forward-Backward Euler is just a slight modification of the Forward-Backward Euler whose convergence is---to our knowledge---still unknown in our very general non-geodesically-convex setting.

paragraphs: This paper studies optimization in Wasserstein space, where the objects being optimized are probability distributions. It considers objectives that are nonconvex along generalized geodesics, the paths used in the analysis of this space. The central question is how to obtain convergence results when the objective lacks convexity along these paths.

The authors focus on objectives with a difference-of-convex structure along generalized geodesics. This means the nonconvexity retains a particular mathematical organization that the algorithm can exploit. Their framework also includes sampling problems whose target distribution has a logarithm with difference-of-convex structure, connecting the optimization setting to the task of generating samples.

They introduce a semi Forward-Backward Euler scheme and derive convergence insights across several nonconvex regimes, including potentially nonsmooth ones. The scheme is only a slight modification of Forward-Backward Euler. According to the authors, convergence of the latter remains unknown in their very general setting. The significance is that this small algorithmic change permits convergence analysis for structured problems beyond the geodesically convex case.
summary.tldr: A modified Forward-Backward Euler scheme yields convergence insights for structured nonconvex optimization over probability distributions.

title: Non-geodesically-convex optimization in the Wasserstein space

abstract: Given a graph $G$ and a positive integer $k$, the Graphlet Sampling problem asks to sample a connected induced $k$-vertex subgraph of $G$ uniformly at random.Graphlet sampling enhances machine learning applications by transforming graph structures into feature vectors for tasks such as graph classification and subgraph identification, boosting neural network performance, and supporting clustered federated learning by capturing local structures and relationships.A recent work has shown that the problem admits an algorithm that preprocesses $G$ in time $O(nk^2 \log k + m)$, and draws one sample in expected time $k^{O(k)} \log n$, where $n=|V(G)|$ and $m=|E(G)|$. Such an algorithm relies on the assumption that the input graph fits into main memory and it does not seem to be straightforward to adapt it to very large graphs. We consider Graphlet Sampling in the semi-streaming setting, where we have a memory of $M = \Omega(n \log n)$ words, and $G$ can be only read through sequential passes over the edge list. We develop a semi-streaming algorithm that preprocesses $G$ in $p={O}(\log n)$ passes and samples $\Theta(M k^{-O(k)})$ independent uniform $k$-graphlets in $O(k)$ passes. For constant $k$, both phases run in time $O((n+m)\log n)$. We also show that the tradeoff between memory and number of passes of our algorithms is near-optimal. Our extensive evaluation on very large graphs shows the effectiveness of our algorithms.

paragraphs: Graphlet sampling selects a connected group of k vertices uniformly at random, including every graph edge between the selected vertices. Such samples capture local structure that can support graph learning and analysis. Earlier efficient algorithms assumed the whole graph fit in main memory, making their use on very large graphs difficult.

This paper studies a semi-streaming setting: memory is limited, and the graph can only be accessed through sequential passes over its edge list. Its algorithm first preprocesses the graph using a number of passes proportional to the logarithm of the vertex count. It then generates a batch of independent, uniformly distributed graphlets using a number of passes proportional to k.

The available memory determines the batch size, with a further dependence on graphlet size. For fixed k, both phases have running time proportional to the graph's combined vertex and edge count times a logarithmic factor. The authors also establish that the memory-versus-pass tradeoff is near-optimal. Evaluations on very large graphs support the effectiveness of obtaining exact uniform samples under these access constraints.
summary.tldr: Semi-streaming algorithms sample independent uniform graphlets from large graphs with a near-optimal tradeoff between memory and sequential passes.

title: Efficient Streaming Algorithms for Graphlet Sampling

abstract: We introduce DiffAug, a simple and efficient diffusion-based augmentation technique to train image classifiers for the crucial yet challenging goal of improved classifier robustness. Applying DiffAug to a given example consists of one forward-diffusion step followed by one reverse-diffusion step. Using both ResNet-50 and Vision Transformer architectures, we comprehensively evaluate classifiers trained with DiffAug and demonstrate the surprising effectiveness of single-step reverse diffusion in improving robustness to covariate shifts, certified adversarial accuracy and out of distribution detection. When we combine DiffAug with other augmentations such as AugMix and DeepAugment we demonstrate further improved robustness. Finally, building on this approach, we also improve classifier-guided diffusion wherein we observe improvements in: (i) classifier-generalization, (ii) gradient quality (i.e., improved perceptual alignment) and (iii) image generation performance. We thus introduce a computationally efficient technique for training with improved robustness that does not require any additional data, and effectively complements existing augmentation approaches.

paragraphs: Image augmentation changes training examples to help a classifier handle variation beyond its original training inputs. DiffAug introduces a diffusion-based augmentation with a short procedure: apply one forward diffusion step, then one reverse diffusion step. The paper investigates whether this simple diffuse-and-denoise transformation can improve robustness efficiently without requiring additional data.

The authors evaluate classifiers using both ResNet-50 and vision-transformer architectures. They report improvements in robustness to changes in the input distribution, certified adversarial accuracy, and detection of out-of-distribution examples. A central finding is that a single reverse diffusion step can already be effective. Combining DiffAug with AugMix or DeepAugment produces further robustness improvements in their evaluations.

The paper also applies the approach to classifier-guided diffusion, where classifier information helps direct image generation. Here, the authors observe better classifier generalization, gradients that align more closely with perceptual information, and improved generated-image performance. These results connect the augmentation's benefits for classification with its usefulness when the classifier actively guides another model's generation process.
summary.tldr: A single diffuse-and-denoise augmentation improves several tested forms of classifier robustness and also benefits classifier-guided image generation.

title: DiffAug: A Diffuse-and-Denoise Augmentation for Training Robust Classifiers

abstract: The architecture of Vision Transformers (ViTs), particularly the Multi-head Attention (MHA) mechanism, imposes substantial hardware demands. Deploying ViTs on devices with varying constraints, such as mobile phones, requires multiple models of different sizes. However, this approach has limitations, such as training and storing each required model separately. This paper introduces HydraViT, a novel approach that addresses these limitations by stacking attention heads to achieve a scalable ViT. By repeatedly changing the size of the embedded dimensions throughout each layer and their corresponding number of attention heads in MHA during training, HydraViT induces multiple subnetworks. Thereby, HydraViT achieves adaptability across a wide spectrum of hardware environments while maintaining performance. Our experimental results demonstrate the efficacy of HydraViT in achieving a scalable ViT with up to 10 subnetworks, covering a wide range of resource constraints. HydraViT achieves up to 5 p.p. more accuracy with the same GMACs and up to 7 p.p. more accuracy with the same throughput on ImageNet-1K compared to the baselines, making it an effective solution for scenarios where hardware availability is diverse or varies over time. The source code is available at https://github.com/ds-kiel/HydraViT.

paragraphs: Vision Transformers can be demanding to deploy, especially when available hardware varies between devices or over time. One response is to train and store separate models at several sizes, but that creates its own burden. HydraViT instead develops a scalable model whose internal subnetworks provide different choices of computational cost within one trained architecture.

The approach stacks attention heads and repeatedly changes embedding dimensions and the corresponding number of attention heads during training. These changes induce multiple subnetworks with different resource requirements. Training across these configurations is intended to preserve useful performance throughout the range, allowing the architecture to adapt to hardware constraints through the available subnetwork choices.

Experiments demonstrate a model with up to ten subnetworks. On ImageNet-1K, HydraViT achieves gains of up to five percentage points in accuracy at the same GMAC count and up to seven percentage points at the same throughput compared with the baselines. These are reported maximum improvements, supporting the usefulness of a scalable Transformer for the evaluated resource constraints.
summary.tldr: HydraViT trains multiple resource-scaled subnetworks within one Vision Transformer by varying embedding dimensions and attention-head counts.

title: HydraViT: Stacking Heads for a Scalable ViT

abstract: In this work, we study the mean-field flow for learning subspace-sparse polynomials using stochastic gradient descent and two-layer neural networks, where the input distribution is standard Gaussian and the output only depends on the projection of the input onto a low-dimensional subspace. We establish a necessary condition for SGD-learnability, involving both the characteristics of the target function and the expressiveness of the activation function. In addition, we prove that the condition is almost sufficient, in the sense that a condition slightly stronger than the necessary condition can guarantee the exponential decay of the loss functional to zero.
originalAbstract: In this work, we study the mean-field flow for learning subspace-sparse polynomials using stochastic gradient descent and two-layer neural networks, where the input distribution is standard Gaussian and the output only depends on the projection of the input onto a low-dimensional subspace. We establish a necessary condition for SGD-learnability, involving both the characteristics of the target function and the expressiveness of the activation function. In addition, we prove that the condition is almost sufficient, in the sense that a condition slightly stronger than the necessary condition can guarantee the exponential decay of the loss functional to zero.

paragraphs: This paper analyzes learning polynomial targets whose outputs depend only on a low-dimensional projection of the input. Although an input can have many coordinates, the target function uses information from a smaller subspace. The analysis assumes standard Gaussian inputs and studies two-layer neural networks trained with stochastic gradient descent through their mean-field flow.

The authors establish a necessary condition for learnability that depends on both the target function and the expressive capabilities of the activation function. This connects successful learning to a relationship between what must be represented and what the network’s nonlinear components can express. The condition is therefore about the learning problem and model together.

They also prove a closely related sufficient result: a slightly stronger condition guarantees that the loss functional decays exponentially to zero. The necessary condition itself is not claimed to be sufficient. By placing these two conditions close together, the work narrows the gap between identifying obstacles to learning and guaranteeing convergence within the stated Gaussian-input, subspace-sparse polynomial setting.
summary.tldr: A mean-field analysis gives closely related necessary and sufficient conditions for learning subspace-sparse polynomials under Gaussian inputs.

title: Mean-Field Analysis for Learning Subspace-Sparse Polynomials with Gaussian Input

abstract: Existing open-set learning methods consider only the single-layer labels of objects and strictly assume no overlap between the training and testing sets, leading to contradictory optimization for superposed categories. In this paper, we introduce a more practical Semi-Open Environment setting for open-set 3D object retrieval with hierarchical labels, in which the training and testing set share a partial label space for coarse categories but are completely disjoint from fine categories. We propose the Hypergraph-Based Hierarchical Equilibrium Representation (HERT) framework for this task. Specifically, we propose the Hierarchical Retrace Embedding (HRE) module to overcome the global disequilibrium of unseen categories by fully leveraging the multi-level category information. Besides, tackling the feature overlap and class confusion problem, we perform the Structured Equilibrium Tuning (SET) module to utilize more equilibrial correlations among objects and generalize to unseen categories, by constructing a superposed hypergraph based on the local coherent and global entangled correlations. Furthermore, we generate four semi-open 3DOR datasets with multi-level labels for benchmarking. Results demonstrate that the proposed method can effectively generate the hierarchical embeddings of 3D objects and generalize them towards semi-open environments.

paragraphs: Open-set 3D object retrieval must handle categories absent from training. This paper introduces a semi-open setting that distinguishes broad categories from fine-grained ones: training and test data share some coarse labels, while their fine labels are completely disjoint. That hierarchy captures overlap that a single layer of labels cannot adequately express.

The proposed HERT framework uses a Hierarchical Retrace Embedding module to exploit category information at multiple levels and address imbalance involving unseen categories. Its Structured Equilibrium Tuning module tackles overlapping features and category confusion. It constructs a superposed hypergraph from local coherent relationships and globally entangled relationships among objects.

The authors also create four datasets with multi-level labels for evaluating semi-open 3D retrieval. Results show that the framework can learn hierarchical object embeddings and generalize them to the proposed setting. The contribution joins a more differentiated evaluation problem with a representation method designed around it, making partial familiarity at the coarse level an explicit part of retrieval.
summary.tldr: HERT learns hierarchical 3D object representations for retrieval where broad categories partly overlap but fine-grained test categories are unseen.

title: Semi-Open 3D Object Retrieval via Hierarchical Equilibrium on Hypergraph

abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) is inherently rife with non-stationarity since the states and rewards the agent observes during training depend on its changing policy.Therefore, networks in deep RL must be capable of adapting to new observations and fitting new targets.However, previous works have observed that networks trained under non-stationarity exhibit an inability to continue learning, termed loss of plasticity, and eventually a collapse in performance.For off-policy deep value-based RL methods, this phenomenon has been correlated with a decrease in representation rank and the ability to fit random targets, termed capacity loss.Although this correlation has generally been attributed to neural network learning under non-stationarity, the connection to representation dynamics has not been carefully studied in on-policy policy optimization methods.In this work, we empirically study representation dynamics in Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO) on the Atari and MuJoCo environments, revealing that PPO agents are also affected by feature rank deterioration and capacity loss.We show that this is aggravated by stronger non-stationarity, ultimately driving the actor's performance to collapse, regardless of the performance of the critic.We ask why the trust region, specific to methods like PPO, cannot alleviate or prevent the collapse and find a connection between representation collapse and the degradation of the trust region, one exacerbating the other.Finally, we present Proximal Feature Optimization (PFO), a novel auxiliary loss that, along with other interventions, shows that regularizing the representation dynamics mitigates the performance collapse of PPO agents.Code and run histories are available at https://github.com/CLAIRE-Labo/no-representation-no-trust.
