paragraphs: An ensemble can estimate uncertainty through variation among its members, but maintaining many deep networks consumes substantial computation and memory. Compressing that ensemble into smaller models can reduce this variation and lose useful uncertainty information. The paper asks how to preserve the ensemble’s distributional behavior during compression.

Gaussian distillation represents the teacher ensemble with a student distribution. It treats each teacher network as a realization of a stochastic process and estimates the ensemble’s distribution using a deep latent factor model, a particular Gaussian process. Its mean describes the central prediction, while its covariance represents variation and how that variation is related. An expectation-maximization procedure estimates these functions stably.

Across multiple benchmark datasets, the authors report better performance than existing distillation baselines. They also demonstrate that the approach works well for language-model fine-tuning and distribution shift problems. The contribution is a way to make uncertainty itself a target of compression, preserving more than a central prediction while addressing the deployment burden that motivates replacing a full ensemble.
summary.tldr: Gaussian distillation compresses an ensemble into a learned probability distribution to better preserve its predictive uncertainty.

title: Knowledge Distillation of Uncertainty using Deep Latent Factor Model

abstract: Modeling reflections from 2D images is essential for photorealistic rendering and novel view synthesis. Recent approaches enhance Gaussian primitives with reflection-related material attributes to enable physically based rendering (PBR) with Gaussian Splatting. However, the material inference often lacks sufficient constraints, especially under limited environment modeling, resulting in illumination aliasing and reduced generalization. In this work, we revisit the problem from a multi-view perspective and show that multi-view consistent material inference with more physically-based environment modeling is key to learning accurate reflections with Gaussian Splatting. To this end, we enforce 2D Gaussians to produce multi-view consistent material maps during deferred shading. We also track photometric variations across views to identify highly reflective regions, which serve as strong priors for reflection strength terms. To handle indirect illumination caused by inter-object occlusions, we further introduce an environment modeling strategy through ray tracing with 2DGS, enabling photorealistic rendering of indirect radiance. Experiments on widely used benchmarks show that our method faithfully recovers both illumination and geometry, achieving state-of-the-art rendering quality in novel views synthesis. Project Page: https://wen-yuan-zhang.github.io/MaterialRefGS.

paragraphs: Reconstructing reflective objects from images requires separating surface properties from lighting effects. Gaussian-splatting methods can attach material attributes to their scene primitives, but insufficient constraints can mix illumination effects into the inferred materials. MaterialRefGS addresses this problem by combining consistency across viewpoints with a more physically grounded representation of the surrounding illumination.

The method requires 2D Gaussians to produce consistent material maps across views during deferred shading. It also examines how image appearance changes between viewpoints to identify strongly reflective regions, using those regions to constrain reflection strength. A ray-tracing environment model built with 2D Gaussian Splatting handles indirect illumination associated with objects occluding one another.

These components tie material estimation to evidence from multiple images and to the way light interacts with the scene. On widely used benchmarks, the authors report faithful recovery of illumination and geometry and state-of-the-art rendering quality for novel views. The findings support their claim that consistent materials and richer environment modeling are important for learning accurate reflections in this representation.
summary.tldr: MaterialRefGS improves reflective Gaussian-splatting reconstructions through consistent material estimates across views and ray-traced environment illumination.

title: MaterialRefGS: Reflective Gaussian Splatting with Multi-view Consistent Material Inference

abstract: Large language models (LLMs) integrated with retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) have improved factuality by grounding outputs in external evidence. However, they remain susceptible to unfaithful generation, where outputs contradict retrieved context despite its relevance and accuracy. Existing approaches aiming to improve faithfulness primarily focus on enhancing the utilization of external context, but often overlook the persistent influence of internal parametric knowledge during generation. In this work, we investigate the internal mechanisms behind unfaithful generation and identify a subset of mid-to-deep feed-forward networks (FFNs) that are disproportionately activated in such cases. Building on this insight, we propose Parametric Knowledge Muting through FFN Suppression (ParamMute), a framework that improves contextual faithfulness by suppressing the activation of unfaithfulness-associated FFNs and calibrating the model toward retrieved knowledge. To evaluate our approach, we introduce CoFaithfulQA, a benchmark specifically designed to evaluate faithfulness in scenarios where internal knowledge conflicts with accurate external evidence. Experimental results show that ParamMute significantly enhances faithfulness across both CoFaithfulQA and the established ConFiQA benchmark, achieving substantial reductions in reliance on parametric memory. These findings underscore the importance of mitigating internal knowledge dominance and provide a new direction for improving LLM trustworthiness in RAG. All codes are available at https://github.com/OpenBMB/ParamMute.

paragraphs: Retrieval-augmented generation supplies a language model with external evidence, but the model can still produce answers that contradict it. This paper examines cases where retrieved information is relevant and accurate yet conflicts with information stored in model parameters. It investigates how internal computations contribute to that failure to follow the supplied evidence.

The authors identify a subset of feed-forward networks in middle-to-deep layers that are disproportionately active during unfaithful generation. ParamMute suppresses activations in these associated networks and calibrates the model toward retrieved knowledge. The intervention therefore targets the influence of internal parametric information alongside the model's use of external context.

The paper introduces CoFaithfulQA to evaluate conflicts between internal knowledge and accurate external evidence. Across that benchmark and ConFiQA, ParamMute significantly improves faithfulness and reduces reliance on parametric memory. These findings support addressing internal knowledge dominance as part of retrieval-augmented generation, particularly in the evidence-conflict scenarios that motivate the method and its evaluation.
summary.tldr: ParamMute suppresses feed-forward networks associated with unfaithful answers to help language models follow accurate retrieved evidence.

title: ParamMute: Suppressing Knowledge-Critical FFNs for Faithful Retrieval-Augmented Generation

abstract: Non-conservative uncertainty bounds are key for both assessing an estimation algorithm’s accuracy and in view of downstream tasks, such as its deployment in safety-critical contexts. In this paper, we derive a tight, non-asymptotic uncertainty bound for kernel-based estimation, which can also handle correlated noise sequences. Its computation relies on a mild norm-boundedness assumption on the unknown function and the noise, returning the worst-case function realization within the hypothesis class at an arbitrary query input location. The value of this function is shown to be given in terms of the posterior mean and covariance of a Gaussian process for an optimal choice of the measurement noise covariance. By rigorously analyzing the proposed approach and comparing it with other results in the literature, we show its effectiveness in returning tight and easy-to-compute bounds for kernel-based estimates.

paragraphs: An estimate is more useful when accompanied by an uncertainty bound that accurately reflects how wrong it could be. Overly conservative bounds can obscure the quality of an estimator. This paper derives a tight bound for kernel-based estimation that applies to finite data and can accommodate noise that is correlated across observations.

The analysis assumes bounds on the norms of the unknown function and the noise. Within those constraints, it identifies the worst-case function in the chosen hypothesis class at any requested input location. The resulting uncertainty therefore has a precise interpretation tied to the permitted functions and disturbances, rather than relying on an unlimited-data approximation.

The authors show that the worst-case value can be expressed through a Gaussian process posterior mean and covariance when the measurement-noise covariance is chosen optimally. Their theoretical analysis and comparisons with prior results support both tightness and ease of computation. The contribution connects constrained worst-case estimation to Gaussian process quantities while retaining the stated norm-boundedness assumptions.
summary.tldr: The paper derives tight finite-data kernel regression uncertainty bounds under norm-bounded function and noise assumptions, including correlated noise.

title: Optimal kernel regression bounds under energy-bounded noise

abstract: Large language model (LLM) benchmarks inform LLM use decisions (e.g., "is this LLM safe to deploy for my use case and context?"). However, benchmarks may be rendered unreliable by various failure modes impacting benchmark bias, variance, coverage, or people's capacity to understand benchmark evidence. Using the National Institute of Standards and Technology's risk management process as a foundation, this research iteratively analyzed 26 popular benchmarks, identifying 57 potential failure modes and 196 corresponding mitigation strategies. The mitigations reduce failure likelihood and/or severity, providing a frame for evaluating "benchmark risk," which is scored to provide a metaevaluation benchmark: BenchRisk. Higher scores indicate benchmark users are less likely to reach an incorrect or unsupported conclusion about an LLM. All 26 scored benchmarks present significant risk within one or more of the five scored dimensions (comprehensiveness, intelligibility, consistency, correctness, and longevity), which points to important open research directions for the field of LLM benchmarking. The BenchRisk workflow allows for comparison between benchmarks; as an open-source tool, it also facilitates the identification and sharing of risks and their mitigations.

title: Risk Management for Mitigating Benchmark Failure Modes: BenchRisk

abstract: A multi-agent system (MAS) enhances its capacity to solve complex natural language processing (NLP) tasks through collaboration among multiple agents, where consensus-seeking serves as a fundamental mechanism. However, existing consensus-seeking approaches typically rely on voting mechanisms to judge consensus, overlooking contradictions in system-internal beliefs that destabilize the consensus. Moreover, these methods often involve agents updating their results through indiscriminate collaboration with every other agent. Such uniform interaction fails to identify the optimal collaborators for each agent, hindering the emergence of a stable consensus. To address these challenges, we provide a theoretical framework for selecting optimal collaborators that maximize consensus stability. Based on the theorems, we propose the Belief-Calibrated Consensus Seeking (BCCS) framework to facilitate stable consensus via selecting optimal collaborators and calibrating the consensus judgment by system-internal beliefs. Experimental results on the MATH and MMLU benchmark datasets demonstrate that the proposed BCCS framework outperforms the best existing results by 2.23\% and 3.95\% of accuracy on challenging tasks, respectively. Our code and data are available at https://github.com/dengwentao99/BCCS.

Agents may choose the same answer while retaining contradictory beliefs, leaving their consensus unstable. This paper also questions whether every agent should interact equally with every other agent, since some collaborators may be more useful for achieving stable agreement.

The authors develop a theoretical framework for choosing collaborators that maximize consensus stability. Their Belief-Calibrated Consensus Seeking framework, BCCS, uses this analysis to select collaboration partners and assess agreement using the system's internal beliefs. Partner selection and consensus assessment therefore work together: the method changes both whom agents consult and how their resulting agreement is judged.

Experiments on MATH and MMLU report accuracy improvements of 2.23% and 3.95%, respectively, over the best existing results. These findings support the value of considering the structure of collaboration and underlying beliefs when coordinating agents on challenging tasks. The contribution connects a theoretical account of stable consensus with empirical improvements in answer accuracy.
summary.tldr: BCCS improves multi-agent collaboration by selecting partners for stable consensus and checking agreement against agents' internal beliefs.

title: Belief-Calibrated Multi-Agent Consensus Seeking for Complex NLP Tasks

abstract: The Schrödinger Bridge (SB) problem has become a fundamental tool in computational optimal transport and generative modeling. To address this problem, ideal methods such as Iterative Proportional Fitting and Iterative Markovian Fitting (IMF) have been proposed—alongside practical approximations like Diffusion Schrödinger Bridge and its Matching (DSBM) variant. While previous work have established asymptotic convergence guarantees for IMF, a quantitative, non-asymptotic understanding remains unknown. In this paper, we provide the first non-asymptotic exponential convergence guarantees for IMF under mild structural assumptions on the reference measure and marginal distributions, assuming a sufficiently large time horizon. Our results encompass two key regimes: one where the marginals are log-concave, and another where they are weakly log-concave. The analysis relies on new contraction results for the Markovian projection operator and paves the way to theoretical guarantees for DSBM.

paragraphs: The Schrödinger Bridge problem is used in computational optimal transport and generative modeling. Iterative Markovian Fitting, or IMF, is an idealized method for solving it. Earlier theory established that IMF converges eventually, but did not quantify its progress after a finite number of iterations. This paper supplies such a quantitative convergence result.

The authors prove exponential convergence under structural assumptions on the reference measure and marginal distributions, with a sufficiently large time horizon. They cover two regimes: log-concave marginals and the broader case of weakly log-concave marginals. The guarantee therefore depends on these conditions; it is a statement about IMF in the analyzed settings rather than unrestricted convergence for every bridge problem.

The analysis develops new contraction results for the Markovian projection operator, providing the mathematical basis for controlling how the iteration progresses. This strengthens an eventual-convergence statement into a finite-iteration rate. The work also lays groundwork for analyzing Diffusion Schrödinger Bridge Matching, a practical approximation, while the stated exponential guarantees apply to IMF itself.
summary.tldr: The paper proves finite-iteration exponential convergence for Iterative Markovian Fitting under structural assumptions and a sufficiently large time horizon.

title: Exponential Convergence Guarantees for Iterative Markovian Fitting

abstract: Growing evidence suggests that synaptic weights in the brain follow heavy-tailed distributions, yet most theoretical analyses of recurrent neural networks (RNNs) assume Gaussian connectivity. We systematically study the activity of RNNs with random weights drawn from biologically plausible Lévy alpha-stable distributions. While mean-field theory for the infinite system predicts that the quiescent state is always unstable---implying ubiquitous chaos---our finite-size analysis reveals a sharp transition between quiescent and chaotic dynamics. We theoretically predict the gain at which the finite system transitions from quiescent to chaotic dynamics, and validate it through simulations. Compared to Gaussian networks, finite heavy-tailed RNNs exhibit a broader gain regime near the edge of chaos, namely, a slow transition to chaos. However, this robustness comes with a tradeoff: heavier tails reduce the Lyapunov dimension of the attractor, indicating lower effective dimensionality. Our results reveal a biologically aligned tradeoff between the robustness of dynamics near the edge of chaos and the richness of high-dimensional neural activity. By analytically characterizing the transition point in finite-size networks---where mean-field theory breaks down---we provide a tractable framework for understanding dynamics in realistically sized, heavy-tailed neural circuits.

This paper studies random networks with Lévy alpha-stable weights. It focuses on how finite network size changes the transition between a quiet state and chaotic activity.

Infinite-system mean-field theory predicts that the quiet state is always unstable. The finite-size analysis instead finds a sharp transition and predicts the gain at which it occurs, with simulations validating the prediction. title: Slow Transition to Low-Dimensional Chaos in Heavy-Tailed Recurrent Neural Networks

abstract: Diffusion models have demonstrated exceptional capabilities in generating high-fidelity images. However, their iterative denoising process results in significant computational overhead during inference, limiting their practical deployment in resource-constrained environments. Existing acceleration methods often adopt uniform strategies that fail to capture the temporal variations during diffusion generation, while the commonly adopted sequential $\textit{pruning-then-fine-tuning strategy}$ suffers from sub-optimality due to the misalignment between pruning decisions made on pretrained weights and the model’s final parameters. To address these limitations, we introduce $\textbf{ALTER}$: $\textbf{A}$ll-in-One $\textbf{L}$ayer Pruning and $\textbf{T}$emporal $\textbf{E}$xpoert $\textbf{R}$outing, a unified framework that transforms diffusion models into a mixture of efficient temporal experts. ALTER achieves a single-stage optimization that unifies layer pruning, expert routing, and model fine-tuning by employing a trainable hypernetwork, which dynamically generates layer pruning decisions and manages timestep routing to specialized, pruned expert sub-networks throughout the ongoing fine-tuning of the UNet. This unified co-optimization strategy enables significant efficiency gains while preserving high generative quality. Specifically, ALTER achieves same-level visual fidelity to the original 50-step Stable Diffusion v2.1 model while utilizing only 25.9\% of its total MACs with just 20 inference steps and delivering a 3.64$\times$ speedup through 35\% sparsity.

paragraphs: Diffusion image generation repeatedly runs a denoising network, making inference expensive. The computational needs can vary across this process, so applying one uniform acceleration strategy may miss useful differences between timesteps. Another difficulty arises when layers are removed before fine-tuning: pruning decisions reflect weights that will subsequently change.

ALTER addresses both issues by jointly learning which layers to remove, which specialized subnetwork to use at each timestep, and how to fine-tune the model. They also report a 3.64-fold speedup with 35% sparsity. These results demonstrate substantial savings in the stated comparison, supporting coordinated pruning and timestep specialization as an effective acceleration approach.
summary.tldr: ALTER jointly optimizes layer pruning, timestep routing, and fine-tuning to accelerate diffusion generation while preserving reported visual fidelity.

title: ALTER: All-in-One Layer Pruning and Temporal Expert Routing for Efficient Diffusion Generation

abstract: Recent methods in language model interpretability employ techniques such as sparse autoencoders to decompose residual stream contributions into linear, semantically-meaningful features. Our work demonstrates that an underlying assumption of these methods—that residual stream contributions build additively upon each other—is insufficient to fully explain model behavior. Specifically, we identify the Transformer Layer Correction Mechanism (TLCM), wherein adjacent transformer layers systematically counteract each other's contributions to the residual stream. TLCM appears in 5 out of 7 major open-source model families and activates across nearly all tokens in diverse texts. To understand TLCM, we show that it emerges during pretraining, operates most strongly on punctuation and numbers, and adaptively calibrates its correction strength based on the preceding layer's output. We further show that TLCM actively corrects a small subspace and promotes other subspaces, different from standard model behavior. We advance the ``propose-and-reject'' hypothesis: layers may propose multiple candidate features, while subsequent layers selectively filter out inappropriate ones. Finally, we discuss how our findings help explain three persistent challenges in feature-based interpretability: why extracted features descriptions often suffer from low specificity; why feature-based interventions for model steering fail at low magnitude; why recent work finds cross-layer transcoders outperform SAEs.

paragraphs: Some interpretability methods decompose a language model's internal updates into meaningful features, assuming that successive contributions build additively. This paper finds that this picture is insufficient: neighboring transformer layers can systematically counteract each other's updates. The authors call this behavior the Transformer Layer Correction Mechanism.

The mechanism appears in five of seven examined open-source model families and operates across nearly all tokens in varied texts. It emerges during pretraining, is strongest on punctuation and numbers, and adjusts its strength according to the preceding layer's output. The correction targets a small subspace while promoting others, giving it a selective structure.

The authors propose that one layer may introduce several candidate features and the next may reject inappropriate ones. This remains a hypothesis for interpreting the observed behavior. They discuss how the findings help explain vague extracted-feature descriptions, weak steering effects from small feature interventions, and the reported advantage of cross-layer transcoders over sparse autoencoders. The broader implication is that interpreting features may require following their interactions across layers.
summary.tldr: Adjacent transformer layers often selectively counteract each other's updates, complicating interpretations that treat features as simply accumulating.

title: LLM Layers Immediately Correct Each Other

abstract: Large Language Model (LLM) agents have demonstrated impressive capabilities for social interaction and are increasingly being deployed in situations where they might engage with both human and artificial agents. These interactions represent a critical frontier for LLM-based agents, yet existing evaluation methods fail to measure how well these capabilities generalize to novel social situations. In this paper, we introduce a method for evaluating the ability of LLM-based agents to cooperate in zero-shot, mixed-motive environments using Concordia, a natural language multi-agent simulation environment. Our method measures general cooperative intelligence by testing an agent's ability to identify and exploit opportunities for mutual gain across diverse partners and contexts. We present empirical results from the NeurIPS 2024 Concordia Contest, where agents were evaluated on their ability to achieve mutual gains across a suite of diverse scenarios ranging from negotiation to collective action problems. Our findings reveal significant gaps between current agent capabilities and the robust generalization required for reliable cooperation, particularly in scenarios demanding persuasion and norm enforcement.

paragraphs: An agent that communicates well in one setting may still struggle to cooperate in an unfamiliar social situation. This paper introduces an evaluation method for that transfer problem, focusing on mixed-motive environments where participants have opportunities for mutual benefit alongside differing interests. The target is cooperation across new partners and contexts.

The method uses Concordia, a multi-agent simulation environment built around natural language. Agents face scenarios in a zero-shot setting, and the evaluation measures their ability to recognize and pursue opportunities for mutual gain. This gives cooperative intelligence a concrete testing focus: whether agents can turn varied social circumstances into outcomes that benefit multiple participants.

Results come from the NeurIPS 2024 Concordia Contest and cover scenarios ranging from negotiation to collective action. The authors find substantial gaps between current abilities and the generalization needed for reliable cooperation. Persuasion and norm enforcement are particularly difficult. These findings identify specific weaknesses in social transfer and provide an evaluation approach for studying whether future agents improve across unfamiliar cooperative situations.
summary.tldr: Concordia evaluations reveal that LLM agents struggle to generalize cooperation, especially when persuasion or norm enforcement is required.

title: Evaluating Generalization Capabilities of LLM-Based Agents in Mixed-Motive Scenarios Using Concordia

abstract: LLMs have demonstrated impressive capabilities across various natural language processing tasks yet remain vulnerable to prompts, known as jailbreak attacks, carefully designed to bypass safety guardrails and elicit harmful responses. Traditional methods rely on manual heuristics that suffer from limited generalizability. Despite being automatic, optimization-based attacks often produce unnatural jailbreak prompts that can be easily detected by safety filters or require high computational costs due to discrete token optimization. This paper introduces *Generative Adversarial Suffix Prompter* (GASP), a novel automated framework that can efficiently generate human-readable jailbreak prompts in a fully black-box setting. In particular, GASP leverages latent Bayesian optimization to craft adversarial suffixes by efficiently exploring continuous latent spaces, gradually optimizing the suffix generator to improve attack efficacy while balancing prompt coherence via a targeted iterative refinement procedure. Through comprehensive experiments, we show that GASP can produce natural adversarial prompts, significantly improving jailbreak success, reducing training times, and accelerating inference speed, thus making it an efficient and scalable solution for red-teaming LLMs.

paragraphs: Language models can remain vulnerable to prompts designed to bypass their safety guardrails. Testing these vulnerabilities is difficult when attacks depend on manual tricks or expensive optimization over discrete tokens. The paper introduces GASP, an automated framework for generating readable adversarial prompt suffixes in a fully black-box setting.

GASP uses latent Bayesian optimization to search a continuous representation space associated with a suffix generator. It progressively improves the generator through an iterative refinement procedure that balances attack effectiveness with prompt coherence. The approach targets a central tension in automated testing: prompts need to expose weaknesses while remaining natural enough to avoid the conspicuous wording produced by some optimization methods.

The authors report that GASP produces natural adversarial prompts while significantly improving jailbreak success, reducing training time, and accelerating inference in their experiments. These findings support its proposed use as an efficient, scalable red-teaming framework. The contribution is a way to automate the generation of coherent test attacks without requiring access to the target model’s internal parameters.
summary.tldr: GASP uses continuous latent-space optimization to generate readable black-box jailbreak suffixes more efficiently for language-model red-teaming.

title: GASP: Efficient Black-Box Generation of Adversarial Suffixes for Jailbreaking LLMs

abstract: Code embedding models attract increasing attention due to the widespread popularity of retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) in software development. These models are expected to capture the rich semantic relationships inherent to code, which differ significantly from those found in text. However, existing models remain severely limited due to the scarcity of high-quality training data. In this work, we introduce \textbf{CodeR} (\underline{Code} \underline{R}etrieval), a state-of-the-art embedding model for general-purpose code retrieval. The superior performance of CodeR is built upon \textbf{CodeR-Pile}, a large-scale synthetic dataset constructed under the DRU (Diversity, Reliability, Usability) principle via a novel data synthesis pipeline. To optimize training effectiveness, we propose \textbf{Annealing}, a curriculum learning strategy that enables effective knowledge transfer across heterogeneous sources of data. We evaluate CodeR based on 16 diverse code retrieval tasks, where it significantly outperforms existing baselines and exhibits strong out-of-domain generalization performance. We have publicly released our code and the well-trained model to facilitate further research in this critical area\footnote{\url{https://github.com/FlagOpen/FlagEmbedding/tree/master/research/BGE_Coder}}.

The paper identifies a shortage of high-quality training data as a major obstacle, particularly as retrieval-augmented generation becomes more widely used in software development.

These findings support the combined data-synthesis and curriculum approach for building a broadly useful code embedding model. The authors also release the code and trained model, making the resulting retrieval system available for further research.
summary.tldr: CodeR combines large-scale synthetic training data with a curriculum strategy to improve general-purpose code retrieval across 16 tasks.

title: Towards A Generalist Code Embedding Model Based On Massive Data Synthesis

abstract: Creativity in AI imagery remains a fundamental challenge, requiring not only the generation of visually compelling content but also the capacity to add novel, expressive, and artistically rich transformations to images. Unlike conventional editing tasks that rely on direct prompt-based modifications, creative image editing demands an autonomous, iterative approach that balances originality, coherence, and artistic intent. To address this, we introduce CREA, a novel multi-agent collaborative framework that mimics the human creative process. Our framework leverages a team of specialized AI agents who dynamically collaborate to conceptualize, generate, critique, and enhance images. Through extensive qualitative and quantitative evaluations, we demonstrate that CREA significantly outperforms state-of-the-art methods in diversity, semantic alignment, and creative transformation. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first work to introduce the task of creative editing.

paragraphs: Creative image editing asks a system to introduce expressive, original transformations while keeping an image coherent and aligned with artistic intent. The paper frames this as a broader problem than executing a direct editing instruction: deciding how an image should evolve is itself part of the work.

CREA organizes that work around a collaborating team of specialized AI agents. Their roles cover developing concepts, generating images, critiquing results, and enhancing them. These activities form an autonomous, iterative process inspired by human creative work, allowing the framework to revisit and develop an image through collaboration.

The authors evaluate CREA both qualitatively and quantitatively, reporting significant improvements over state-of-the-art methods in diversity, semantic alignment, and creative transformation. These dimensions matter together because originality alone does not establish that an edit remains meaningful or coherent. The reported findings support organizing image creation around an ongoing cycle of proposals and critique. The authors also position the paper, to their knowledge, as the first introduction of creative editing as a task.
summary.tldr: CREA uses collaborating agents to conceive, generate, critique, and refine images, improving evaluated creative editing outcomes.

title: CREA: A Collaborative Multi-Agent Framework for Creative Image Editing and Generation

abstract: In this paper, we introduce LangSplatV2, which achieves high-dimensional feature splatting at 476.2 FPS and 3D open-vocabulary text querying at 384.6 FPS for high-resolution images, providing a 42 × speedup and a 47 × boost over LangSplat respectively, along with improved query accuracy. LangSplat employs Gaussian Splatting to embed 2D CLIP language features into 3D, significantly enhancing speed and learning a precise 3D language field with SAM semantics. Such advancements in 3D language fields are crucial for applications that require language interaction within complex scenes. However, LangSplat does not yet achieve real- time performance (8.2 FPS), even with advanced A100 GPUs, severely limiting its broader application. In this paper, we first conduct a detailed time analysis of LangSplat, identifying the heavyweight decoder as the primary speed bottleneck. Our solution, LangSplatV2 assumes that each Gaussian acts as a sparse code within a global dictionary, leading to the learning of a 3D sparse coefficient field that entirely eliminates the need for a heavyweight decoder. By leveraging this sparsity, we further propose an efficient sparse coefficient splatting method with CUDA optimization, rendering high-dimensional feature maps at high quality while incurring only the time cost of splatting an ultra-low-dimensional feature. Our experimental results demonstrate that LangSplatV2 not only achieves better or competitive query accuracy but is also significantly faster. Codes and demos are available at our project page: https://langsplat-v2.github.io.

abstract: We propose a novel accelerated exact k-means algorithm, which outperforms the current state-of-the-art low-dimensional algorithm in 18 of 22 experiments, running up to 3 times faster. We also propose a general improvement of existing state-of-the-art accelerated exact k-means algorithms through better estimates of the distance bounds used to reduce the number of distance calculations, obtaining speedups in 36 of 44 experiments, of up to 1.8 times. We have conducted experiments with our own implementations of existing methods to ensure homogeneous evaluation of performance, and we show that our implementations perform as well or better than existing available implementations. Finally, we propose simplified variants of standard approaches and show that they are faster than their fully-fledged counterparts in 59 of 62 experiments.

paragraphs: Accelerated exact k-means algorithms use distance bounds to avoid unnecessary distance calculations while retaining exact computation. This paper develops a new algorithm and improves the bounds used by existing approaches. Its central idea is that more accurate estimates can eliminate additional calculations and thereby reduce clustering time.

The new algorithm beats the compared leading low-dimensional method in 18 of 22 experiments, with speedups reaching threefold. The more general bound improvement speeds up existing accelerated methods in 36 of 44 experiments, reaching a factor of 1.8. These results distinguish a new standalone algorithm from a modification that can benefit other algorithms.

The authors also examine simplified versions of standard approaches, which outperform their fuller counterparts in 59 of 62 experiments. For consistency, they evaluate their own implementations of existing methods and show that those implementations match or exceed available ones. Together, the findings indicate that tighter bounds and simpler implementations can both matter for runtime; the reported gains remain empirical outcomes across the tested cases.
summary.tldr: Tighter distance bounds and simpler algorithm variants accelerate exact k-means across most of the reported experiments.

title: Fast k-means with accurate bounds

abstract: We introduce Bayesian Poisson Tucker decomposition (BPTD) for modeling country–country interaction event data. These data consist of interaction events of the form “country i took action a toward country j at time t.” BPTD discovers overlapping country–community memberships, including the number of latent communities. In addition, it discovers directed community–community interaction networks that are specific to “topics” of action types and temporal “regimes.” We show that BPTD yields an efficient MCMC inference algorithm and achieves better predictive performance than related models. We also demonstrate that it discovers interpretable latent structure that agrees with our knowledge of international relations.

paragraphs: The paper models international interaction records that specify an acting country, an action, a receiving country, and a time. Bayesian Poisson Tucker decomposition uses these linked dimensions to uncover hidden organization in the events. The aim is to represent relationships among countries alongside patterns in what they do and when.

The model discovers country communities and allows a country to belong to multiple communities. It also discovers the number of latent communities. Beyond membership, it learns directed networks of interactions between communities, with different networks associated with action topics and temporal regimes. This lets the representation distinguish who interacts, the kinds of actions involved, and the relevant time patterns.

The authors provide an efficient Markov chain Monte Carlo inference algorithm and report better predictive performance than related models. They also find interpretable latent structure that agrees with their knowledge of international relations. These results support both predictive and descriptive uses of the model: forecasting event patterns and organizing observed interactions into understandable communities and relationships.
summary.tldr: Bayesian Poisson Tucker decomposition discovers overlapping country communities and interaction patterns across action topics and temporal regimes.

title: Bayesian Poisson Tucker Decomposition for Learning the Structure of International Relations

abstract: Common nonlinear activation functions used in neural networks can cause training difficulties due to the saturation behavior of the activation function, which may hide dependencies that are not visible to vanilla-SGD (using first order gradients only). Gating mechanisms that use softly saturating activation functions to emulate the discrete switching of digital logic circuits are good examples of this. We propose to exploit the injection of appropriate noise so that the gradients may flow easily, even if the noiseless application of the activation function would yield zero gradients. Large noise will dominate the noise-free gradient and allow stochastic gradient descent to explore more. By adding noise only to the problematic parts of the activation function, we allow the optimization procedure to explore the boundary between the degenerate saturating) and the well-behaved parts of the activation function. We also establish connections to simulated annealing, when the amount of noise is annealed down, making it easier to optimize hard objective functions. We find experimentally that replacing such saturating activation functions by noisy variants helps optimization in many contexts, yielding state-of-the-art or competitive results on different datasets and task, especially when training seems to be the most difficult, e.g., when curriculum learning is necessary to obtain good results.

paragraphs: Saturating activation functions can make neural networks hard to train because their gradients become uninformative or vanish. Dependencies may then be invisible to ordinary stochastic gradient descent, which uses first-order gradients. The paper highlights gating mechanisms as one setting where functions intended to resemble discrete switches can create this difficulty.

The proposed remedy is to inject suitable noise into the problematic portions of the activation function. This can let gradients flow even where the noiseless function would give zero gradients. Larger noise encourages greater exploration, and concentrating it around troublesome regions helps optimization explore the boundary between saturated and better-behaved parts of the function.

The authors also connect gradually reducing the noise to simulated annealing as a way to ease optimization of difficult objectives. Experiments find that noisy replacements help optimization in many settings and achieve competitive or state-of-the-art results across different datasets and tasks. The reported benefits are especially pronounced in difficult training situations, including cases where curriculum learning is needed for good results.
summary.tldr: Adding targeted noise to saturating activations helps gradients and exploration, improving optimization in the reported experiments.

title: Noisy Activation Functions

abstract: We propose a generic framework based on a new stochastic variance-reduced gradient descent algorithm for accelerating nonconvex low-rank matrix recovery. Starting from an appropriate initial estimator, our proposed algorithm performs projected gradient descent based on a novel semi-stochastic gradient specifically designed for low-rank matrix recovery. Based upon the mild restricted strong convexity and smoothness conditions, we derive a projected notion of the restricted Lipschitz continuous gradient property, and prove that our algorithm enjoys linear convergence rate to the unknown low-rank matrix with an improved computational complexity. Moreover, our algorithm can be employed to both noiseless and noisy observations, where the (near) optimal sample complexity and statistical rate can be attained respectively. We further illustrate the superiority of our generic framework through several specific examples, both theoretically and experimentally.

paragraphs: The paper develops a common optimization framework for recovering an unknown low-rank matrix. Its focus is computational efficiency in a nonconvex formulation: how to make progress toward the desired matrix while reducing the cost of the gradient calculations used during optimization. The approach is intended to support multiple recovery problems within one framework.

The algorithm combines projected gradient descent with a specially designed semi-stochastic gradient and variance reduction. Its guarantees require an appropriate starting estimator and restricted strong convexity and smoothness conditions. From these assumptions, the authors establish a projected gradient regularity property and prove linear convergence, together with improved computational complexity.

The framework accommodates observations both with and without noise. The authors report near-optimal or optimal sample complexity in the noiseless setting and statistical convergence rates in the noisy setting. These results connect computational progress with the amount and quality of available information. Specific examples provide theoretical and experimental support for the advantages of the general approach.
summary.tldr: A variance-reduced projected gradient framework accelerates low-rank matrix recovery under suitable initialization and restricted regularity conditions.

title: A Unified Variance Reduction-Based Framework for Nonconvex Low-Rank Matrix Recovery

abstract: We use deep learning to model interactions across two or more sets of objects, such as user{–}movie ratings or protein{–}drug bindings. The canonical representation of such interactions is a matrix (or tensor) with an exchangeability property: the encoding’s meaning is not changed by permuting rows or columns. We argue that models should hence be Permutation Equivariant (PE): constrained to make the same predictions across such permutations. We present a parameter-sharing scheme and prove that it is maximally expressive under the PE constraint. This scheme yields three benefits. First, we demonstrate performance competitive with the state of the art on multiple matrix completion benchmarks. Second, our models require a number of parameters independent of the numbers of objects and thus scale well to large datasets. Third, models can be queried about new objects that were not available at training time, but for which interactions have since been observed. We observed surprisingly good generalization performance on this matrix extrapolation task, both within domains (e.g., new users and new movies drawn from the same distribution used for training) and even across domains (e.g., predicting music ratings after training on movie ratings).

paragraphs: Interactions between sets of objects can be represented as matrices or tensors, such as users rating movies or proteins binding drugs. Reordering the objects changes their positions in this representation without changing the interactions themselves. This paper builds deep models around that symmetry: predictions should follow the same reordering rather than depend on arbitrary row or column positions.

The authors introduce a parameter-sharing scheme and prove it is maximally expressive under the permutation-equivariance constraint. Its parameter count does not depend on the number of objects, supporting use with large collections. The models can also answer queries about objects absent during training when interactions involving those objects have subsequently been observed.

Experiments show performance competitive with leading methods on matrix completion benchmarks. The authors also report strong generalization when extending predictions to new objects, both within the training domain and across domains, including transfer from movie ratings to music ratings. These findings connect a structural symmetry to practical scalability and reuse, while the new-object capability still relies on having observed interactions for those objects.
summary.tldr: Permutation-equivariant interaction models combine expressive parameter sharing with competitive matrix completion and promising generalization to new objects and domains.

title: Deep Models of Interactions Across Sets

abstract: One of the most challenging machine learning problems is a particular case of data classification in which classes are hierarchically structured and objects can be assigned to multiple paths of the class hierarchy at the same time. This task is known as hierarchical multi-label classification (HMC), with applications in text classification, image annotation, and in bioinformatics problems such as protein function prediction. In this paper, we propose novel neural network architectures for HMC called HMCN, capable of simultaneously optimizing local and global loss functions for discovering local hierarchical class-relationships and global information from the entire class hierarchy while penalizing hierarchical violations. We evaluate its performance in 21 datasets from four distinct domains, and we compare it against the current HMC state-of-the-art approaches. Results show that HMCN substantially outperforms all baselines with statistical significance, arising as the novel state-of-the-art for HMC.

paragraphs: Hierarchical multi-label classification assigns an object several labels organized within a hierarchy, potentially spanning multiple paths. This structure matters in tasks such as text classification, image annotation, and protein function prediction. A useful model must learn which labels apply while accounting for relationships among labels at different positions in the hierarchy.

The paper introduces HMCN, a family of neural-network architectures that optimize local and global losses simultaneously. Local objectives capture relationships within parts of the hierarchy, while global objectives use information from the hierarchy as a whole. The training objective also penalizes hierarchical violations, making consistency with the label structure part of learning.

The authors evaluate HMCN on 21 datasets covering four domains and compare it with established hierarchical classification approaches. They report substantial, statistically significant improvements over every tested baseline. These results support combining local and global learning signals in one architecture, and establish the claimed state-of-the-art performance within the comparisons reported in the paper.
summary.tldr: HMCN combines local and global hierarchy-aware objectives and significantly outperforms tested hierarchical multi-label classification baselines.

title: Hierarchical Multi-Label Classification Networks

abstract: We provide theoretical investigation of curriculum learning in the context of stochastic gradient descent when optimizing the convex linear regression loss. We prove that the rate of convergence of an ideal curriculum learning method is monotonically increasing with the difficulty of the examples. Moreover, among all equally difficult points, convergence is faster when using points which incur higher loss with respect to the current hypothesis. We then analyze curriculum learning in the context of training a CNN. We describe a method which infers the curriculum by way of transfer learning from another network, pre-trained on a different task. While this approach can only approximate the ideal curriculum, we observe empirically similar behavior to the one predicted by the theory, namely, a significant boost in convergence speed at the beginning of training. When the task is made more difficult, improvement in generalization performance is also observed. Finally, curriculum learning exhibits robustness against unfavorable conditions such as excessive regularization.

paragraphs: Curriculum learning changes which training examples a model encounters as learning proceeds. This paper first examines an ideal curriculum mathematically for stochastic gradient descent on a convex linear regression loss. That setting provides a tractable way to study how example difficulty and the model's current errors relate to convergence.

The analysis proves that the convergence rate of the ideal method increases monotonically with example difficulty. Among examples of equal difficulty, those producing greater loss under the current hypothesis lead to faster convergence. The authors then construct a practical curriculum for a convolutional network using information transferred from another network pretrained on a different task.

This transferred curriculum only approximates the ideal one, so the neural-network findings are empirical. The experiments nevertheless show a substantial acceleration early in training, resembling the behavior predicted by the theory. Generalization also improves when the task is made harder, and curriculum learning shows robustness to unfavorable conditions such as excessive regularization. These results connect a restricted theoretical analysis with a practical curriculum-building method.
summary.tldr: The paper analyzes ideal curricula for linear regression and uses transfer learning to build practical curricula that accelerate early CNN training.

title: Curriculum Learning by Transfer Learning: Theory and Experiments with Deep Networks

abstract: Although adversarial examples and model robust-ness have been extensively studied in the context of neural networks, research on this issue in tree-based models and how to make tree-based models robust against adversarial examples is still limited. In this paper, we show that tree-based models are also vulnerable to adversarial examples and develop a novel algorithm to learn robust trees. At its core, our method aims to optimize the performance under the worst-case perturbation of input features, which leads to a max-min saddle point problem. Incorporating this saddle point objective into the decision tree building procedure is non-trivial due to the discrete nature of trees{—}a naive approach to finding the best split according to this saddle point objective will take exponential time. To make our approach practical and scalable, we propose efficient tree building algorithms by approximating the inner minimizer in the saddlepoint problem, and present efficient implementations for classical information gain based trees as well as state-of-the-art tree boosting systems such as XGBoost. Experimental results on real world datasets demonstrate that the proposed algorithms can significantly improve the robustness of tree-based models against adversarial examples.

paragraphs: Decision trees can also be vulnerable to adversarial examples: changes to input features chosen to undermine a model's predictions. This paper demonstrates that vulnerability and develops a training approach intended to improve robustness. Its central idea is to choose tree behavior according to performance under worst-case feature perturbations.

This turns tree construction into a max-min saddle-point problem, combining the learner's choices with an opposing choice of perturbations. Trees make discrete split decisions, and a direct search for the best robust split would require exponential time. The authors make the procedure practical by approximating the inner minimization, reducing the computational obstacle to using the robust objective.

They provide efficient implementations for both classical information-gain trees and boosted tree systems such as XGBoost. Experiments on real-world datasets show significant improvements in adversarial robustness. The result extends robustness-oriented training to widely used tree models and demonstrates that approximating the difficult inner problem can yield useful empirical gains within scalable tree-building procedures.
summary.tldr: Approximate worst-case split optimization makes adversarially robust training practical for decision trees and boosted tree systems.

title: Robust Decision Trees Against Adversarial Examples

abstract: We address the problem of any-code completion - generating a missing piece of source code in a given program without any restriction on the vocabulary or structure. We introduce a new approach to any-code completion that leverages the strict syntax of programming languages to model a code snippet as a tree - structural language modeling (SLM). SLM estimates the probability of the program’s abstract syntax tree (AST) by decomposing it into a product of conditional probabilities over its nodes. We present a neural model that computes these conditional probabilities by considering all AST paths leading to a target node. Unlike previous techniques that have severely restricted the kinds of expressions that can be generated in this task, our approach can generate arbitrary code in any programming language. Our model significantly outperforms both seq2seq and a variety of structured approaches in generating Java and C# code. Our code, data, and trained models are available at http://github.com/tech-srl/slm-code-generation/. An online demo is available at http://AnyCodeGen.org.

paragraphs: Completing a missing program fragment can require generating expressions with varied vocabulary and structure. This paper addresses any-code completion, which does not restrict those possibilities in advance. Its approach uses the strict syntax of programming languages to represent the missing code and its context through an abstract syntax tree.

Structural language modeling assigns a probability to the program's tree by combining conditional probabilities for its nodes. A neural model computes each node's probability using all abstract-syntax-tree paths leading to that node. This makes the tree structure central to how the model represents context and predicts the pieces of a program.

The approach is presented as capable of generating arbitrary code in any programming language, overcoming restrictions on expression types imposed by earlier completion methods. The reported evaluations are on Java and C#, where the model significantly outperforms sequence-to-sequence models and several structured approaches. These findings support syntax-based modeling as an effective basis for flexible code completion in the tested languages.
summary.tldr: Structural language modeling generates missing code through syntax-tree node probabilities and outperforms sequence and structured approaches on Java and C#.

title: Structural Language Models of Code

abstract: We study the iteration complexity of stochastic gradient descent (SGD) for minimizing the gradient norm of smooth, possibly nonconvex functions. We provide several results, implying that the classical $\mathcal{O}(\epsilon^{-4})$ upper bound (for making the average gradient norm less than $\epsilon$) cannot be improved upon, unless a combination of additional assumptions is made. Notably, this holds even if we limit ourselves to convex quadratic functions. We also show that for nonconvex functions, the feasibility of minimizing gradients with SGD is surprisingly sensitive to the choice of optimality criteria.
originalAbstract: We study the iteration complexity of stochastic gradient descent (SGD) for minimizing the gradient norm of smooth, possibly nonconvex functions. We provide several results, implying that the classical $\mathcal{O}(\epsilon^{-4})$ upper bound (for making the average gradient norm less than $\epsilon$) cannot be improved upon, unless a combination of additional assumptions is made. Notably, this holds even if we limit ourselves to convex quadratic functions. We also show that for nonconvex functions, the feasibility of minimizing gradients with SGD is surprisingly sensitive to the choice of optimality criteria.

paragraphs: The paper asks how many stochastic gradient descent iterations are needed to make gradients small when optimizing a smooth function. A small gradient indicates approximate stationarity, which is a useful target even when a function is nonconvex. The analysis focuses on gradient norms rather than treating every notion of optimization success as interchangeable.

The authors provide results showing that the classical O(epsilon to the power minus four) upper bound for making the average gradient norm smaller than epsilon cannot generally be improved without a combination of additional assumptions. This obstacle persists even when attention is restricted to convex quadratic functions. Thus, simply choosing that familiar function class does not remove the stated worst-case difficulty.

For nonconvex functions, the paper also finds that whether SGD can minimize gradients is highly sensitive to the chosen optimality criterion. This makes the precise definition of success consequential when comparing guarantees. The results identify limits on improving SGD's iteration complexity and explain why stronger conclusions require careful attention to both assumptions and the quantity being controlled.
summary.tldr: SGD's classical gradient-norm complexity cannot generally improve without combined additional assumptions, even for convex quadratics.

title: The Complexity of Finding Stationary Points with Stochastic Gradient Descent

abstract: The way that people make choices or exhibit preferences can be strongly affected by the set of available alternatives, often called the choice set. Furthermore, there are usually heterogeneous preferences, either at an individual level within small groups or within sub-populations of large groups. Given the availability of choice data, there are now many models that capture this behavior in order to make effective predictions—however, there is little work in understanding how directly changing the choice set can be used to influence the preferences of a collection of decision-makers. Here, we use discrete choice modeling to develop an optimization framework of such interventions for several problems of group influence, namely maximizing agreement or disagreement and promoting a particular choice. We show that these problems are NP-hard in general, but imposing restrictions reveals a fundamental boundary: promoting a choice can be easier than encouraging consensus or sowing discord. We design approximation algorithms for the hard problems and show that they work well on real-world choice data.

Given the availability of choice data, there are now many models that capture this behavior in order to make effective predictions—however, there is little work in understanding how directly changing the choice set can be used to influence the preferences of a collection of decision-makers. Here, we use discrete choice modeling to develop an optimization framework of such interventions for several problems of group influence, namely maximizing agreement or disagreement and promoting a particular choice. We design approximation algorithms for the hard problems and show that they work well on real-world choice data.

paragraphs: People’s preferences can depend on which alternatives they are offered, and different people may respond differently to the same menu. This paper asks how changing that menu can influence a group’s choices. It moves from predicting decisions with discrete choice models to optimizing the alternatives presented to decision-makers.

The framework considers three objectives: increasing agreement, increasing disagreement, and encouraging a particular choice. The authors show that these optimization problems are NP-hard in general, establishing a computational obstacle to solving every instance efficiently. They then examine restricted settings that reveal differences between the objectives.

Under some restrictions, promoting one option can be easier than making a group converge or divide. This distinguishes changing support for a particular alternative from reshaping agreement across the group. For the difficult problems, the authors develop approximation algorithms and report that they work well on real-world choice data. The result is both a framework for designing choice-set interventions and an account of where their computational difficulty arises.
summary.tldr: Optimizing which choices a group sees is generally hard, but promoting one option can be easier than encouraging agreement or disagreement.

title: Choice Set Optimization Under Discrete Choice Models of Group Decisions

abstract: Thompson sampling is one of the most widely used algorithms in many online decision problems due to its simplicity for implementation and superior empirical performance over other state-of-the-art methods. Despite its popularity and empirical success, it has remained an open problem whether Thompson sampling can achieve the minimax optimal regret O(\sqrt{TK}) for K-armed bandit problems, where T is the total time horizon. In this paper we fill this long open gap by proposing a new Thompson sampling algorithm called MOTS that adaptively truncates the sampling result of the chosen arm at each time step. We prove that this simple variant of Thompson sampling achieves the minimax optimal regret bound O(\sqrt{TK}) for finite time horizon T and also the asymptotic optimal regret bound when $T$ grows to infinity as well. This is the first time that the minimax optimality of multi-armed bandit problems has been attained by Thompson sampling type of algorithms.

paragraphs: Thompson sampling is widely used for sequential decisions because it is simple to implement and has strong empirical performance. The paper addresses a theoretical question left open by that success: whether a Thompson-sampling-style algorithm can attain the best possible worst-case regret rate for multi-armed bandits.

The proposed method, MOTS, modifies Thompson sampling by adaptively truncating the sampling result associated with the chosen arm at each time step. This is a targeted change to the sampling procedure. The authors prove that it achieves regret of order the square root of T times K, where T is the decision horizon and K is the number of arms.

That rate is minimax optimal for finite horizons, matching the best achievable worst-case order. The paper also proves asymptotic regret optimality as the horizon grows without bound. These are complementary guarantees about finite-horizon worst-case behavior and long-run performance. The contribution establishes both for the proposed variant, resolving the stated minimax question for Thompson-sampling-type algorithms.
summary.tldr: MOTS adds adaptive truncation to Thompson sampling and achieves both minimax-optimal finite-horizon regret and asymptotically optimal regret.

title: MOTS: Minimax Optimal Thompson Sampling

abstract: Among dissimilarities between probability distributions, the Kernel Stein Discrepancy (KSD) has received much interest recently. We investigate the properties of its Wasserstein gradient flow to approximate a target probability distribution $\pi$ on $\mathbb{R}^d$, known up to a normalization constant. This leads to a straightforwardly implementable, deterministic score-based method to sample from $\pi$, named KSD Descent, which uses a set of particles to approximate $\pi$. Remarkably, owing to a tractable loss function, KSD Descent can leverage robust parameter-free optimization schemes such as L-BFGS; this contrasts with other popular particle-based schemes such as the Stein Variational Gradient Descent algorithm. We study the convergence properties of KSD Descent and demonstrate its practical relevance. However, we also highlight failure cases by showing that the algorithm can get stuck in spurious local minima.

paragraphs: This paper studies how to approximate a target probability distribution when its density is known only up to a normalization constant. It starts from Kernel Stein Discrepancy, a measure of difference between distributions, and investigates the associated Wasserstein gradient flow. This turns the problem of matching a distribution into a process for moving an approximation toward the target.

The resulting algorithm, KSD Descent, represents the target with a collection of particles and moves them deterministically using score information. A central practical feature is its tractable loss function. That explicit objective allows the use of robust optimization schemes such as L-BFGS, an advantage the authors contrast with other particle methods, including Stein Variational Gradient Descent.

The paper examines convergence properties and demonstrates practical relevance, but also establishes concrete failure cases. KSD Descent can become trapped in spurious local minima, so optimizing its loss does not invariably produce the desired distribution. The contribution therefore combines an implementable sampling approach with an analysis of both its useful optimization structure and its possible failure behavior.
summary.tldr: KSD Descent approximates distributions with deterministically optimized particles and a tractable loss, but can get stuck in spurious local minima.

title: Kernel Stein Discrepancy Descent

abstract: Ratio maximization has applications in areas as diverse as finance, reward shaping for reinforcement learning (RL), and the development of safe artificial intelligence, yet there has been very little exploration of RL algorithms for ratio maximization. This paper addresses this deficiency by introducing two new, model-free RL algorithms for solving cost-aware Markov decision processes, where the goal is to maximize the ratio of long-run average reward to long-run average cost. The first algorithm is a two-timescale scheme based on relative value iteration (RVI) Q-learning and the second is an actor-critic scheme. The paper proves almost sure convergence of the former to the globally optimal solution in the tabular case and almost sure convergence of the latter under linear function approximation for the critic. Unlike previous methods, the two algorithms provably converge for general reward and cost functions under suitable conditions. The paper also provides empirical results demonstrating promising performance and lending strong support to the theoretical results.

paragraphs: Some decision problems call for maximizing reward relative to cost. This paper studies cost-aware Markov decision processes, whose objective is the ratio of long-run average reward to long-run average cost. That objective evaluates sustained reward efficiency and motivates reinforcement-learning methods designed specifically for ratios.

The authors introduce two model-free algorithms. One uses a two-timescale scheme based on relative value iteration Q-learning; the other uses an actor-critic approach. Both have convergence results for general reward and cost functions under suitable conditions, expanding the range of functions covered by previous methods.

The guarantees differ between the algorithms. In the tabular case, the Q-learning-based method converges almost surely to a globally optimal solution. The actor-critic method has an almost-sure convergence result when its critic uses linear function approximation, without the same stated global-optimality claim. Empirical evaluations show promising performance and support the theoretical results. Together, these contributions give ratio maximization dedicated learning algorithms while making the conditions and strength of their respective convergence claims explicit.
summary.tldr: Two model-free reinforcement-learning algorithms optimize long-run reward-to-cost ratios with distinct convergence guarantees under suitable conditions.

title: Reinforcement Learning for Cost-Aware Markov Decision Processes

abstract: As humans, our goals and our environment are persistently changing throughout our lifetime based on our experiences, actions, and internal and external drives. In contrast, typical reinforcement learning problem set-ups consider decision processes that are stationary across episodes. Can we develop reinforcement learning algorithms that can cope with the persistent change in the former, more realistic problem settings? While on-policy algorithms such as policy gradients in principle can be extended to non-stationary settings, the same cannot be said for more efficient off-policy algorithms that replay past experiences when learning. In this work, we formalize this problem setting, and draw upon ideas from the online learning and probabilistic inference literature to derive an off-policy RL algorithm that can reason about and tackle such lifelong non-stationarity. Our method leverages latent variable models to learn a representation of the environment from current and past experiences, and performs off-policy RL with this representation. We further introduce several simulation environments that exhibit lifelong non-stationarity, and empirically find that our approach substantially outperforms approaches that do not reason about environment shift.

paragraphs: The paper studies reinforcement learning in environments that continue changing over an agent’s lifetime. Typical formulations instead assume the decision process stays fixed across episodes. Persistent change creates a particular difficulty for off-policy learning, which reuses past experiences: those experiences may have been collected under different environmental conditions.

The authors formalize this setting and derive an off-policy algorithm using ideas from online learning and probabilistic inference. A latent variable model learns a representation of the environment from both current and past experiences. The reinforcement learning algorithm then uses this representation, giving it a mechanism for reasoning about environmental change while still drawing on earlier data.

The paper also introduces simulation environments with lifelong non-stationarity. In those evaluations, the method substantially outperforms approaches that do not reason about environment shifts. This is an empirical finding in the introduced settings. It supports the value of explicitly representing change when reusing experience, and makes continual adaptation part of the learning problem rather than assuming a fixed environment.
summary.tldr: A latent-variable off-policy reinforcement learning method reasons about persistent environment changes and improves performance in non-stationary simulations.

title: Deep Reinforcement Learning amidst Continual Structured Non-Stationarity

abstract: This paper studies task adaptive pre-trained model selection, an underexplored problem of assessing pre-trained models for the target task and select best ones from the model zoo \emph{without fine-tuning}. A few pilot works addressed the problem in transferring supervised pre-trained models to classification tasks, but they cannot handle emerging unsupervised pre-trained models or regression tasks. In pursuit of a practical assessment method, we propose to estimate the maximum value of label evidence given features extracted by pre-trained models. Unlike the maximum likelihood, the maximum evidence is \emph{immune to over-fitting}, while its expensive computation can be dramatically reduced by our carefully designed algorithm. The Logarithm of Maximum Evidence (LogME) can be used to assess pre-trained models for transfer learning: a pre-trained model with a high LogME value is likely to have good transfer performance. LogME is \emph{fast, accurate, and general}, characterizing itself as the first practical method for assessing pre-trained models. Compared with brute-force fine-tuning, LogME brings at most $3000\times$ speedup in wall-clock time and requires only $1%$ memory footprint. It outperforms prior methods by a large margin in their setting and is applicable to new settings. It is general enough for diverse pre-trained models (supervised pre-trained and unsupervised pre-trained), downstream tasks (classification and regression), and modalities (vision and language). Code is available at this repository: \href{https://github.com/thuml/LogME}{https://github.com/thuml/LogME}.

The authors distinguish this evidence criterion from maximum likelihood, describing maximum evidence as immune to overfitting. They develop an algorithm that greatly reduces its computational cost. A high LogME score indicates that a candidate is likely to transfer well, providing a predictive assessment of downstream performance.

The method covers supervised and unsupervised pre-training, classification and regression, and vision and language. The authors report outperforming prior methods in their settings, with speedups of up to 3,000 times and a memory footprint of only 1% compared with brute-force fine-tuning. These findings support using inexpensive evidence-based assessment to guide model selection.
summary.tldr: LogME cheaply estimates a pre-trained model’s likely transfer performance from features and target labels without fine-tuning.

title: LogME: Practical Assessment of Pre-trained Models for Transfer Learning

abstract: Generating functions, which are widely used in combinatorics and probability theory, encode function values into the coefficients of a polynomial. In this paper, we explore their use as a tractable probabilistic model, and propose probabilistic generating circuits (PGCs) for their efficient representation. PGCs are strictly more expressive efficient than many existing tractable probabilistic models, including determinantal point processes (DPPs), probabilistic circuits (PCs) such as sum-product networks, and tractable graphical models. We contend that PGCs are not just a theoretical framework that unifies vastly different existing models, but also show great potential in modeling realistic data. We exhibit a simple class of PGCs that are not trivially subsumed by simple combinations of PCs and DPPs, and obtain competitive performance on a suite of density estimation benchmarks. We also highlight PGCs’ connection to the theory of strongly Rayleigh distributions.
