paragraphs: This paper develops probabilistic models based on generating functions, which encode values as polynomial coefficients. The authors introduce probabilistic generating circuits, or PGCs, as an efficient way to represent these functions. Their aim is to combine tractable probabilistic modeling with a broader ability to represent distributions compactly.

The theoretical result is greater expressive efficiency than several existing tractable model families, including determinantal point processes, probabilistic circuits such as sum-product networks, and tractable graphical models. This concerns how efficiently distributions can be represented, making the contribution more than a shared notation for existing approaches. The framework also provides a way to connect previously different kinds of probabilistic models.

To investigate practical relevance, the authors construct a simple PGC class that is not trivially captured by simple combinations of probabilistic circuits and determinantal point processes. It achieves competitive performance on density-estimation benchmarks. The paper also identifies a connection to strongly Rayleigh distributions, linking the circuit framework with an established theoretical family while providing empirical evidence of modeling potential.
summary.tldr: Probabilistic generating circuits use polynomial generating functions to offer greater expressive efficiency than several tractable model families and competitive density estimation.

title: Probabilistic Generating Circuits

abstract: Distributions over discrete sets capture the essential statistics including the high-order correlation among elements. Such information provides powerful insight for decision making across various application domains, e.g., product assortment based on product distribution in shopping carts. While deep generative models trained on pre-collected data can capture existing distributions, such pre-trained models are usually not capable of aligning with a target domain in the presence of distribution shift due to reasons such as temporal shift or the change in the population mix. We develop a general framework to adapt a generative model subject to a (possibly counterfactual) target data distribution with both sampling and computation efficiency. Concretely, instead of re-training a full model from scratch, we reuse the learned modules to preserve the correlations between set elements, while only adjusting corresponding components to align with target marginal constraints. We instantiate the approach for three commonly used forms of discrete set distribution—latent variable, autoregressive, and energy based models—and provide efficient solutions for marginal-constrained optimization in either primal or dual forms. Experiments on both synthetic and real-world e-commerce and EHR datasets show that the proposed framework is able to practically align a generative model to match marginal constraints under distribution shift.

paragraphs: Distributions over discrete sets describe both how often individual elements occur and how elements appear together. A model of shopping carts, for example, can capture relationships among products. When populations or conditions change, a pretrained generative model may no longer match the desired distribution.

This paper develops a framework for adapting such models to target marginal constraints, including possibly counterfactual targets. It reuses learned modules to preserve correlations among set elements while adjusting the components responsible for matching those constraints. The approach aims to retain useful learned structure without retraining an entire generative model from the beginning.

Experiments use synthetic data and real e-commerce and electronic health record datasets. The results show practical alignment with target marginal constraints under distribution shift. This supports modular adaptation as a sampling- and computation-efficient way to update selected distributional properties while retaining learned dependencies.
summary.tldr: Modular adaptation updates discrete-set generative models to match target marginals while reusing learned correlations.

title: Marginal Distribution Adaptation for Discrete Sets via Module-Oriented Divergence Minimization

abstract: Approaches to policy optimization have been motivated from diverse principles, based on how the parametric model is interpreted (e.g. value versus policy representation) or how the learning objective is formulated, yet they share a common goal of maximizing expected return. To better capture the commonalities and identify key differences between policy optimization methods, we develop a unified perspective that re-expresses the underlying updates in terms of a limited choice of gradient form and scaling function. In particular, we identify a parameterized space of approximate gradient updates for policy optimization that is highly structured, yet covers both classical and recent examples, including PPO. As a result, we obtain novel yet well motivated updates that generalize existing algorithms in a way that can deliver benefits both in terms of convergence speed and final result quality. An experimental investigation demonstrates that the additional degrees of freedom provided in the parameterized family of updates can be leveraged to obtain non-trivial improvements both in synthetic domains and on popular deep RL benchmarks.

paragraphs: Policy optimization methods can begin from different interpretations of a model or different learning objectives, even though they all seek higher expected return. This paper looks for shared structure in the updates these methods actually perform. The aim is to make their similarities and differences easier to identify within a common mathematical description.

The authors express those updates through a limited selection of gradient forms and scaling functions. This produces a structured, parameterized family of approximate gradient updates that includes both classical and recent methods, including PPO. The parameters describe meaningful choices within the update, providing a way to move beyond the specific combinations used by established algorithms.

Using this family, the paper derives new updates that generalize existing approaches. Experiments in synthetic settings and popular deep reinforcement learning benchmarks show that the additional flexibility can improve convergence speed and final performance. The contribution is therefore both an organizing framework and a route to useful algorithm variants, with benefits demonstrated empirically.
summary.tldr: A unified family of approximate policy gradients reveals connections between algorithms and enables updates with demonstrated learning improvements.

title: A Parametric Class of Approximate Gradient Updates for Policy Optimization

abstract: Off-policy evaluation and learning (OPE/L) use offline observational data to make better decisions, which is crucial in applications where online experimentation is limited. However, depending entirely on logged data, OPE/L is sensitive to environment distribution shifts — discrepancies between the data-generating environment and that where policies are deployed. Si et al., (2020) proposed distributionally robust OPE/L (DROPE/L) to address this, but the proposal relies on inverse-propensity weighting, whose estimation error and regret will deteriorate if propensities are nonparametrically estimated and whose variance is suboptimal even if not. For standard, non-robust, OPE/L, this is solved by doubly robust (DR) methods, but they do not naturally extend to the more complex DROPE/L, which involves a worst-case expectation. In this paper, we propose the first DR algorithms for DROPE/L with KL-divergence uncertainty sets. For evaluation, we propose Localized Doubly Robust DROPE (LDR$^2$OPE) and show that it achieves semiparametric efficiency under weak product rates conditions. Thanks to a localization technique, LDR$^2$OPE only requires fitting a small number of regressions, just like DR methods for standard OPE. For learning, we propose Continuum Doubly Robust DROPL (CDR$^2$OPL) and show that, under a product rate condition involving a continuum of regressions, it enjoys a fast regret rate of $O(N^{-1/2})$ even when unknown propensities are nonparametrically estimated. We empirically validate our algorithms in simulations and further extend our results to general $f$-divergence uncertainty sets.

paragraphs: Off-policy evaluation and learning use recorded decisions and outcomes to assess or improve policies without fresh online experiments. Deployment conditions can differ from those represented in the records, motivating evaluation against a range of possible distributions. Existing distributionally robust approaches rely on weighting by action probabilities, which can introduce unfavorable variance and estimation behavior.

The paper develops doubly robust algorithms for uncertainty sets defined through KL divergence. Its evaluation algorithm uses localization so that only a small number of regressions must be fitted. Under weak conditions on products of estimation rates, it achieves semiparametric efficiency. This supplies a statistical efficiency result while retaining a manageable regression workload.

For policy learning, a second algorithm achieves regret of order one over the square root of the sample size under a product-rate condition involving a continuum of regressions. The result allows unknown action probabilities to be estimated nonparametrically. Simulations support the methods, and the authors extend their results to general f-divergence uncertainty sets. The guarantees remain tied to their stated estimation-rate conditions.
summary.tldr: Doubly robust methods improve the statistical guarantees of off-policy evaluation and learning under specified distribution-shift uncertainty sets and estimation conditions.

title: Doubly Robust Distributionally Robust Off-Policy Evaluation and Learning

abstract: Many problems in machine learning involve data sets in which each data point is a point cloud in $\mathbb{R}^D$. A growing number of applications require a means of measuring not only distances between point clouds, but also angles, volumes, derivatives, and other more advanced concepts. To formulate and quantify these concepts in a coordinate-invariant way, we develop a Riemannian geometric framework for point cloud data. By interpreting each point in a point cloud as a sample drawn from some given underlying probability density, the space of point cloud data can be given the structure of a statistical manifold – each point on this manifold represents a point cloud – with the Fisher information metric acting as a natural Riemannian metric. Two autoencoder applications of our framework are presented: (i) smoothly deforming one 3D object into another via interpolation between the two corresponding point clouds; (ii) learning an optimal set of latent space coordinates for point cloud data that best preserves angles and distances, and thus produces a more discriminative representation space. Experiments with large-scale standard benchmark point cloud data show greatly improved classification accuracy vis-á-vis existing methods. Code is available at https://github.com/seungyeon-k/SMF-public.

paragraphs: A point cloud represents an object or observation through a collection of points. Comparing such collections often requires more than a distance: applications may also need meaningful angles, volumes, or derivatives. This paper develops a geometric framework that defines these quantities without making their meaning depend on the chosen coordinates.

The authors interpret the points within each cloud as samples from an underlying probability density. Each entire cloud then becomes a point on a statistical manifold, a space whose elements represent probability-based objects. The Fisher information metric supplies the geometry of this space, providing a common mathematical basis for measuring and manipulating point clouds.

The framework is applied to two autoencoder tasks. One smoothly transforms a three-dimensional object into another by interpolating between their point clouds. The other learns latent coordinates that preserve angles and distances, aiming for a more discriminative representation. Experiments on large standard point-cloud benchmarks report substantial classification improvements over existing methods. The results connect richer geometric descriptions to useful learned representations.
summary.tldr: Treating point clouds as probability-based geometric objects enables smooth interpolation and latent representations with improved classification results.

title: A Statistical Manifold Framework for Point Cloud Data

abstract: In federated learning (FL), model performance typically suffers from client drift induced by data heterogeneity, and mainstream works focus on correcting client drift. We propose a different approach named virtual homogeneity learning (VHL) to directly “rectify” the data heterogeneity. In particular, VHL conducts FL with a virtual homogeneous dataset crafted to satisfy two conditions: containing no private information and being separable. The virtual dataset can be generated from pure noise shared across clients, aiming to calibrate the features from the heterogeneous clients. Theoretically, we prove that VHL can achieve provable generalization performance on the natural distribution. Empirically, we demonstrate that VHL endows FL with drastically improved convergence speed and generalization performance. VHL is the first attempt towards using a virtual dataset to address data heterogeneity, offering new and effective means to FL.

paragraphs: Federated learning can suffer when clients hold different data distributions. These differences induce client drift, which can harm the shared model. Virtual homogeneity learning, or VHL, addresses the heterogeneity through an additional virtual dataset intended to help calibrate features across clients.

The virtual dataset is designed to meet two conditions: it contains no private information and is separable. It can be generated from pure noise shared among the clients. By introducing homogeneous virtual data into federated training, the method aims to align features learned from the clients' otherwise heterogeneous data. The shared reference therefore does not require sharing their private examples.

The authors prove a generalization result on the natural data distribution and empirically demonstrate substantially improved convergence speed and generalization. These findings support using virtual data as a mechanism for addressing differences between clients. The contribution is the connection between a carefully constructed homogeneous dataset and improved federated training on the actual heterogeneous distributions.
summary.tldr: VHL uses shared, nonprivate virtual data to calibrate client features, improving federated convergence and generalization in the reported experiments.

title: Virtual Homogeneity Learning: Defending against Data Heterogeneity in Federated Learning

abstract: Correlation clustering is a widely studied framework for clustering based on pairwise similarity and dissimilarity scores, but its best approximation algorithms rely on impractical linear programming relaxations. We present faster approximation algorithms that avoid these relaxations, for two well-studied special cases: cluster editing and cluster deletion. We accomplish this by drawing new connections to edge labeling problems related to the principle of strong triadic closure. This leads to faster and more practical linear programming algorithms, as well as extremely scalable combinatorial techniques, including the first combinatorial approximation algorithm for cluster deletion. In practice, our algorithms produce approximate solutions that nearly match the best algorithms in quality, while scaling to problems that are orders of magnitude larger.

Its strongest approximation algorithms can depend on linear-programming relaxations that are too expensive for large instances. This paper targets two established versions of the problem, cluster editing and cluster deletion, with the aim of retaining useful solution quality while making computation more practical.

These connections yield more practical linear-programming approaches and highly scalable combinatorial methods that avoid the expensive relaxations. The latter include what the authors identify as the first combinatorial approximation algorithm for cluster deletion.

The finding is a trade-off improvement rather than a claim of exact optimization: the methods produce approximate clusterings, but make high-quality approximation accessible at substantially larger scales through a different formulation of the underlying problem.
summary.tldr: Connections to strong triadic closure yield scalable approximation algorithms for cluster editing and deletion with near-leading empirical solution quality.

title: Correlation Clustering via Strong Triadic Closure Labeling: Fast Approximation Algorithms and Practical Lower Bounds

abstract: We study the problem of offline Imitation Learning (IL) where an agent aims to learn an optimal expert behavior policy without additional online environment interactions. Instead, the agent is provided with a supplementary offline dataset from suboptimal behaviors. Prior works that address this problem either require that expert data occupies the majority proportion of the offline dataset, or need to learn a reward function and perform offline reinforcement learning (RL) afterwards. In this paper, we aim to address the problem without additional steps of reward learning and offline RL training for the case when demonstrations contain a large proportion of suboptimal data. Built upon behavioral cloning (BC), we introduce an additional discriminator to distinguish expert and non-expert data. We propose a cooperation framework to boost the learning of both tasks, Based on this framework, we design a new IL algorithm, where the outputs of the discriminator serve as the weights of the BC loss. Experimental results show that our proposed algorithm achieves higher returns and faster training speed compared to baseline algorithms.

paragraphs: The paper studies how an agent can learn expert behavior using an existing dataset without further interaction with its environment. The difficult case is a dataset containing a large proportion of suboptimal behavior. Learning to copy that data indiscriminately would give substantial influence to demonstrations that do not represent the desired expert policy.

The method builds on behavioral cloning and adds a discriminator that distinguishes expert from non-expert data. Its outputs become weights in the behavioral-cloning loss, changing how strongly individual demonstrations contribute to training. A cooperative framework is designed to improve both discrimination and policy learning, linking the assessment of demonstration quality to the process of learning behavior.

This design addresses the problem without separate reward-learning and offline reinforcement-learning stages. It also targets a setting where expert demonstrations need not dominate the dataset, unlike some earlier approaches described by the authors. Experiments report higher returns and faster training than the compared baselines. The findings support weighting demonstrations as a practical way to learn from mixed-quality offline behavior.
summary.tldr: A discriminator weights behavioral-cloning examples to improve offline imitation learning from datasets containing substantial suboptimal behavior.

title: Discriminator-Weighted Offline Imitation Learning from Suboptimal Demonstrations

abstract: Transfer learning is a de facto standard method for efficiently training machine learning models for data-scarce problems by adding and fine-tuning new classification layers to a model pre-trained on large datasets. Although numerous previous studies proposed to use homomorphic encryption to resolve the data privacy issue in transfer learning in the machine learning as a service setting, most of them only focused on encrypted inference. In this study, we present HETAL, an efficient Homomorphic Encryption based Transfer Learning algorithm, that protects the client’s privacy in training tasks by encrypting the client data using the CKKS homomorphic encryption scheme. HETAL is the first practical scheme that strictly provides encrypted training, adopting validation-based early stopping and achieving the accuracy of nonencrypted training. We propose an efficient encrypted matrix multiplication algorithm, which is 1.8 to 323 times faster than prior methods, and a highly precise softmax approximation algorithm with increased coverage. The experimental results for five well-known benchmark datasets show total training times of 567–3442 seconds, which is less than an hour.

paragraphs: Transfer learning adapts a pretrained model to a new task, often by training additional classification layers when labeled data are scarce. In a machine-learning service, that training can involve private client data. This paper addresses encrypted training, extending beyond the encrypted inference that had been the focus of most earlier work in this setting.

HETAL encrypts client data using the CKKS homomorphic encryption scheme, allowing the training computation to operate on encrypted data. These results provide concrete evidence for the practicality of the proposed encrypted transfer-learning procedure in the evaluated settings.
summary.tldr: HETAL enables encrypted transfer-learning training that matches nonencrypted accuracy in its evaluation and finishes within an hour on five benchmarks.

title: HETAL: Efficient Privacy-preserving Transfer Learning with Homomorphic Encryption

abstract: The study of universal approximation properties (UAP) for neural networks (NN) has a long history. When the network width is unlimited, only a single hidden layer is sufficient for UAP. In contrast, when the depth is unlimited, the width for UAP needs to be not less than the critical width $w^*_{\min}=\max(d_x,d_y)$, where $d_x$ and $d_y$ are the dimensions of the input and output, respectively. Recently, (Cai, 2022) shows that a leaky-ReLU NN with this critical width can achieve UAP for $L^p$ functions on a compact domain $\mathcal{K}$, i.e., the UAP for $L^p(\mathcal{K},\mathbb{R}^{d_y})$. This paper examines a uniform UAP for the function class $C(\mathcal{K},\mathbb{R}^{d_y})$ and gives the exact minimum width of the leaky-ReLU NN as $w_{\min}=\max(d_x+1,d_y)+1_{d_y=d_x+1}$, which involves the effects of the output dimensions. To obtain this result, we propose a novel lift-flow-discretization approach that shows that the uniform UAP has a deep connection with topological theory.

paragraphs: Universal approximation asks whether a neural network family can approximate every function in a specified class arbitrarily well. This paper studies how narrow leaky-ReLU networks can be when depth is unrestricted. Its target is uniform approximation of continuous functions on a compact domain, where the approximation must be accurate throughout the domain.

The authors derive the exact minimum width: max(d_x + 1, d_y), with one additional unit when d_y equals d_x + 1. Here d_x and d_y are the input and output dimensions. The formula shows that the output dimension affects the threshold, including a special case that requires more width than the maximum expression alone would indicate.

To prove the result, the paper introduces a lift-flow-discretization approach and connects uniform approximation to topology. The result distinguishes this setting from earlier approximation guarantees for Lp functions at the critical width max(d_x, d_y). It establishes a precise architectural threshold for representational capability under the stated approximation criterion and unrestricted depth.
summary.tldr: The paper establishes the exact minimum width for uniform universal approximation by arbitrarily deep leaky-ReLU networks on compact domains.

title: Minimum Width of Leaky-ReLU Neural Networks for Uniform Universal Approximation

abstract: We observe that the mapping between an image’s representation in one model to its representation in another can be learned surprisingly well with just a linear layer, even across diverse models. Building on this observation, we propose text-to-concept , where features from a fixed pretrained model are aligned linearly to the CLIP space, so that text embeddings from CLIP’s text encoder become directly comparable to the aligned features. With text-to-concept, we convert fixed off-the-shelf vision encoders to surprisingly strong zero-shot classifiers for free, with accuracy at times even surpassing that of CLIP, despite being much smaller models and trained on a small fraction of the data compared to CLIP. We show other immediate use-cases of text-to-concept, like building concept bottleneck models with no concept supervision, diagnosing distribution shifts in terms of human concepts, and retrieving images satisfying a set of text-based constraints. Lastly, we demonstrate the feasibility of concept-to-text , where vectors in a model’s feature space are decoded by first aligning to the CLIP before being fed to a GPT-based generative model. Our work suggests existing deep models, with presumably diverse architectures and training, represent input samples relatively similarly, and a two-way communication across model representation spaces and to humans (through language) is viable.

After alignment, the vision model’s features can be directly compared with embeddings produced by CLIP’s text encoder.

Together, these results suggest that models with different architectures and training can encode inputs in relatively compatible ways. The evidence supports practical communication across representation spaces and with people through language, rather than establishing that all models have identical internal representations.
summary.tldr: Linear alignment with CLIP connects pretrained vision models to language, enabling zero-shot classification, concept-based analysis, and feature-to-text generation.

title: Text-To-Concept (and Back) via Cross-Model Alignment

abstract: We develop information geometric techniques to understand the representations learned by deep networks when they are trained on different tasks using supervised, meta-, semi-supervised and contrastive learning. We shed light on the following phenomena that relate to the structure of the space of tasks: (1) the manifold of probabilistic models trained on different tasks using different representation learning methods is effectively low-dimensional; (2) supervised learning on one task results in a surprising amount of progress even on seemingly dissimilar tasks; progress on other tasks is larger if the training task has diverse classes; (3) the structure of the space of tasks indicated by our analysis is consistent with parts of the Wordnet phylogenetic tree; (4) episodic meta-learning algorithms and supervised learning traverse different trajectories during training but they fit similar models eventually; (5) contrastive and semi-supervised learning methods traverse trajectories similar to those of supervised learning. We use classification tasks constructed from the CIFAR-10 and Imagenet datasets to study these phenomena. Code is available at https://github.com/grasp-lyrl/picture_of_space_of_tasks.

paragraphs: This paper investigates how representations learned for different tasks relate to one another. The authors use information geometry to study probabilistic models produced by supervised, meta-learning, semi-supervised, and contrastive approaches. Their analysis examines both the models reached after training and the paths taken to reach them, using classification tasks constructed from CIFAR-10 and ImageNet.

A central finding is that the resulting collection of models is effectively low-dimensional. Despite the variety of tasks and training methods, their relationships can therefore be described through a relatively compact structure. Training on one task also produces progress on apparently dissimilar tasks, with greater progress when the training task contains diverse classes. Parts of the observed task structure agree with the WordNet hierarchy.

The training paths reveal another distinction: episodic meta-learning and supervised learning follow different trajectories but eventually fit similar models. Contrastive and semi-supervised methods follow paths resembling supervised learning. Together, these observations connect task transfer, representation similarity, and training dynamics within the studied classification settings.
summary.tldr: Information geometry reveals compact relationships between learned tasks and shows how different training methods can reach similar models.

title: A Picture of the Space of Typical Learnable Tasks

abstract: We consider solving sequential decision-making problems in the scenario where the agent has access to two supervision sources: $\textit{reward signal}$ and a $\textit{teacher}$ that can be queried to obtain a $\textit{good}$ action for any state encountered by the agent. Learning solely from rewards, or reinforcement learning, is data inefficient and may not learn high-reward policies in challenging scenarios involving sparse rewards or partial observability. On the other hand, learning from a teacher may sometimes be infeasible. For instance, the actions provided by a teacher with privileged information may be unlearnable by an agent with limited information (i.e., partial observability). In other scenarios, the teacher might be sub-optimal, and imitating their actions can limit the agent’s performance. To overcome these challenges, prior work proposed to jointly optimize imitation and reinforcement learning objectives but relied on heuristics and problem-specific hyper-parameter tuning to balance the two objectives. We introduce Teacher Guided Reinforcement Learning (TGRL), a principled approach to dynamically balance following the teacher’s guidance and leveraging RL. TGRL outperforms strong baselines across diverse domains without hyperparameter tuning.

paragraphs: An agent learning sequential decisions may have both rewards and a teacher that can recommend actions. Each source has weaknesses. Reward-based learning can require substantial data, especially with sparse rewards or partial observability. A teacher may be suboptimal, or may use privileged information that the agent cannot observe and therefore cannot reliably imitate.

TGRL addresses the decision of how much to follow the teacher and how much to learn from rewards. Earlier combined approaches balanced imitation and reinforcement learning through heuristics and problem-specific tuning. The paper proposes a principled method that adjusts this balance dynamically, allowing the two supervision sources to play different roles during learning.

The authors report that TGRL outperforms strong baselines across diverse domains without hyperparameter tuning. The significance is tied to the stated setting: teacher guidance is available, but its usefulness may be limited by information differences or imperfect actions. Dynamically balancing guidance and reward learning provides a way to benefit from teaching while accounting for those reasons that imitation alone may fall short.
summary.tldr: TGRL dynamically balances teacher imitation and reward-based learning, outperforming strong baselines across the reported domains without hyperparameter tuning.

title: TGRL: An Algorithm for Teacher Guided Reinforcement Learning

abstract: Semi-supervised learning is a powerful technique for leveraging unlabeled data to improve machine learning models, but it can be affected by the presence of “informative" labels, which occur when some classes are more likely to be labeled than others. In the missing data literature, such labels are called missing not at random. In this paper, we propose a novel approach to address this issue by estimating the missing-data mechanism and using inverse propensity weighting to debias any SSL algorithm, including those using data augmentation. We also propose a likelihood ratio test to assess whether or not labels are indeed informative. Finally, we demonstrate the performance of the proposed methods on different datasets, in particular on two medical datasets for which we design pseudo-realistic missing data scenarios.

paragraphs: Semi-supervised learning combines labeled and unlabeled examples, but the labeled examples may not represent all classes equally. If one class is more likely to receive labels than another, the presence of a label itself carries information. The paper studies this missing-not-at-random setting, where ignoring the labeling process can bias learning.

The proposed approach first estimates the mechanism that determines which examples receive labels. It then uses inverse propensity weighting to compensate for unequal labeling probabilities. The correction is presented as applicable to any semi-supervised learning algorithm, including methods that use data augmentation. This makes the labeling mechanism an explicit part of the learning procedure.

The authors also introduce a likelihood ratio test for assessing whether label availability is informative. Together, the test and correction address both recognizing the problem and responding to it. Evaluations cover several datasets, including two medical datasets with constructed, pseudo-realistic missing-data scenarios. Those scenarios examine the methods under deliberately modeled labeling patterns rather than establishing performance for every naturally occurring medical labeling process.
summary.tldr: Estimating how labels go missing enables a weighting correction for class-dependent labeling bias in semi-supervised learning.

title: Are labels informative in semi-supervised learning? Estimating and leveraging the missing-data mechanism.

abstract: We introduce a new family of physics-inspired generative models termed PFGM++ that unifies diffusion models and Poisson Flow Generative Models (PFGM). These models realize generative trajectories for N dimensional data by embedding paths in N+D dimensional space while still controlling the progression with a simple scalar norm of the D additional variables. The new models reduce to PFGM when D=1 and to diffusion models when D$\to\infty$. The flexibility of choosing D allows us to trade off robustness against rigidity as increasing D results in more concentrated coupling between the data and the additional variable norms. We dispense with the biased large batch field targets used in PFGM and instead provide an unbiased perturbation-based objective similar to diffusion models. To explore different choices of D, we provide a direct alignment method for transferring well-tuned hyperparameters from diffusion models (D$\to\infty$) to any finite D values. Our experiments show that models with finite D can be superior to previous state-of-the-art diffusion models on CIFAR-10/FFHQ 64$\times$64 datasets/LSUN Churches 256$\times$256, with median Ds. In class-conditional setting, D=2048 yields current state-of-the-art FID of 1.74 on CIFAR-10 without additional training. Furthermore, we demonstrate that models with smaller $D$ exhibit improved robustness against modeling errors. Code is available at https://github.com/Newbeeer/pfgmpp

summary.tldr: PFGM++ unifies Poisson flow and diffusion models through an adjustable dimensionality that trades rigidity against robustness.

title: PFGM++: Unlocking the Potential of Physics-Inspired Generative Models

abstract: Utilizing machine learning to address partial differential equations (PDEs) presents significant challenges due to the diversity of spatial domains and their corresponding state configurations, which complicates the task of encompassing all potential scenarios through data-driven methodologies alone. Moreover, there are legitimate concerns regarding the generalization and reliability of such approaches, as they often overlook inherent physical constraints. In response to these challenges, this study introduces a novel machine-learning architecture that is highly generalizable and adheres to conservation laws and physical symmetries, thereby ensuring greater reliability. The foundation of this architecture is graph neural networks (GNNs), which are adept at accommodating a variety of shapes and forms. Additionally, we explore the parallels between GNNs and traditional numerical solvers, facilitating a seamless integration of conservative principles and symmetries into machine learning models. Our findings from experiments demonstrate that the model’s inclusion of physical laws significantly enhances its generalizability, i.e., no significant accuracy degradation for unseen spatial domains while other models degrade. The code is available at https://github.com/yellowshippo/fluxgnn-icml2024.

paragraphs: Learning to solve partial differential equations is difficult when spatial shapes and physical states vary widely. Training data alone may not cover the possible configurations, and predictions can become unreliable when a model ignores physical constraints. This paper develops a graph neural architecture that incorporates conservation laws and physical symmetries into the solver.

Graphs provide a foundation for handling different spatial forms. The authors also examine connections between graph neural networks and traditional numerical solvers, using those connections to integrate conservative principles and symmetries into the architecture. This makes physical structure part of the model’s design, reducing its dependence on learning every relevant behavior solely from examples.

Experiments report substantially better generalization when physical laws are included. In particular, the proposed model shows no significant accuracy degradation on unseen spatial domains in the reported tests, while other models degrade. The finding supports the architectural choice: respecting physical structure can help a learned PDE solver transfer across domain shapes, with the evidence established through the experiments presented.
summary.tldr: A graph neural PDE solver incorporates conservation and physical symmetries, showing stronger generalization to unseen spatial domains in experiments.

title: Graph Neural PDE Solvers with Conservation and Similarity-Equivariance

abstract: The k-means with outliers problem is one of the most extensively studied clustering problems in the field of machine learning, where the goal is to discard up to z outliers and identify a minimum k-means clustering on the remaining data points. Most previous results for this problem have running time dependent on the aspect ratio Δ (the ratio between the maximum and the minimum pairwise distances) to achieve fast approximations. To address the issue of aspect ratio dependency on the running time, we propose sampling-based algorithms with almost linear running time in the data size, where a crucial component of our approach is an algorithm called Fast-Sampling. Fast-Sampling algorithm can find inliers that well approximate the optimal clustering centers without relying on a guess for the optimal clustering costs, where a 4-approximate solution can be obtained in time $O(\frac{ndk\log\log n}{\epsilon^2})$ with O(k/ϵ) centers opened and (1+ϵ)z outliers discarded. To reduce the number of centers opened, we propose a center reduction algorithm, where an O(1/ϵ)-approximate solution can be obtained in time $O(\frac{ndk\log \log n}{\epsilon^2} + dpoly(k, \frac{1}{\epsilon})\log(n\Delta))$ with (1+ϵ)z outliers discarded and exactly k centers opened. Empirical experiments suggest that our proposed sampling-based algorithms outperform state-of-the-art algorithms for the k-means with outliers problem.

To address the issue of aspect ratio dependency on the running time, we propose sampling-based algorithms with almost linear running time in the data size, where a crucial component of our approach is an algorithm called Fast-Sampling. Fast-Sampling algorithm can find inliers that well approximate the optimal clustering centers without relying on a guess for the optimal clustering costs, where a 4-approximate solution can be obtained in time $O(\frac{ndk\log\log n}{\epsilon^2})$ with O(k/ϵ) centers opened and (1+ϵ)z outliers discarded. To reduce the number of centers opened, we propose a center reduction algorithm, where an O(1/ϵ)-approximate solution can be obtained in time $O(\frac{ndk\log \log n}{\epsilon^2} + dpoly(k, \frac{1}{\epsilon})\log(n\Delta))$ with (1+ϵ)z outliers discarded and exactly k centers opened. Empirical experiments suggest that our proposed sampling-based algorithms outperform state-of-the-art algorithms for the k-means with outliers problem.

paragraphs: Clustering with outliers aims to discard up to z points and cluster the remainder around k centers. Fast approximation methods have often had runtimes depending on the aspect ratio, the largest pairwise distance divided by the smallest. This paper develops sampling-based algorithms to reduce that dependence and achieve nearly linear scaling in data size.

Its Fast-Sampling component identifies useful inliers without guessing the optimal clustering cost. It gives a 4-approximation while opening O(k/epsilon) centers and discarding up to (1+epsilon)z outliers. Its runtime is O(ndk log log n / epsilon²), where n is the number of points and d their dimension.

A second procedure reduces the result to exactly k centers, obtaining an O(1/epsilon)-approximation with the same relaxed outlier allowance. This adds a runtime term involving log(n times the aspect ratio), so aspect-ratio dependence remains in that stage. Experiments suggest better performance than state-of-the-art methods. The guarantees expose a useful trade-off between speed, approximation quality, the number of centers, and permission to discard slightly more outliers.
summary.tldr: Sampling-based algorithms accelerate k-means with outliers through explicit trade-offs in approximation quality, center count, and the allowed number of discarded points.

title: Near-Linear Time Approximation Algorithms for k-means with Outliers

abstract: Deep Neural Networks (DNN) have shown great promise in many classification applications, yet are widely known to have poorly calibrated predictions when they are over-parametrized. Improving DNN calibration without comprising on model accuracy is of extreme importance and interest in safety critical applications such as in the health-care sector. In this work, we show that decoupling the training of feature extraction layers and classification layers in over-parametrized DNN architectures such as Wide Residual Networks (WRN) and Vision Transformers (ViT) significantly improves model calibration whilst retaining accuracy, and at a low training cost. In addition, we show that placing a Gaussian prior on the last hidden layer outputs of a DNN, and training the model variationally in the classification training stage, even further improves calibration. We illustrate these methods improve calibration across ViT and WRN architectures for several image classification benchmark datasets.

paragraphs: A classifier's confidence is useful only when it reflects how often its predictions are correct. Large neural networks can classify images accurately while reporting poorly calibrated confidence. This paper investigates whether changing how different parts of the network are trained can improve that alignment while preserving classification accuracy.

The authors separate training of the feature extraction layers from training of the classification layers. These components serve different roles: one builds representations of the input, while the other converts those representations into predictions. Decoupling their training improves calibration in the studied over-parameterized architectures, with low training cost and retained accuracy.

A further modification places a Gaussian prior on the outputs of the last hidden layer and uses variational training during the classification stage. This produces additional calibration improvements. Experiments cover Vision Transformers and Wide Residual Networks on several image classification benchmarks. The findings indicate that training organization, together with probabilistic treatment of the final representation, can improve confidence estimates without requiring an observed accuracy tradeoff in these evaluations.
summary.tldr: Training feature extraction and classification separately improves neural-network calibration while retaining accuracy in the reported image experiments.

title: Decoupling Feature Extraction and Classification Layers for Calibrated Neural Networks

abstract: Knowledge distillation is a widely adopted model compression technique that has been successfully applied to object detection. In feature distillation, it is common practice for the student model to imitate the feature responses of the teacher model, with the underlying objective of improving its own abilities by reducing the disparity with the teacher. However, it is crucial to recognize that the disparities between the student and teacher are inconsistent, highlighting their varying abilities. In this paper, we explore the inconsistency in the disparity between teacher and student feature maps and analyze their impact on the efficiency of the distillation. We find that regions with varying degrees of difference should be treated separately, with different distillation constraints applied accordingly. We introduce our distillation method called Disparity Feature Distillation(DFD). The core idea behind DFD is to apply different treatments to regions with varying learning difficulties, simultaneously incorporating leniency and strictness. It enables the student to better assimilate the teacher’s knowledge. Through extensive experiments, we demonstrate the effectiveness of our proposed DFD in achieving significant improvements. For instance, when applied to detectors based on ResNet50 such as RetinaNet, FasterRCNN, and RepPoints, our method enhances their mAP from 37.4%, 38.4%, 38.6% to 41.7%, 42.4%, 42.7%, respectively. Our approach also demonstrates substantial improvements on YOLO and ViT-based models. The code is available at https://github.com/luckin99/DFD.

paragraphs: Knowledge distillation trains a smaller student model using a teacher model’s responses. For object detection, one common approach asks the student to imitate the teacher’s feature maps. This paper examines a complication: the gap between those maps varies across regions, reflecting different levels of student ability and different learning difficulties.

Disparity Feature Distillation, or DFD, applies different constraints to regions with different degrees of teacher–student disagreement. Its central idea is to combine stricter and more lenient treatment within the same distillation process. The authors argue that accounting for uneven disparities helps the student absorb the teacher’s knowledge more effectively than treating the entire feature map uniformly.

For ResNet50-based RetinaNet, FasterRCNN, and RepPoints detectors, reported mAP rises from 37.4%, 38.4%, and 38.6% to 41.7%, 42.4%, and 42.7%, respectively. The paper also reports substantial improvements for YOLO and vision-transformer-based models. These experiments support the practical value of adapting distillation constraints to local learning difficulty across several detector architectures, rather than viewing every teacher–student difference as an equivalent training signal.
summary.tldr: DFD improves detector distillation by applying different constraints to feature regions with different teacher–student disparities.

title: DFD: Distilling the Feature Disparity Differently for Detectors

abstract: Shuffling gradient methods are widely used in modern machine learning tasks and include three popular implementations: Random Reshuffle (RR), Shuffle Once (SO), and Incremental Gradient (IG). Compared to the empirical success, the theoretical guarantee of shuffling gradient methods was not well-understood for a long time. Until recently, the convergence rates had just been established for the average iterate for convex functions and the last iterate for strongly convex problems (using squared distance as the metric). However, when using the function value gap as the convergence criterion, existing theories cannot interpret the good performance of the last iterate in different settings (e.g., constrained optimization). To bridge this gap between practice and theory, we prove the first last-iterate convergence rates for shuffling gradient methods with respect to the objective value even without strong convexity. Our new results either (nearly) match the existing last-iterate lower bounds or are as fast as the previous best upper bounds for the average iterate.

paragraphs: Shuffling gradient methods include Random Reshuffle, Shuffle Once, and Incremental Gradient. Although widely used, their practical performance has been only partly explained by convergence theory. This paper focuses on the final iterate produced by optimization and asks how quickly its objective value approaches the optimum, a criterion distinct from distance to an optimal solution.

Previous results covered averaged iterates for convex objectives and final iterates for strongly convex problems using squared distance. Those guarantees did not adequately explain final-iterate performance measured through the objective-value gap in settings such as constrained optimization. The authors establish last-iterate convergence rates for this gap even without requiring strong convexity.

The new bounds either nearly match existing last-iterate lower bounds or match the speed of previous best upper bounds for averaged iterates. This gives a stronger theoretical account of the final result returned by shuffling methods. The contribution is specifically about convergence guarantees and their performance criterion: it connects the final iterate’s objective value to rates previously unavailable under the studied conditions.
summary.tldr: The paper establishes objective-value convergence rates for the final iterate of shuffling gradient methods without requiring strong convexity.

title: On the Last-Iterate Convergence of Shuffling Gradient Methods

abstract: Most text-to-3D generators build upon off-the-shelf text-to-image models trained on billions of images. They use variants of Score Distillation Sampling (SDS), which is slow, somewhat unstable, and prone to artifacts. A mitigation is to fine-tune the 2D generator to be multi-view aware, which can help distillation or can be combined with reconstruction networks to output 3D objects directly. In this paper, we further explore the design space of text-to-3D models. We significantly improve multi-view generation by considering video instead of image generators. Combined with a 3D reconstruction algorithm which, by using Gaussian splatting, can optimize a robust image-based loss, we directly produce high-quality 3D outputs from the generated views. Our new method, IM-3D, reduces the number of evaluations of the 2D generator network 10-100$\times$, resulting in a much more efficient pipeline, better quality, fewer geometric inconsistencies, and higher yield of usable 3D assets.

paragraphs: Many text-to-3D systems depend on pretrained image generators and a procedure called score distillation sampling. That procedure can be slow, unstable, and prone to visual artifacts. IM-3D explores a different route: generate multiple views of an object and reconstruct a 3D asset from those views.

The key generation choice is to use a video generator rather than an image generator. The authors report that this substantially improves multiview generation. They combine the generated views with a reconstruction algorithm based on Gaussian splatting, which allows optimization of a robust image-based loss. The resulting pipeline directly converts the views into high-quality 3D outputs.

IM-3D reduces evaluations of the 2D generator network by a factor of 10 to 100. The paper reports a more efficient pipeline together with improved quality, fewer geometric inconsistencies, and a larger proportion of usable assets. These outcomes connect computational savings with practical output quality: reducing generator calls accompanies improvements in how successfully the views form a coherent 3D object.
summary.tldr: IM-3D combines video-based multiview generation with Gaussian-splatting reconstruction to produce better 3D assets using 10–100 times fewer generator evaluations.

title: IM-3D: Iterative Multiview Diffusion and Reconstruction for High-Quality 3D Generation

abstract: Guaranteeing the correctness and factuality of language model (LM) outputs is a major open problem. In this work, we propose conformal factuality, a framework that can ensure high probability correctness guarantees for LMs by connecting language modeling and conformal prediction. Our insight is that the correctness of an LM output is equivalent to an uncertainty quantification problem, where the uncertainty sets are defined as the entailment set of an LM’s output. Using this connection, we show that conformal prediction in language models corresponds to a back-off algorithm that provides high probability correctness guarantees by progressively making LM outputs less specific (and expanding the associated uncertainty sets). This approach applies to any black-box LM and requires very few human-annotated samples. Evaluations of our approach on closed book QA (FActScore, NaturalQuestions) and reasoning tasks (MATH) show that our approach can provide 80-90% correctness guarantees while retaining the majority of the LM’s original output.

paragraphs: The paper treats language-model factuality as a problem of quantifying uncertainty. Its key connection is between whether an output is correct and an uncertainty set defined through what that output entails. This allows the authors to bring conformal prediction into the task of controlling the correctness of generated language.

The resulting framework uses a back-off procedure that gradually makes an output less specific. As details are removed or weakened, the associated uncertainty set becomes larger. This provides a mechanism for obtaining high-probability correctness guarantees while preserving useful content, with specificity acting as the quantity the procedure can adjust.

The approach works with a black-box language model and requires only a small number of human-annotated examples. Evaluations on closed-book question answering and mathematical reasoning report correctness guarantees of 80–90% while retaining most of the original output. The contribution is therefore a method for trading some detail for a stated probabilistic correctness level, rather than requiring access to the model’s internal computation or treating every generated statement as certain.
summary.tldr: Conformal factuality progressively reduces output specificity to obtain probabilistic correctness guarantees while retaining most generated content in evaluations.

title: Language Models with Conformal Factuality Guarantees

abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have recently been used for sequential decision making in interactive environments. However, leveraging environment reward signals for continual LLM actor improvement is not straightforward. We propose Skill Set Optimization (SSO) for improving LLM actor performance through constructing and refining sets of transferable skills. SSO constructs skills by extracting common subtrajectories with high rewards and generating subgoals and instructions to represent each skill. These skills are provided to the LLM actor in-context to reinforce behaviors with high rewards. Then, SSO further refines the skill set by pruning skills that do not continue to result in high rewards. We evaluate our method in the classic videogame NetHack and the text environment ScienceWorld to demonstrate SSO’s ability to optimize a set of skills and perform in-context policy improvement. SSO outperforms baselines by 40% in our custom NetHack task and outperforms the previous state-of-the-art in ScienceWorld by 35%.

paragraphs: Skill Set Optimization improves a language-model actor by turning rewarding experience into a reusable collection of skills. The problem is how to use feedback from an interactive environment for continued improvement. SSO makes that feedback actionable through instructions placed in the actor’s context, allowing successful behaviors to inform later decisions.

The method identifies recurring segments of trajectories associated with high rewards. It then generates subgoals and instructions that describe each segment as a skill. Refinement continues after construction: skills that stop producing high rewards are pruned from the collection. This gives the skill set a feedback-driven update process rather than leaving it as a fixed record of past successes.

The authors evaluate SSO in NetHack and ScienceWorld, demonstrating optimization of the skill collection and in-context policy improvement. They report a 40% improvement over baselines on their custom NetHack task and a 35% improvement over the previous state of the art in ScienceWorld. These results support the use of constructed and selectively retained skills to improve the tested language-model actors.
summary.tldr: SSO converts rewarding behavior into reusable in-context skills and prunes ineffective skills to improve language-model actors.

title: Skill Set Optimization: Reinforcing Language Model Behavior via Transferable Skills

abstract: We propose a novel formalism for describing Structural Causal Models (SCMs) as fixed-point problems on causally ordered variables, eliminating the need for Directed Acyclic Graphs (DAGs), and establish the weakest known conditions for their unique recovery given the topological ordering (TO). Based on this, we design a two-stage causal generative model that first infers in a zero-shot manner a valid TO from observations, and then learns the generative SCM on the ordered variables. To infer TOs, we propose to amortize the learning of TOs on synthetically generated datasets by sequentially predicting the leaves of graphs seen during training. To learn SCMs, we design a transformer-based architecture that exploits a new attention mechanism enabling the modeling of causal structures, and show that this parameterization is consistent with our formalism. Finally, we conduct an extensive evaluation of each method individually, and show that when combined, our model outperforms various baselines on generated out-of-distribution problems.

paragraphs: Structural causal models describe how variables are generated through causal relationships. This paper expresses these models as fixed-point problems over causally ordered variables, removing the need for a directed acyclic graph in the formalism. Given the topological ordering, the authors establish what they describe as the weakest known conditions for uniquely recovering the model.

Their generative approach separates finding an ordering from learning the causal relationships. First, a model infers a valid ordering from observations in a zero-shot manner. Its training experience comes from synthetic datasets, where it learns to predict graph leaves sequentially. This transfers the work of learning how to order variables into a reusable inference procedure.

Second, a transformer learns the structural causal model using the ordered variables. A new attention mechanism represents causal structure, and the authors show that this parameterization agrees with their fixed-point formalism. They evaluate both stages individually and report that the combined model outperforms various baselines on generated problems outside the training distribution.
summary.tldr: A fixed-point formulation supports a two-stage causal generator that infers variable orderings and then learns causal relationships.

title: A Fixed-Point Approach for Causal Generative Modeling

abstract: Deep neural networks are applied in more and more areas of everyday life. However, they still lack essential abilities, such as robustly dealing with spatially transformed input signals. Approaches to mitigate this severe robustness issue are limited to two pathways: Either models are implicitly regularised by increased sample variability (data augmentation) or explicitly constrained by hard-coded inductive biases. The limiting factor of the former is the size of the data space, which renders sufficient sample coverage intractable. The latter is limited by the engineering effort required to develop such inductive biases for every possible scenario. Instead, we take inspiration from human behaviour, where percepts are modified by mental or physical actions during inference. We propose a novel technique to emulate such an inference process for neural nets. This is achieved by traversing a sparsified inverse transformation tree during inference using parallel energy-based evaluations. Our proposed inference algorithm, called Inverse Transformation Search (ITS), is model-agnostic and equips the model with zero-shot pseudo-invariance to spatially transformed inputs. We evaluated our method on several benchmark datasets, including a synthesised ImageNet test set. ITS outperforms the utilised baselines on all zero-shot test scenarios.

paragraphs: A classifier can recognize an object in one orientation yet fail after a spatial transformation. Training-time augmentation and built-in architectural invariances address this problem, but both have limits. This paper instead studies whether inference can actively transform the input to expose recognition ability already present in a model.

Inverse Transformation Search traverses a sparse tree of inverse transformations using parallel energy-based evaluations. The procedure is model-agnostic and operates during inference. It aims to provide zero-shot pseudo-invariance, meaning improved behavior on transformed inputs without requiring the classifier to have been trained specifically for those test transformations.

Tests include several benchmarks and a synthesized ImageNet test set. ITS outperforms the selected baselines in all reported zero-shot scenarios. The contribution is an inference-time search strategy for spatial robustness; pseudo-invariance is a performance objective here, not a proof of exact invariance to every possible transformation or a guarantee of zero additional inference cost.
summary.tldr: Inverse Transformation Search improves spatial robustness by exploring input transformations during inference without task-specific retraining.

title: Tilt your Head: Activating the Hidden Spatial-Invariance of Classifiers

abstract: An open challenge in reinforcement learning (RL) is the effective deployment of a trained policy to new or slightly different situations as well as semantically-similar environments. We introduce Symmetry-Invariant Transformer (SiT), a scalable vision transformer (ViT) that leverages both local and global data patterns in a self-supervised manner to improve generalisation. Central to our approach is Graph Symmetric Attention, which refines the traditional self-attention mechanism to preserve graph symmetries, resulting in invariant and equivariant latent representations. We showcase SiT’s superior generalization over ViTs on MiniGrid and Procgen RL benchmarks, and its sample efficiency on Atari 100k and CIFAR10.

We showcase SiT’s superior generalization over ViTs on MiniGrid and Procgen RL benchmarks, and its sample efficiency on Atari 100k and CIFAR10.

paragraphs: A reinforcement-learning policy can struggle when deployed in a situation that differs from its training environment, even if the new situation has similar meaning. SiT addresses this generalization problem through the visual representations used by the policy. It is a scalable vision transformer that learns from both local and global patterns through self-supervision.

Its central component is Graph Symmetric Attention, a modification of ordinary self-attention designed to preserve graph symmetries. This produces invariant and equivariant latent representations: representations that remain unchanged or change in a corresponding way under the relevant symmetries. The architecture therefore incorporates structure into how visual information is represented.

The authors report better generalization than vision transformers on MiniGrid and Procgen reinforcement-learning benchmarks. They also demonstrate sample efficiency on Atari 100k and CIFAR10. Together, these results support symmetry-aware attention as a useful design choice for learning transferable representations. The evidence spans generalization and sample efficiency in the named evaluations, connecting the architectural change to practical learning behavior.
summary.tldr: SiT incorporates graph symmetries into transformer attention to improve reported generalization and sample efficiency.

title: SiT: Symmetry-invariant Transformers for Generalisation in Reinforcement Learning

abstract: Molecular surfaces imply fingerprints of interaction patterns between proteins. However, non-equivalent efforts have been paid to incorporating the abundant protein surface information for analyzing proteins’ biological functions in juxtaposition to amino acid sequences and 3D structures. We propose a novel surface-based unsupervised learning algorithm termed Surface-VQMAE to overcome this obstacle. In light of surface point clouds’ sparsity and disorder properties, we first partition them into patches and obtain the sequential arrangement via the Morton curve. Successively, a Transformer-based architecture named SurfFormer was introduced to integrate the surface geometry and capture patch-level relations. At last, we enhance the prevalent masked auto-encoder (MAE) with the vector quantization (VQ) technique, which establishes a surface pattern codebook to enforce a discrete posterior distribution of latent variables and achieve more condensed semantics. Our work is the foremost to implement pretraining purely on molecular surfaces and extensive experiments on diverse real-life scenarios including binding site scoring, binding affinity prediction, and mutant effect estimation demonstrate its effectiveness. The code is available at https://github.com/smiles724/VQMAE.

paragraphs: Protein surfaces contain information about how proteins interact, but surface-based learning has received less attention than learning from amino acid sequences or three-dimensional structures. Surface-VQMAE explores unsupervised pretraining using molecular surfaces alone. Its design addresses the fact that surface point clouds are sparse and have no inherent sequence ordering.

The method divides a surface into patches and arranges them using a Morton curve. A Transformer architecture called SurfFormer then integrates surface geometry and models relationships between patches. The framework adds vector quantization to a masked autoencoder, creating a codebook of surface patterns and a discrete representation of latent variables intended to capture more compact semantic information.

The resulting pipeline turns unordered surface measurements into structured, reusable representations of interaction-related patterns. Evaluations include binding-site scoring, binding-affinity prediction, and mutation-effect estimation, with extensive experiments demonstrating effectiveness across these tasks. The findings support molecular surfaces as a useful basis for pretraining and show how patch organization, geometric modeling, and a discrete pattern codebook can work together.
summary.tldr: Surface-VQMAE learns discrete molecular-surface patterns through unsupervised pretraining for protein interaction and mutation-related prediction tasks.

title: Surface-VQMAE: Vector-quantized Masked Auto-encoders on Molecular Surfaces

abstract: Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback (RLHF) is currently the most widely used method to align large language models (LLMs) with human preferences. Existing RLHF methods can be roughly categorized as either reward-based or reward-free. Novel applications such as ChatGPT and Claude leverage reward-based methods that first learn a reward model and apply actor-critic algorithms, such as Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO). However, in academic benchmarks, state-of-the-art results are often achieved via reward-free methods, such as Direct Preference Optimization (DPO). Is DPO truly superior to PPO? Why does PPO perform poorly on these benchmarks? In this paper, we first conduct both theoretical and empirical studies on the algorithmic properties of DPO and show that DPO may have fundamental limitations. Moreover, we also comprehensively examine PPO and reveal the key factors for the best performances of PPO in fine-tuning LLMs. Finally, we benchmark DPO and PPO across a collection of RLHF testbeds, ranging from dialogue to code generation. Experiment results demonstrate that PPO is able to surpass other alignment methods in all cases and achieve state-of-the-art results in challenging code competitions.

summary.tldr: A theoretical and empirical comparison finds possible DPO limitations and shows that well-performing PPO can surpass other alignment methods across the evaluated testbeds.

abstract: Significant progress has been achieved on the improvement and downstream usages of the Contrastive Language-Image Pre-training (CLIP) vision-language model, while less attention is paid to the interpretation of CLIP. We propose a Gradient-based visual Explanation method for CLIP (Grad-ECLIP), which interprets the matching result of CLIP for specific input image-text pair. By decomposing the architecture of the encoder and discovering the relationship between the matching similarity and intermediate spatial features, Grad-ECLIP produces effective heat maps that show the influence of image regions or words on the CLIP results. Different from the previous Transformer interpretation methods that focus on the utilization of self-attention maps, which are typically extremely sparse in CLIP, we produce high-quality visual explanations by applying channel and spatial weights on token features. Qualitative and quantitative evaluations verify the superiority of Grad-ECLIP compared with the state-of-the-art methods. A series of analysis are conducted based on our visual explanation results, from which we explore the working mechanism of image-text matching, and the strengths and limitations in attribution identification of CLIP. Codes are available here: https://github.com/Cyang-Zhao/Grad-Eclip.

paragraphs: CLIP assigns a matching score to an image and a piece of text, but that score alone does not reveal which parts of either input influenced the match. Grad-ECLIP aims to explain a specific image–text pairing by producing heat maps that highlight influential image regions or words. The focus is interpretation of the matching result.

The method examines the encoder architecture and relates the final similarity score to intermediate spatial features. It applies channel and spatial weights to token features to construct visual explanations. This choice responds to a problem with attention-based explanations: CLIP's self-attention maps are typically extremely sparse, making them a difficult basis for informative attribution.

The researchers also use those explanations to investigate how image–text matching works and to explore strengths and limitations in CLIP's attribution identification. The contribution therefore includes both an explanation method and an analytical tool for examining what contributes to a particular match.
summary.tldr: Grad-ECLIP explains image–text matches with gradient-based weighting of token features, producing stronger visual explanations in the reported evaluations.

title: Gradient-based Visual Explanation for Transformer-based CLIP

abstract: Speculative sampling is a popular technique for accelerating inference in Large Language Models by generating candidate tokens using a fast draft model and then accepting or rejecting them based on the target model’s distribution. While speculative sampling was previously limited to discrete sequences, we extend it to diffusion models, which generate samples via continuous, vector-valued Markov chains. In this context, the target model is a high-quality but computationally expensive diffusion model. We propose various drafting strategies, including a simple and effective approach that does not require training a draft model and is applicable out-of-the-box to any diffusion model. We demonstrate significant generation speedup on various diffusion models, halving the number of function evaluations while generating exact samples from the target model. Finally, we also show how this procedure can be used to accelerate Langevin diffusions to sample unnormalized distributions.

paragraphs: Diffusion models generate outputs through a sequence of continuous, vector-valued states, with repeated evaluations of an expensive model. This paper adapts speculative sampling to accelerate that process. The basic idea is to propose candidate steps cheaply and then accept or reject them using the distribution specified by the higher-quality target model.

Speculative sampling had previously been applied to discrete sequences such as language-model tokens. Extending it to diffusion requires handling continuous Markov chains instead. The authors propose several ways to draft candidate steps, including an approach that needs no separately trained draft model and can be applied directly to an existing diffusion model.

Across the diffusion models evaluated, the method speeds generation and halves the number of function evaluations while retaining exact sampling from the target model. That combination matters because the stated acceleration preserves the target distribution rather than merely producing similar-looking outputs. The authors also show that the procedure can accelerate Langevin diffusions used to sample from unnormalized distributions, extending its use beyond generative diffusion models.
summary.tldr: Speculative sampling accelerates continuous diffusion processes, halving function evaluations in experiments while preserving exact samples from the target model.

title: Accelerated Diffusion Models via Speculative Sampling

abstract: This paper examines multiplayer symmetric constant-sum games with more than two players in a competitive setting, such as Mahjong, Poker, and various board and video games. In contrast to two-player zero-sum games, equilibria in multiplayer games are neither unique nor non-exploitable, failing to provide meaningful guarantees when competing against opponents who play different equilibria or non-equilibrium strategies. This gives rise to a series of long-lasting fundamental questions in multiplayer games regarding suitable objectives, solution concepts, and principled algorithms. This paper takes an initial step towards addressing these challenges by focusing on the natural objective of equal share—securing an expected payoff of $C/n$ in an $n$-player symmetric game with a total payoff of $C$. We rigorously identify the theoretical conditions under which achieving an equal share is tractable and design a series of efficient algorithms, inspired by no-regret learning, that provably attain approximate equal share across various settings. Furthermore, we provide complementary lower bounds that justify the sharpness of our theoretical results. Our experimental results highlight worst-case scenarios where meta-algorithms from prior state-of-the-art systems for multiplayer games fail to secure an equal share, while our algorithm succeeds, demonstrating the effectiveness of our approach.

This paper therefore studies a concrete performance objective: securing an expected payoff of C/n when n players share a total payoff of C.

The authors identify theoretical conditions under which achieving this equal-share objective is computationally tractable. The guarantee concerns expected payoff and approximate attainment in the relevant settings, providing a principled objective for situations where equilibrium-based reasoning alone offers insufficient protection.
summary.tldr: The paper establishes conditions and efficient learning algorithms for securing approximately equal expected payoff in multiplayer symmetric constant-sum games.

title: Securing Equal Share: A Principled Approach for Learning Multiplayer Symmetric Games

abstract: Medical image segmentation is a critical task in computer vision, with UNet serving as a milestone architecture. The typical component of UNet family is the skip connection, however, their skip connections face two significant limitations: (1) they lack effective interaction between features at different scales, and (2) they rely on simple concatenation or addition operations, which constrain efficient information integration. While recent improvements to UNet have focused on enhancing encoder and decoder capabilities, these limitations remain overlooked. To overcome these challenges, we propose a novel multi-scale feature fusion method that reimagines the UNet decoding process as solving an initial value problem (IVP), treating skip connections as discrete nodes. By leveraging principles from the linear multistep method, we propose an adaptive ordinary differential equation method to enable effective multi-scale feature fusion. Our approach is independent of the encoder and decoder architectures, making it adaptable to various U-Net-like networks. Experiments on ACDC, KiTS2023, MSD brain tumor, and ISIC2017/2018 skin lesion segmentation datasets demonstrate improved feature utilization, reduced network parameters, and maintained high performance. The code is available at https://github.com/nayutayuki/FuseUNet.
